## Deliberate non-feature: on-demand start

`capabilities.ensure_qwen25_vl_runtime()` starts `llama-server.exe` for a
**media** job after VRAM planning. That is not a chat-picker pattern, and
it is the wrong place to copy for PowerInfer:

- `powerinfer_openai_proxy.py` is specified **not** to start/stop
  `server.exe`. Wiring auto-start into `decide()` would violate that
  contract from the caller side.
- A real start needs a production-registry bundle, GPU-gateway grant,
  VRAM budget, and thread/context flags. Those live in the PowerInfer
  pipeline, which another session is running; this change must not
  touch `tools/powerinfer/run_pipeline.ps1`, `pipeline_lib.py`,
  `vault.py`, or `init_vault.py`.
- Starting `server.exe` from a status poll or first token would race
  ComfyUI and the live pipeline.

If PowerInfer is down, the picker shows it disabled and `decide()` says
so. The operator starts `server.exe` and the proxy themselves, then the
same picker row becomes selectable. That is the gap: **the router can
detect a missing backend cleanly; it cannot own PowerInfer process
lifecycle without a new supervisor, and this change will not invent one.**

chunks.heading: # PowerInfer Control-Plane plan — 2026-08-29
chunks.text:
# PowerInfer Control-Plane plan — 2026-08-29

## Decision

Evaluate PowerInfer as an **opt-in interactive inference backend** on the Ryzen CPU + RTX 5080 control plane. It is not enabled, installed, downloaded, or routed into the local agent yet.

PowerInfer is a CPU/GPU hybrid engine that keeps frequently activated neurons on GPU and computes the remainder on CPU/RAM. Its sparse performance path requires a PowerInfer GGUF plus matching predictor and activation files; an ordinary llama.cpp-compatible GGUF may run in compatibility mode but does not gain the sparse acceleration. The upstream project currently lists sparse Llama-2, ProSparse Llama-2, Falcon/ReLU, and Bamboo families—not the existing Qwen/Ollama chat models. See the [upstream PowerInfer README](https://github.com/Tiiny-AI/PowerInfer) and [its server API documentation](https://github.com/Tiiny-AI/PowerInfer/blob/main/examples/server/README.md).

Model preparation is a separate mandatory track. See
`docs/MODEL_CONVERSION_AND_PROFILING_PLAN_2026-08-29.md`: a PowerInfer-ready
bundle needs model/predictor/activation lineage and acceptance evidence. Do not
assume a normal GGUF, arbitrary abliterated checkpoint, or post-LoRA merge can
be automatically profiled into a sparse PowerInfer model.

**Do not promise 70B “real-time” performance from the 16 GB GPU alone.** A suitable sparse model can shift hot activations to VRAM, but the rest still needs substantial system RAM and CPU/PCIe bandwidth. The operator's reported 32 GB system RAM may be insufficient for a 70B-class quantized model plus runtime and OS headroom. Profile a supported model and record RAM, VRAM, prefill, decode, and first-token latency before changing any production route.

## Local-only API boundary

`local_agent/powerinfer_openai_proxy.py` is a standard-library OpenAI-style adapter. It remains separate from `START_LOCAL_AGENT_GUI.ps1` and binds only to `127.0.0.1:8091` by default:

```text
Interactive Python agent
        │  OpenAI-style /v1/chat/completions
        ▼
PowerInfer OpenAI proxy (127.0.0.1:8091)
        │  PowerInfer /completion
        ▼
PowerInfer server (127.0.0.1:8080)
        │
 RTX 5080 hot neurons + Ryzen DDR5 cold neurons
```

The proxy accepts text-only `system`, `user`, and `assistant` messages and renders the Llama-2-family chat format used by currently supported sparse models. It supports normal and SSE streaming replies, model discovery, optional loopback API-key checking, bounded request/prompt/completion sizes, and prompt caching. It deliberately rejects image content and tools: PowerInfer's existing sparse model support does not establish safe multimodal or native tool-call semantics for this agent.

The existing local-agent GPU permission gateway remains the owner of permission to start/keep a PowerInfer workload. Do not expose this endpoint on Wi-Fi, LoRa, LXMF, LAN, or `0.0.0.0`.

The existing local-agent GPU permission gateway remains the owner of permission to start/keep a PowerInfer workload. Do not expose this endpoint on Wi-Fi, LoRa, LXMF, LAN, or `0.0.0.0`.

## Allocation strategy

| Workload | Route | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Real-time general chat, tool planning, difficult interactive coding | Existing Ollama tiers by default; PowerInfer only after a supported sparse model passes benchmarks and GPU approval | Preserve known chat/tool behavior until measured replacement quality exists. |
| Interactive Teacher turns and immediate critique/rewrite | Candidate for PowerInfer after acceptance | Latency-sensitive, human-in-the-loop requests can benefit from a large supported sparse model. |
| Harmon Town / Nothing Forever Stage generation | Candidate for PowerInfer only for text-only real-time stage dialogue after format and safety tests | It needs low response latency, but the Stage must retain its own moderation, pacing, state, and tool boundaries. |
| Judge evaluation, web/PDF/repository processing, embeddings, export distillation, bulk Teacher/Student generation | Celery/Redis worker farm and later cluster queues | Asynchronous, batchable tasks should not reserve the interactive GPU. |
| ComfyUI renders, VLM/video/audio analysis | Existing guarded media/ComfyUI paths | PowerInfer does not replace multimodal runtimes or render workflows. |

The worker farm receives compact encrypted artifact references, not live chat prompts or PowerInfer process control. It may consume completed logs for batch evaluation, but it must never start or stop the PowerInfer server.

## Build prerequisites and Windows commands

Use a Visual Studio **x64 Native Tools** PowerShell after confirming CUDA **12.8+** (Blackwell / RTX 5080), CMake 3.17+, Python 3.8+, Git, and the C++ desktop build tools are installed.

**Native Windows is the intended runtime**, not WSL2. The OpenAI proxy binds `127.0.0.1:8091` in native Python and expects `server.exe` on `127.0.0.1:8080`. WSL2 localhost forwarding can reach a Linux `./server`, but that is a fallback only if the native `sm_120` build cannot compile.

The upstream CUDA flag is `LLAMA_CUBLAS=ON`. For CUDA 12.8+, `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120` is the documented Blackwell arch (`sm_120`); pass it explicitly on this workstation.

```powershell
cd A:\Users\rhine\Documents\Codex\2026-08-07\referenced-chatgpt-conversation-this-is-an-2\COMFYUI_STORY_HANDOFF_2026-08-09
.\tools\powerinfer\run_pipeline.ps1 -ModelId prosparse-7b -Stage setup -Execute
# equivalent manual cmake:
# cmake -S external\PowerInfer -B external\PowerInfer\build -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64 -DLLAMA_CUBLAS=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120

select an explicit VRAM budget below what the gateway reports as free. Example
only after model verification:

```powershell

  --vram-budget <approved-GiB> -t <Ryzen-CPU-thread-count> -c <verified-context> `

Then, in a separate terminal, start the unlaunched adapter only on loopback:

$env:POWERINFER_PROXY_API_KEY = '<local-secret>'
python local_agent\powerinfer_openai_proxy.py
```

No command above should be run while ComfyUI owns the GPU. The adapter is implemented and tested but is not wired into launchers or routes automatically.

## Model sourcing and conversion

1. Prefer an upstream PowerInfer model repository containing `*.powerinfer.gguf` **and** the sibling `activation/` directory. Preserve that directory layout: PowerInfer generates a `*.generated.gpuidx` index beside the model at first use.
2. For an upstream-supported 70B experiment, use only the matching original sparse model and predictor pair listed by upstream, then convert with:

   ```powershell
   python convert.py --outfile D:\PowerInferModels\<model>.powerinfer.gguf `
     D:\PowerInferModels\<original-sparse-model> D:\PowerInferModels\<predictor>
   ```

3. Record SHA-256 hashes, source repository commit/revision, model license, predictor revision, activation-file inventory, Windows/CUDA/CMake versions, RAM/VRAM, and benchmark results before accepting it.
4. Never convert an arbitrary existing Qwen/Ollama model and label it PowerInfer-ready. The predictor is a required learned component, not a generic conversion option.

chunks.text:
# PowerInfer FATReLU operator decision — 2026-08-29

**Status:** waiting on an operator choice. The relu-gate stays closed.
**This note does not authorize a download, a GPU stage, a gate bypass, or a ReluLLaMA intake.**

Written 2026-08-29 at 5:28 PM ET. The existing ProSparse intake is already on disk; this session only read it and ran the gate.

## Finding

`SparseLLM/prosparse-llama-2-7b` is a **FATReLU / `SparseLlamaForCausalLM`** checkpoint. PowerInfer's conversion pipeline **rejects** it. The weights are already ingested and must be treated as parked evidence, not as a conversion source.

On-disk `config.json` at
`C:\PowerInferVault\prosparse-7b\20260829-prosparse\source\hf\config.json`:

| field | value |
|---|---|
| `_name_or_path` | `SparseLLM/prosparse-llama-2-7b` |
| `hidden_act` | `fatrelu` |
| `hidden_act_param` | `0.01` |
| `model_type` | `sparsellama` |
| `architectures` | `["SparseLlamaForCausalLM"]` |
| `hidden_size` / `intermediate_size` / `num_hidden_layers` | `4096` / `11008` / `32` |

FATReLU is not plain ReLU. With `hidden_act_param: 0.01` the activation is a floored ReLU (`max(x, 0.01)`), so neurons that would be exactly zero under ReLU stay at the floor. PowerInfer's CUDA solver builds GPU index tensors from a ReLU sparsity map (a neuron is either zero or positive). Feeding it FATReLU activations would produce an incorrect sparsity map. The failure mode is not a reliable crash; it is plausible-looking wrong output.

## Intake already on disk

Do not re-download. Do not delete.

| item | path |
|---|---|
| vault / bundle | `C:\PowerInferVault\prosparse-7b\20260829-prosparse` |
| HuggingFace snapshot | `C:\PowerInferVault\prosparse-7b\20260829-prosparse\source\hf` |
| source manifest | `C:\PowerInferVault\prosparse-7b\20260829-prosparse\source\source_manifest.json` |

`source_manifest.json` records:

- `created_at`: `2026-08-29T21:11:52Z` (5:11 PM ET)
- `repo`: `SparseLLM/prosparse-llama-2-7b`
- `count`: 35 files
- `combined_sha256`: `6654eb0ea085082895792cb8ef635c60f0ae205edfd89008c758dd3746b446ab`
- six weight shards totaling ~26.9 GB (`model-00001-of-00006.safetensors` is 4,840,396,416 bytes)

This is the correct HuggingFace ProSparse-LLaMA-2-7B snapshot. The gate is rejecting a real property of that model, not a corrupt download.

## Gate that refused it

The pipeline fails closed unless `hidden_act` is exactly the expected ReLU-family string **and** the activation is not FATReLU **and** the recorded shapes / `model_type` match the target.

### `tools/powerinfer/pipeline_lib.py` — `relu_gate()` (lines 226–252)

```python
def relu_gate(source_dir: Path, expected_act: str = "relu") -> dict[str, Any]:
    config_path = source_dir / "config.json"
    ...
    act = str(config.get("hidden_act") or "").lower()
    ...
    fatrelu = act.startswith("fatrelu")
    ok = act == expected_act.lower() and not fatrelu
    return {
        "ok": ok,
        ...
        "reason": None
        if ok
        else (
            "FATReLU is not supported by PowerInfer"
            if fatrelu
            else f"hidden_act={act!r} is not {expected_act!r}; ReLUfy before dump/train/convert"
        ),
    }
```

The `startswith("fatrelu")` check is deliberate: a value such as `fatrelu` or `fatrelu_0.01` is refused even if someone later aliases it toward `"relu"`.

### `tools/powerinfer/check_relu_gate.py` (lines 17–31)

Wraps `relu_gate()`, then also fails on shape / `model_type` mismatches against `models.json`:

- expected `hidden_act`: `"relu"`
- expected `model_type`: `"llama"`
- expected shapes: `4096 / 11008 / 32`

`model_type='sparsellama'` is therefore a second, independent refusal. Exit code `2` means closed.

### `tools/powerinfer/run_pipeline.ps1` — `Invoke-ReluGate` (lines 202–206)

function Invoke-ReluGate {
    $src = Get-Source $Target $Bundle
    if (-not $src) { throw 'no source checkpoint. Pass -SourceDir or run intake.' }

}

chunks.heading: # No repetition in prompts — rule and the bug that produced it
chunks.text:
# No repetition in prompts — rule and the bug that produced it

Recorded 2026-08-10 after a live observation during manual ComfyUI testing.

## The observation

Testing the first clip by hand, the speaker direction *"Narrator, measured Twilight-Zone-like cadence"* appeared **twice** in the prompt that reached the model. The suspicion was that the repetition itself confused MiniMax H3.

That suspicion checks out, and the underlying cause is structural rather than a one-off typo. It affects most of the film.

## The rule

**Never state the same instruction twice in a prompt. This applies most strictly to the dialogue timing section.**

A repeated instruction is not emphasis. The model has to reconcile two copies of the same directive, and when the copies differ even slightly — different wording, different scope, different tense — it has to guess which one governs. Repeating a spoken line is worse still: the model can read it as the line being said twice.

Say each thing once, in the section that owns it:

| Information | Belongs in | Never repeat in |
|---|---|---|
| Who speaks, and the exact words | `DIALOGUE TIMING` | anywhere else |
| Tone and delivery ("calm", "measured cadence") | `DIALOGUE TIMING`, attached to the line | the shot list |
| Physical staging ("looking at Kent", "turning to Avery") | `SHOT LIST` | the dialogue block |
| Identity features | `IDENTITY` | the action text |
| Cast count | `CAST` | the prohibitions |

Physical staging in the shot list and delivery in the dialogue block are **not** repetition — they are different facts about the same beat. Stating "Faith White speaks, looking at Kent" in the shot list and "Faith White, calm: '…'" in the dialogue block is correct. Stating "Faith White speaks, calm, looking at Kent" in both is not.

## The structural bug behind it

`outputs/minimax_story_runner.py` line 305:

```python
h3_inputs["prompt"] = prompt + "\n\n" + strict_audio_prompt(audio_scene)
```

The prompt that reaches the model is **not** the `prompt` field in `story_config.json`. The runner appends an AUDIO LOCK block built by `strict_audio_prompt()` in `dialogue_validator.py`, and that block restates every line of dialogue verbatim:

> AUDIO LOCK (overrides every earlier audio instruction): No music, song, melody, score… From 1s to 14s, the named speaker says exactly once in clear intelligible American English: "…"

Meanwhile 121 of the 124 stored prompts already contain their own `Dialogue timing:` block carrying the same lines.

**Measured across the config: 73 of the 78 clips that have dialogue send the spoken line to the model twice.** Once in the body, once in the appended AUDIO LOCK.

That is very likely a contributor to the invented and garbled speech that dominated the opening sequence's retries — the model was being handed each line twice and told the second copy overrides the first.

That is very likely a contributor to the invented and garbled speech that dominated the opening sequence's retries — the model was being handed each line twice and told the second copy overrides the first.

### Two clips actively contradict themselves

`00A` and one other say in the body:

> Dialogue is added in post-production; no one vocalizes in this render. Quiet room tone only.

and then receive an appended AUDIO LOCK instructing the narrator to speak the line. The body says silence, the suffix says speak, and the suffix claims to override. The model cannot satisfy both.

`00A` is the film's opening shot. It took seven attempts.

### One thing the pipeline gets right

`expected_dialogue()` correctly strips the stage direction and passes only the quoted words into the AUDIO LOCK, so the model is never asked to *say* "Narrator, measured Twilight-Zone-like cadence". The stage direction reaches it as context in the body, which is correct. The duplication is of the quoted line, not the direction.

## Fixes applied

The optimized prompts on the Desktop now come in two variants, because the correct text depends on how the prompt is delivered:

- **`optimized_prompt`** — for pasting into ComfyUI by hand. Dialogue appears once, in `DIALOGUE TIMING`. Nothing appends an AUDIO LOCK in this path, so the line has to be present.
- **`optimized_prompt_for_runner`** — for going back into `story_config.json`. The quoted line is **omitted**; the dialogue block names the speaker and the window and defers to the audio lock. The runner then supplies the line exactly once.

Within both variants, tone and delivery now appear only in the dialogue block, and the shot list carries physical staging only.

## Fixes still outstanding in the live config

These are in `story_config.json` and the runner, and have not been changed:

1. **73 clips still double their dialogue** when rendered through `minimax_story_runner.py`. Either strip the `Dialogue timing:` block from the stored prompts, or stop `strict_audio_prompt()` restating lines that the body already carries. Stripping the stored block is the smaller change and keeps the audio lock as the single source of truth.
2. **`00A` and its twin still contradict themselves.** Decide whether those clips speak or are silent, and make the body agree with the audio lock.
3. **`AUDIO LOCK (overrides every earlier audio instruction)`** is itself an admission that the prompt contains conflicting audio direction. Once the duplication is removed, that parenthetical should go — nothing should need overriding.

- Does any sentence appear twice?
- Does any spoken line appear outside `DIALOGUE TIMING`?
- Does any tonal direction appear outside `DIALOGUE TIMING`?
- After the runner appends its AUDIO LOCK, is anything stated twice?
- Does any instruction contradict another?

chunks.heading: # Prompt style rules
chunks.text:
# Prompt style rules

Derived from live testing on 2026-08-10, including two failures found by hand. Apply to
every clip. These sit on top of `PROMPT_REPETITION_RULE.md`, which still holds.

## 1. Quotation marks mean speech. Nothing else may be quoted.

**This is the most important rule on the page, and breaking it makes characters speak at
random.**

The model treats a quoted string as a line to be spoken and assigns it to the nearest
named person. A shot list beat like:

```
[1-2.5 s] "If there's one chair in a room" - Male Visitor One steps through the doorway
```

reads to the model as *Visitor One says "If there's one chair in a room."* He then speaks
narration that was only ever meant to time the picture.

It is made worse by the speech-lock sentence, which tells the model that quoted text is
what gets spoken. Once that is established, any quotation mark anywhere is an instruction.

**Narration is never quoted.** Write it plain, with a label:

```
[1-2.5 s] Narration over, off screen: If there's one chair in a room. Male Visitor One
steps through the doorway at screen-right...
```

And open the shot list with:

> Narration timing below is for pacing only. The Narrator is off screen. Nobody visible in
> frame speaks the narration, and nobody's lips move to it.

**The narration does not need to be spoken at all.** Every H3 audio track is discarded and
the real narration is added in post. Narration text exists in the prompt only to time the
visuals, so there is no reason to let the model try to perform it.

## 2. Never put two quoted strings in one beat.

A beat containing both a quoted narration line and a quoted character line is the worst
case observed. The model has to choose an owner for each and frequently gets both wrong.
One beat, at most one line, with the speaker named immediately before it.

## 3. On-camera dialogue lives in its own block, not scattered through the shot list.

The shot list says *that* someone speaks. A single `DIALOGUE` block says *what*, *when* and
*who*:

```
DIALOGUE
Exactly two lines are spoken on camera in this shot, one each, and nothing else:
[3s-5s] Male Visitor Two, politely insistent: "No, please, I insist."
[5s-7s] Male Visitor One, quietly pressing: "Really, please."
Those are the only words spoken by anyone in frame. The receptionist never speaks. Neither
man speaks outside his own window. Nobody else's lips move at any point.
```

State the count. Name who stays silent. In the shot list, refer to it as "speaks his
assigned line" rather than repeating the words — repeating them is a rule-1 violation and a
repetition violation at once.

## 4. No section may reference a section that does not exist.

The stock trailing line, *"Nobody in frame speaks except where DIALOGUE TIMING assigns a
line,"* becomes nonsense if the dialogue block was renamed or removed. Both hand-edited
clips carried this fault. If you move dialogue, fix every sentence that points at it.

chunks.heading: ## 3. On-camera dialogue lives in its own block, not scattered through the shot list.
chunks.text:

repetition violation at once.

## 4. No section may reference a section that does not exist.

The stock trailing line, *"Nobody in frame speaks except where DIALOGUE TIMING assigns a
line,"* becomes nonsense if the dialogue block was renamed or removed. Both hand-edited
clips carried this fault. If you move dialogue, fix every sentence that points at it.

## 5. No blanket denial that contradicts a line you just wrote.

Both hand-edited clips ended with a flourish that cancelled their own dialogue:

- *"The entire check-in is transacted through the form, the stamp and the nod. Nobody speaks
  to anybody."* — while Visitor One says "After you, please."
- *"The whole negotiation is carried by hands, heads and shoulders."* — while both men speak.

Narrow the denial to what is actually true: *"The check-in at the window is transacted
entirely through the form, the stamp and the nod"* is fine, because the window exchange
really is silent.

## 6. `LOOK` describes only what is in this shot.

Several opening clips described *"even television lighting on the Narrator, the room behind
him"* in shots the Narrator is not in. Anything the model is told to light, it may decide
to draw.

## 7. Every beat with a visible face carries a mouth state.

"Mouth closed" or "mouths closed" belongs in the beat, not only in a rule at the bottom.
The model decides what a face is doing at the same moment it decides what the body is
doing. The beat that names the speaker also names who stays silent.

## 8. Counted actions get a number.

"They repeatedly offer the chair" produces either one limp gesture or a blur. "There are
exactly three offer-and-refusal exchanges, no more and no fewer" produces three. Same for
people, props and repetitions of any kind.

## 9. Staging must support its own claims.

An edit that removed the first offer's staging left a later beat asserting *"two offers have
now been made, one each"* when only one had been shown. If a beat counts something, the
beats before it must have shown that many.

## Checklist before sending a prompt

- Every quoted string has a named speaker immediately before it.
- No narration is inside quotation marks.
- No beat contains two quoted strings.
- The dialogue block states how many lines are spoken and who stays silent.
- No sentence refers to a section that is not present.
- No blanket "nobody speaks" while somebody speaks.
- `LOOK`, `SET` and `CAST` describe only people and objects present in this shot.
- Every counted action states its number.
- Any beat that counts prior actions is preceded by that many actions.

chunks.heading: # Sideband / RNode delivery experiment protocol
chunks.text:
# Sideband / RNode delivery experiment protocol

This protocol measures **observed** workstation-to-phone delivery. It does not
claim a queued LXMF message was delivered merely because the workstation called
the outbound transport.

## Controlled run

1. Start the existing bridge; do not start a second bridge.
2. From the paired phone, request 20 counter messages at 30-second intervals.
3. On the phone, record every received counter with the phone's Unix timestamp
   or an exported timestamp. Save JSON Lines on the workstation as:

```json
{"job_id":"phone_schedule_example","counter":0,"received_at":1788000000.0}
```

4. After the final wait window, note the workstation Unix close time.
5. Run, without changing any bridge or schedule data:

```powershell
python local_agent\radio_metrics.py --receipts path\to\phone_receipts.jsonl --close-at 1788000900
```

The report calculates observed unconfirmed messages only after `--close-at`.
Without phone receipts it explicitly reports `not_measured_without_phone_receipts`.
Clock skew can distort latency; record it as an experimental limitation unless
both timestamps are synchronized. Do not describe queue events as delivery.

---

## How to judge it

Compare against `A:\Users\rhine\ComfyUI-Shared\output\video\2.mp4`, your existing `00B`.

**The one question:** does the Narrator sound like the same man in the new `00B` as he does
in `1.mp4`? Play `1.mp4` then the new render back to back.

Then, in order:

1. **Voice** — same person? That is pass or fail for this test.
2. **Lip sync** — should be inherent; video and audio are generated together.
3. **Face** — did the identity reference help, if you connected one?
4. **Picture quality** — nvfp4 is more aggressive quantisation than your int8 fl2va. Softer?
5. **Opening frame** — did it start exactly on `boundary_00_v2`?

---

## Report back

- the actual input names on `MiniMaxH3ReferenceToVideo`
- whether video-with-audio worked as a reference, or whether it needed audio alone
- whether frame-exact anchoring survived
- voice verdict, face verdict, quality verdict
- render time versus your usual ~8 minutes

That is enough to decide whether this replaces the fl2va path, supplements it, or gets
dropped.

chunks.heading: # MiniMax H3 in ComfyUI: T2V, I2V, and R2V Video Workflows
chunks.text:
# MiniMax H3 in ComfyUI: T2V, I2V, and R2V Video Workflows

**Verbatim copy of <https://docs.comfy.org/tutorials/video/minimax/minimax-h3>,
captured 2026-08-16.** Saved locally so the pipeline does not depend on network
access or on a page that may change. Sections irrelevant to this project
(download cards, Comfy Cloud links) are trimmed; every prompting and settings
statement is intact.

For what this project concluded from it, see `docs/OFFICIAL_H3_DOCS_FINDINGS.md`.
For the rules actually in force, see `docs/H3_PROMPT_RULES.md`.

---

MiniMax H3 is MiniMax's general-purpose, omni-modal generation model, now
available as open weights. It jointly understands text, images, video, and audio
in a single context, and generates video with **native stereo audio**: voice,
sound effects, and music are modeled together in a single forward pass instead of
being layered on afterward. Output is up to 2K resolution, 24fps, and about 15
seconds.

Three example workflows ship in the template library, one per generation mode:

* **Text-to-Video (T2V)**
* **Image-to-Video (I2V)** — with optional first/last-frame control
* **Reference-to-Video (R2V)** — lock in a character, style, motion, camera move,
  or voice from reference images, videos, and audio

These are examples, not an exhaustive list. The model supports more modes through
the native nodes: first/last-frame image-to-video (fl2va) via
`MiniMaxH3ImageToVideo`, and reference-driven generation with images, videos and
audio (ref2va) via `MiniMaxH3ReferenceToVideo`.

## Key features

* **Native stereo audio** — dialogue, sound effects and music generated together
  with the video, synced in one MP4
* **Multimodal context** — text, images, video and audio references combined in
  one generation
* **Reference-driven generation** — lock a character's identity, a style, a
  motion, a camera move, or a voice
* **Instruction following** — describe the relationship between references and
  the target shot in natural language
* **Accurate text rendering** — spelled-out text and brand elements render cleanly
* **Open weights**

chunks.heading: ## Key features
chunks.text:
io references combined in
  one generation
* **Reference-driven generation** — lock a character's identity, a style, a
  motion, a camera move, or a voice
* **Instruction following** — describe the relationship between references and
  the target shot in natural language
* **Accurate text rendering** — spelled-out text and brand elements render cleanly
* **Open weights**

## Setting the output resolution

Each workflow uses a **Resolution Selector** node. It computes `width` and
`height` from three settings, and its outputs connect directly to the `width` and
`height` inputs of the MiniMax H3 node:

* **Aspect ratio** — `16:9 (Widescreen)`, `9:16 (Portrait Widescreen)`,
  `1:1 (Square)`, etc.
* **Megapixels** — target total pixel count. Higher gives larger frames; lower
  runs faster
* **Multiple** — the computed resolution is rounded to the nearest multiple of
  this number. **Keep it at `32`** to match H3's resolution grid

> The template ships with a fast preview size. For full-quality output, raise
> Megapixels to about **`1.0` at 16:9**, which yields roughly **1344×768**: H3's
> native canvas, a 768px short edge capped at 768×1344 pixels.

*Project note: this project runs 0.9 MP, deliberately just under native, because
1.0 MP was measured breaking camera control on clip 11. See
`docs/H3_PROMPT_RULES.md`.*

## Models

| Mode | Diffusion model |
|---|---|
| T2V / I2V | `minimax_h3_fl2va_pruned_int8_convrot.safetensors` |
| **R2V** | `minimax_h3_ref2va_pruned_int8_convrot.safetensors` |

Shared by all modes:

```
models/text_encoders/qwen3vl_32b_minimax_h3_nvfp4_awq.safetensors
models/vae/minimax_h3_video_vae_fp16.safetensors
models/vae/minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32.safetensors
```

*Project note: this install runs `minimax_h3_ref2va_pruned_nvfp4`, a more
aggressively quantised variant than the `int8_convrot` the docs name. Untested
against int8, and a multi-GB download.*

## Prompting tips — T2V

1. **Describe the whole scene**: state the overall scene first (location,
   character, what is happening), then break it into timed shots
2. **Shots, camera, and audio**: describe the shots, camera moves, and the
   accompanying audio (dialogue, SFX, music) in one prompt block
3. **Resolution**: H3's native canvas is a 768px short edge, capped at 768×1344
   and rounded to a multiple of 32
4. **Duration**: the duration input snaps to the model's **17-frame-per-block
   (17k+5) grid at 24fps**
5. **First/last frame**: connect images to `first_frame` and/or `last_frame` on
   `MiniMaxH3ImageToVideo` to turn this into first/last-frame image-to-video

## Prompting tips — I2V

1. **Keyframes**: `first_frame` and `last_frame` are optional; the model
   generates the motion between them
2. **Prompt**: describe the shots, motion, and accompanying audio in one block
3. **Resolution**: as above
4. **Duration**: snaps to the 17k+5 grid at 24fps

## Prompting tips — I2V

1. **Keyframes**: `first_frame` and `last_frame` are optional; the model
   generates the motion between them
2. **Prompt**: describe the shots, motion, and accompanying audio in one block
3. **Resolution**: as above
4. **Duration**: snaps to the 17k+5 grid at 24fps

## Prompting tips — R2V  *(the mode this project uses)*

1. **Reference by tag**: reference each input by tag **in the exact order it was
   connected**, for example `<Picture 1>`, `<Video 1>`, `<Audio 1>`
2. **Assign each reference a job**: state which reference drives which part of
   the shot (identity, style, motion, camera, voice). **Explicit assignments tend
   to work much better**
3. **Limits**: up to **9 reference images, 3 reference videos** (each can carry
   its own soundtrack), and **3 standalone reference audio clips**
4. **`ref_image_size`**: `match` scales references down to the generation
   resolution for speed; **`max` keeps up to a 2048px short edge for stronger
   identity fidelity** at the cost of speed
5. **Note**: R2V uses the `ref2va` diffusion model, a different set of weights
   from the `fl2va` model used by T2V and I2V

## Official prompt writing guides

MiniMax publishes two, both saved alongside this file:

| Guide | Modes | Local copy |
|---|---|---|
| base | T2VA, I2VA, FL2VA, L2VA | `MINIMAX_PROMPT_GUIDE_base.md` |
| **full-reference** | **R2V** | `MINIMAX_PROMPT_GUIDE_ref.md` |

The reference guide covers the rewrite output structure — subject definitions,
reference labels, and **retention analysis** — and how to assign each reference a
role in the target shot. MiniMax also publishes installable H3 skills at
<https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/MiniMax-H3/tree/main/skills>, including a
prompt-writing skill that packages these guides for agent use.

## Speeding up generation with Sage Attention

Roughly doubles generation speed with minimal quality loss. Optional dependency:

1. Install the `sageattention` package — download the wheel matching your PyTorch
   and CUDA versions from the SageAttention releases page, then
   `pip install <wheel-file>`
2. Install the KJNodes custom nodes, which provide `Patch Sage Attention KJ`
3. Add that node between `UNETLoader` and `BasicGuider`: its `model` input takes
   the model from `UNETLoader`, its `model` output feeds `BasicGuider`. Set
   `sage_attention` to `auto`
4. Only the guider needs the patch; the scheduler generates sigmas and can stay

**Expected console noise:** Sage Attention requires float16 or bfloat16 tensors.
H3 runs some layers in other dtypes, so you may see *"Input tensors must be in
dtype of torch.float16 or torch.bfloat16, using pytorch attention instead"*.
**These messages are expected** — the affected layers fall back to standard
attention and generation still works. Do not debug them.

Alternatively launch ComfyUI with `--use-sage-attention` instead of adding the
node.

chunks.heading: # Video Prompt Writing Guide (T2VA / I2VA / FL2VA / L2VA)
chunks.text:
# Video Prompt Writing Guide (T2VA / I2VA / FL2VA / L2VA)

**Verbatim copy of MiniMax's official base-mode guide, captured 2026-08-16 from**
`https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3/blob/main/docs/VIDEO_PROMPT_WRITING_GUIDE_base_en.md`

This project uses R2V, so `MINIMAX_PROMPT_GUIDE_ref.md` is the governing
document. **But the ref guide defers to this one** for shots, cuts, camera
vocabulary, speaker IDs, and dialogue format — so those rules come from here.

---

## 1. Task Overview

- **T2VA**: builds a complete audiovisual timeline from text.
- **I2VA**: T2VA body + first-frame instruction + a visual path developing forward
  from the first frame.
- **FL2VA**: T2VA body + first-and-last-frame instruction + a continuous path from
  the first frame to the last.
- **L2VA**: T2VA body + last-frame instruction + a path converging from a
  plausible preceding state to the last frame.

## 2. Final Prompt Structure

### 2.1 Part One Is the Instruction

**T2VA** has no image-alignment instruction and begins directly with the three
core fields.

**I2VA**:

```text
For the target video, at 0.00 seconds into the target video, <Picture 1> (from
[Shot 1]) is fully referenced.
```

**FL2VA**:

```text
How the reference pictures align with the target video — Picture 1 (from Shot 1)
aligns with the 0.00-second mark of the target video; Picture 2 (from Shot N)
aligns with the S.SS-second mark of the target video.
```

**L2VA**:

```text
How the reference pictures align with the target video — <Picture 1> (from
[Shot N]) aligns with the S.SS-second mark of the target video.
```

`N` is the index of the actual final shot; `S.SS` is the effective video duration
to exactly two decimal places. The instruction must be the first line, followed by
one blank line before the core fields.

### 2.2 Part Two Contains the Three Core Fields

```text
integrated_multimodal_description: [Shot 1] ...

overall_soundscape: ...

non_diegetic_music: ...
```

## 3. Incorporating Keyframes

**I2VA** — begin from the image and develop forward. `<Picture 1>` is the actual
first frame at 0.00 s and belongs to `[Shot 1]`. Recommended structure:
**first-frame anchor → action onset → continuous development → result or
reaction**.

**FL2VA** — describe the path between first and last frames. The body should not
repeat two static image descriptions; it should supply the motion path connecting
them. **FL2VA generally favors a single shot** so the model can interpolate
continuously. Recommended: **first-frame state → observable intermediate changes →
progressively narrowing differences → last-frame state**.

**L2VA** — infer the opening and land on the image at the end. Recommended:
**plausible preceding state → explicit action and transition path → gradual
convergence → last-frame landing**.

## 4. The Three Shared Core Sections

chunks.heading: ## 3. Incorporating Keyframes
chunks.text:

continuously. Recommended: **first-frame state → observable intermediate changes →
progressively narrowing differences → last-frame state**.

**L2VA** — infer the opening and land on the image at the end. Recommended:
**plausible preceding state → explicit action and transition path → gradual
convergence → last-frame landing**.

## 4. The Three Shared Core Sections

### 4.1 Develop the Description Along the Timeline

Every detail should correspond to something visible or audible. At the beginning
of `[Shot 1]`, state the overall style and initial composition. Common styles:
`Cinematic`, `live-action`, `2D-animated`, `3D CG`, `claymation`, `watercolor`,
`vintage film`.

```text
[Shot 1] Live-action, cinematic, a medium-wide shot frames...
```

### 4.2 Shots and Cuts

**Do not add a timestamp to the first shot.** Later shots use sequential numbers
and begin with a strictly increasing cut time within the video duration:

```text
[Shot 2] At 00:03.500, the camera cuts to...
```

For ordinary cuts use `the camera cuts to`, `the shot cuts to`, `the shot
transitions to`, `the shot changes to`, or `the shot switches to`. **A cut should
introduce new information** about subject, space, state, viewpoint, or time. If
only distance or a slight angle needs to change, **prefer camera motion**.

### 4.3 Camera Motion: Motion Type + Amplitude + Speed

Add amplitude and speed only when meaningful; medium amplitude and normal speed
are usually omitted.

| Dimension | Expression | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Motion type | `Zoom In / Zoom Out` | Focal length changes, camera body stationary |
| Motion type | `Push In / Pull Out` | The camera moves forward / backward |
| Motion type | `Pan Left / Pan Right` | Camera in place, lens pivots horizontally |
| Motion type | `Truck Left / Truck Right` | The camera translates horizontally |
| Motion type | `Tilt Up / Tilt Down` | Camera in place, lens pivots vertically |
| Motion type | `Pedestal Up / Pedestal Down` | The entire camera moves up / down |
| Motion type | `Arc Shot` | The camera moves in an arc around the subject |
| Motion type | `Tracking Shot` | The camera follows a moving subject |
| Motion type | `Static Shot` | Camera position and lens remain still |
| Motion type | `Shake Slightly / Shake Strongly` | Slight / strong camera shake |
| Motion type | `POV` | The subject's point of view |
| Motion type | `Roll Clockwise / Roll Counterclockwise` | Rolls around the lens axis |
| Amplitude | `with small amplitude` / `with large amplitude` | |
| Speed | `at slow speed` / `at fast speed` | |

Write camera motion as a natural English action within the shot, not stacked as
labels at the end:

```text
The camera pushes in with small amplitude at slow speed toward the folded letter.
The camera pans right with large amplitude at fast speed, revealing the doorway.
The camera holds a static shot as the runner exits the frame.
```

chunks.heading: ### 4.3 Camera Motion: Motion Type + Amplitude + Speed
chunks.text:

Write camera motion as a natural English action within the shot, not stacked as
labels at the end:

```text
The camera pushes in with small amplitude at slow speed toward the folded letter.
The camera pans right with large amplitude at fast speed, revealing the doorway.
The camera holds a static shot as the runner exits the frame.
```

### 4.4 Speakers, Dialogue, and Singing

Subjects who speak, sing, or produce an off-screen human voice use stable IDs
such as `(S1)` and `(S2)`. When multiple numbered speakers speak together, use a
compound ID such as `(S1,S2)`. **A speaker keeps the same ID across shots;
characters who never vocalize receive no speaker ID.**

When a speaker first appears, provide enough information to establish a stable
identity: character type, age, gender, whether on-screen, pitch, timbre, speaking
rate, or accent. **Place the speaker's identifying phrase, ID, action, and
delivery outside `<d>`.** Inside `<d>`, include only the language tag and the
actual spoken content. Preserve every original word and punctuation mark
verbatim; do not translate or rewrite.

```text
The young woman with a quiet, breathy voice (S1) says: <d>[English] I get off at
the next station.</d>
The two children (S1,S2) shout together, <d>[English] Wait for us!</d>
```

For voiceover, use the exact phrase `says in an off-screen voiceover`.
**Immediately after every voiceover `<d>` block, state that the corresponding
on-screen character's lips remain closed:**

```text
The man (S1) says in an off-screen voiceover: <d>[English] I still remember that
road.</d> while his lips remain completely closed.
```

When the same line crosses a cut, use `<scenetrans>` at the connecting points in
both parts and state that the audio continues across the cut. Use `<cutoff>` when
speech is truncated by the end of the video.

### 4.5 On-Screen Text

Place any banner, sign, label, subtitle, or neon text **actually visible on
screen** in English double quotation marks, preserving original text and
punctuation without translation.

```text
A red neon sign reading "营业中" glows above the doorway.
```

### 4.6 `overall_soundscape`

1–4 English sentences in one paragraph summarizing ambient sound, physical action
sounds, and non-verbal human sounds — wind, rain, traffic, footsteps, fabric
movement, impacts, breathing, laughter, panting. Dialogue, singing, and diegetic
music belong in the multimodal description and **should not be repeated here**.
Use `N/A` only when the user explicitly requests complete silence throughout.

### 4.7 `non_diegetic_music`

1–3 English sentences describing background music only the audience hears. Focus
on instrumentation, speed, rhythm, and dynamic changes; **do not use abstract
mood words** or explain emotional function. Singing, instruments, radio,
television, or phone music audible to the characters are diegetic events and
appear in the multimodal description. Use `N/A` when there is none.

## 5. Cases

chunks.heading: ### 4.7 `non_diegetic_music`
chunks.text:
ences describing background music only the audience hears. Focus
on instrumentation, speed, rhythm, and dynamic changes; **do not use abstract
mood words** or explain emotional function. Singing, instruments, radio,
television, or phone music audible to the characters are diegetic events and
appear in the multimodal description. Use `N/A` when there is none.

## 5. Cases

### Case 2: I2VA

```text
For the target video, at 0.00 seconds into the target video, <Picture 1> (from
[Shot 1]) is fully referenced.

integrated_multimodal_description: [Shot 1] Live-action, cinematic, the young
woman shown in <Picture 1> remains beside the rain-covered train window,
preserving her appearance, clothing, seat position, and the carriage layout. The
camera trucks right with small amplitude at slow speed as she lifts her gaze from
the folded letter toward the passing city lights. Her reflection moves across the
glass while the quiet, breathy young woman (S1) says: <d>[English] I get off at
the next station.</d> She folds the letter along its existing crease.

overall_soundscape: The train wheels produce a steady metallic rhythm beneath a
low ventilation hum. Rain ticks against the window while paper rustles softly in
her hands.

non_diegetic_music: Sustained cello notes at a slow tempo with widely spaced piano
tones, gradually decreasing in volume.
```

### Case 3: FL2VA — an eight-second single shot

```text
How the reference pictures align with the target video — Picture 1 (from Shot 1)
aligns with the 0.00-second mark of the target video; Picture 2 (from Shot 1)
aligns with the 8.00-second mark of the target video.

integrated_multimodal_description: [Shot 1] Live-action, cinematic, a rain-soaked
cyclist begins in the position and framing established by Picture 1, holding a
closed black umbrella beside a silver bicycle. The camera pulls out with small
amplitude at slow speed as she releases the bicycle handle, raises the umbrella
above her shoulder, and presses the runner upward until the canopy opens. Water
rolls from the expanding fabric while she steps beneath it, rotates the handle
into the final angle, and settles into the pose, spacing, and composition
established by Picture 2 at the end of the shot.

overall_soundscape: Rain falls steadily on the pavement, followed by the metallic
click of the umbrella runner and the soft snap of the canopy opening. Water drips
from the bicycle frame as distant traffic passes.

non_diegetic_music: N/A
```

---

chunks.text:

established by Picture 2 at the end of the shot.

overall_soundscape: Rain falls steadily on the pavement, followed by the metallic

non_diegetic_music: N/A

---

## What this project takes from this guide

- **`[Shot N]` marks a cut, not a beat.** A continuous take is one `[Shot 1]`
  with no timestamp. The old `[0-1 s]` bracket notation was never H3's grammar.
- **Dialogue is `<d>[English] …</d>`.** Double quotes mean on-screen lettering.
- **Delivery goes outside `<d>`, before the tag.**
- **Voiceover uses the exact phrase** `says in an off-screen voiceover`, followed
  immediately by a lips-closed statement.
- **Camera uses the controlled vocabulary above**, written as natural English.

chunks.heading: # Full-Reference Mode Rewrite Output Format Guide (R2V)
chunks.text:
# Full-Reference Mode Rewrite Output Format Guide (R2V)

**Verbatim copy of MiniMax's official guide, captured 2026-08-16 from**
`https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3/blob/main/docs/VIDEO_PROMPT_WRITING_GUIDE_ref_en.md`

**This is the guide that governs every prompt in this project.** All 124 clips
use R2V (`MiniMaxH3ReferenceToVideo`). Section 4.2 — the audio relationship
markers — is what fixed the doubled-voice bug.

---

This guide explains how rewrite outputs are organized and written in
full-reference mode.

Write all six rewrite sections in English. Preserve the original language only
for dialogue and lyrics inside `<d>` and for text visibly present in the scene.

**Description detail:** Make `detailed_description` as detailed and explicit as
possible. For each shot, clearly establish the current composition, subject
appearance and position, environment and lighting, actions and state changes,
camera movement, current sound, and the points where referenced content actually
appears or takes effect. Avoid reducing the description to a plot summary or a
list of reference relationships.

> The basic formats for shots, camera movement, speakers, dialogue, and ordinary
> sound are shared with the Video Prompt Writing Guide (T2VA / I2VA / FL2VA /
> L2VA). This guide focuses on the reference labels, analysis sections, and
> format differences specific to full-reference mode.

## 1. Overall Structure

A complete rewrite output consists of six sections in the following order:

| Section | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `subject_definitions` | Defines referenced content and its reference labels |
| `summary` | Summarizes the task type, target video, and main reference relationships |
| `retention_analysis` | Describes how referenced content is preserved, transferred, or reused |
| `detailed_description` | Describes visuals, actions, shots, sound, and dialogue in playback order |
| `overall_soundscape` | Summarizes ambience and physical sounds |
| `non_diegetic_music` | Describes background music audible only to the audience |

chunks.heading: ## 1. Overall Structure
chunks.text:
eference relationships |
| `retention_analysis` | Describes how referenced content is preserved, transferred, or reused |
| `detailed_description` | Describes visuals, actions, shots, sound, and dialogue in playback order |
| `overall_soundscape` | Summarizes ambience and physical sounds |
| `non_diegetic_music` | Describes background music audible only to the audience |

## 2. Reference Labels and Definitions (`subject_definitions`)

Four types of labels identify the source and role of referenced content:

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `<Subject N>` | Visible content abstracted from reference assets that can be reused or modified in the target video |
| `<Picture N>` | A reference image used as a concrete target frame or shot-planning anchor |
| `<Video N>` | A reference video that provides an editing source, continuation starting point, or whole-video temporal structure |
| `<Audio N>` | An audio signal that is copied or referenced |

> Once a reference label is assigned to a piece of content, it keeps the same
> meaning across `subject_definitions`, `summary`, `retention_analysis`,
> `detailed_description`, and the audio sections.

`subject_definitions` defines each piece of referenced content that must be
tracked separately later, such as a person, an environment, a source video's
structure, or an audio track. Give each item its own line and explain what its
label denotes, its reference role, and the main features to follow; name the
corresponding source asset when its provenance needs to be made explicit. If
`<Picture N>` or `<Video N>` only identifies the source of another referenced
item and will not be analyzed or used separately later, cite it inside that
item's definition without adding a separate line. `retention_analysis` records
where each referenced item appears and whether it is fully preserved, partially
preserved, transferred, or reused.

### 2.1 `<Subject N>`

Used for reusable visible content, including:

- People, animals, or objects
- Scenes, backgrounds, or environments
- Clothing, props, interfaces, or visual effects
- Styles, actions, expressions, or poses

It represents a content unit that will actually be used in the target video,
rather than the source file itself. One subject may be defined by multiple
reference assets, and one reference asset may provide multiple subjects.

```text
<Subject 1> is the young woman in <Picture 1>, with long dark hair, a blue
cardigan, and a thin silver necklace.
```

When the same subject comes from multiple assets, combine the sources and state
what each asset provides:

```text
<Subject 1> is the woman whose appearance comes from <Picture 1> and whose
walking motion comes from <Video 1>.
```

chunks.heading: ### 2.1 `<Subject N>`
chunks.text:
tiple subjects.

```text
<Subject 1> is the young woman in <Picture 1>, with long dark hair, a blue
cardigan, and a thin silver necklace.
```

When the same subject comes from multiple assets, combine the sources and state
what each asset provides:

```text
<Subject 1> is the woman whose appearance comes from <Picture 1> and whose
walking motion comes from <Video 1>.
```

### 2.2 `<Picture N>`

Use a standalone `<Picture N>` when the reference image itself serves as a shot's
first frame, keyframe, last frame, edited keyframe, or composition anchor:

```text
<Picture 2> is the first frame of [Shot 1], showing a woman seated beside a café
window.
```

**If an image is used only to define a character, scene, costume, or style, do
not create a standalone picture entry.** Instead, cite the image source inside
the corresponding `<Subject N>` definition.

When an image acts as a storyboard or shot-planning reference, state which shots
it maps to and what planning information it provides:

```text
<Picture 3> is a storyboard reference for [Shot 1] and [Shot 2], defining their
viewpoint, subject placement, and shot order.
```

### 2.3 `<Video N>`

Reserved for whole-video relationships, such as editing an original video,
continuing from the end of one, or referencing its camera movement, cuts, rhythm,
or temporal structure.

```text
<Video 1> is the source video for the target video edit.
```

If a person, object, scene, action, or effect from a reference video is reused as
visible content, it still belongs under `<Subject N>`. `<Video N>` identifies the
asset or structural source and does not replace subject labels.

### 2.4 `<Audio N>`

Represents a standalone audio asset or an enabled synchronized audio track from a
reference video. Common uses:

- Copying all or part of an audio signal
- Referencing a background-music style
- **Referencing a speaker's voice timbre and delivery**
- Using dialogue, lyrics, or sound effects from the original audio
- Referencing beat, rhythm, or audio continuity

When an `<Audio N>` explicitly corresponds to a target speaker, reuse that
speaker's global ID in the definition: write `<Subject N> (Sx)` when the speaker
maps to a defined subject, or use a stable voice description followed by `(Sx)`
otherwise. The ID comes from the target video's global speaker order and is not
independently assigned or renumbered in the audio definition.

```text
<Audio 1> is the voice-timbre reference for <Subject 1> (S1).
```

When one audio asset serves multiple roles, describe those roles in one natural
sentence rather than creating additional subsections.

When one audio asset serves multiple roles, describe those roles in one natural

### 2.5 Visual and Audio Tracks from the Same Reference Video

`<Video N>` and `<Audio N>` are numbered independently. Each index indicates only
the label's order within its own category and does not encode a pairing between
the two categories. The same reference video may therefore correspond to
`<Video 1>` and `<Audio 2>`.

An ordinary reference video does not create `<Audio N>` merely because the file
contains sound.

```text
<Video 1> is the source video for the target video edit.
<Audio 2> is the synchronized audio track of <Video 1> and is reused in the
target video.
```

## 3. `summary`

One short English paragraph summarizing the target video and its reference
relationships, beginning with a square-bracketed task-type prefix:

```text
[reference generation] ...
[video editing + reference generation + audio reuse] ...
```

| Task type | When to use it |
|---|---|
| `keyframe completion` | An image serves as the target video's first frame, keyframe, last frame, edited keyframe, or another concrete frame anchor |
| `reference generation` | An image, video, or audio asset provides generation guidance for a character, scene, style, action, camera movement, storyboard, and so on, without serving as a concrete frame or as the source video being edited or continued |
| `video editing` | An existing source video is directly modified |
| `video continuation` | New content continues, extends, resumes, or transitions from an existing source video |
| `audio reuse` | The same audio signal is reused in full or in part |
| **`audio reference`** | **The audio signal is not copied directly; only its music style, timbre, dialogue or lyric content, sound-effect texture, beat, or continuity is referenced** |

When a task satisfies multiple relationships, combine with `+` and do not repeat
a type. The mere presence of video or audio does not automatically create a
corresponding task type.

The summary uses the previously defined labels to describe the main subjects,
shot flow, and roles of the reference assets. Do not introduce new reference
labels in this section.

## 4. `retention_analysis`

Describes how each piece of referenced content is preserved, transferred,
copied, or referenced. **Use one line for each reference label** and preserve the
meaning established in `subject_definitions`.

## 4. `retention_analysis`

Describes how each piece of referenced content is preserved, transferred,
copied, or referenced. **Use one line for each reference label** and preserve the
meaning established in `subject_definitions`.

### 4.1 Visible Content

`<Subject N>`, `<Picture N>`, and `<Video N>` use these fixed markers:

| Marker | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `fully_preserved` | The defined role of the referenced content is fully preserved |
| `partially_preserved` | Still used, but some defined characteristics are changed or only partially retained |
| `attribute_transfer` | Referenced characteristics are transferred to a different identifiable target subject |
| `weak_reference` | Only broad similarity in style, category, composition, or atmosphere is retained |

```text
<Subject 1> (appears in [Shot 1], [Shot 3]): fully_preserved - ...
<Picture 2> ([Shot 1] first frame): fully_preserved - ...
<Video 1> (cut and pacing structure): weak_reference - ...
```

### 4.2 Audio  ← **the section that fixed this project's doubled voice**

`<Audio N>` uses these markers:

| Marker | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `fully_copy` | The complete source audio serves as the target video's complete final audio track |
| `partially_copy` | Only part of the timeline or selected audio layers are copied, or other sounds are added, removed, or replaced after copying |
| **`reference`** | **The signal is not copied directly; only timbre, rhythm, music style, dialogue content, or sound texture is referenced** |
| `weak_reference` | Only broad similarity in category or atmosphere is retained |

```text
<Audio 1>: fully_copy - <Audio 1> is reused 1:1 as the target video's complete
final audio track.
```

```text
<Audio 2>: reference - the target speaker follows <Audio 2>'s voice timbre and
measured delivery without copying the original signal.
```

Choose each relationship marker only within the reference role already defined
for that label in `subject_definitions`. Do not treat newly added actions,
backgrounds, or plot events in the target video as losses of reference fidelity.

## 5. `detailed_description`

The main body. Describes visuals, actions, sound, and dialogue shot by shot in
target-video playback order, inserting reference labels where they apply.

## 5. `detailed_description`

The main body. Describes visuals, actions, sound, and dialogue shot by shot in
target-video playback order, inserting reference labels where they apply.

### 5.1 Basic Format

- Write the body in English. Preserve the original language of dialogue, lyrics,
  and visible text.
- **`[Shot 1]` marks the opening shot and has no timestamp.** Later shots use
  `[Shot N] At MM:SS.mmm, ...` to mark cut times.
- Write camera movement as natural English within the current shot, including
  movement type, amplitude, and speed when they need to be expressed.
- Give vocal sources stable `(S1)`, `(S2)`, and subsequent IDs. Write dialogue
  and lyrics as `<d>[Language] ...</d>`.
- Use `<scenetrans>`, `<cutoff>`, and the corresponding continuity descriptions
  for dialogue crossing a cut, speech truncated by the video ending, and
  continuous audio across shots.

### 5.2 Full-Reference Mode Differences

| Dimension | T2VA | Full-reference mode |
|---|---|---|
| Main field | `integrated_multimodal_description` | `detailed_description` |
| Style opening | Written after `[Shot 1]` | Established in one or two English sentences **before** `[Shot 1]` |
| Reference information | Does not use full-reference labels | Inserts `<Subject N>`, `<Picture N>`, `<Video N>`, `<Audio N>` at their first appearance and where their roles apply |
| Audio relationships | Describes the target video's own sound | Cites `<Audio N>` in the corresponding shot or audio phase and states whether the signal is copied or referenced |

```text
The target video is in a cinematic, literary music-video style with soft lighting
and a slightly desaturated color palette.
[Shot 1] The scene opens in a crowded urban street...
[Shot 2] At 00:09.000, the shot cuts to an extreme close-up...
```

For generation tasks, `detailed_description` is normally **350–500 English
words**. Dialogue-dense content prioritizes fitting the complete spoken timeline
rather than mechanically reaching a word count.

### 5.3 Using Reference Labels in Shots

At the first clear appearance of an important `<Subject N>`, describe its
referenced characteristics, position in the frame, and current action within what
is actually visible. Continue using the same label in later shots without
redefining it.

Natural phrasing for concrete frame anchors:

```text
the shot begins from <Picture 1>
the shot's keyframe corresponds to <Picture 2>
the shot ends on <Picture 3>
```

### 5.4 Speakers, Audio Sources, and Dialogue

When a referenced subject physically speaks, retain both the visual reference
label and the speaker ID:

```text
<Subject 2> (S1) turns toward the woman and says, <d>[English] Last summer, I
went to my grandfather's house. He talked about you.</d>
```

`<Subject N>` identifies the referenced subject, `(Sx)` identifies the actual
speaker. If the same subject speaks off-screen, keep the same form and mark it as
`off-screen`. When the speaker does not correspond to a defined subject, use a
stable voice description followed by `(Sx)`.

When verbal content is only a cue within a directly reused BGM or complete
soundtrack, and no person, character, narrator, or other independent vocal source
physically produces it, use `<Audio N>` as the audible source and do not invent an
additional `(Sx)`.

When dialogue, narration, or lyrics from reference audio are directly reused, or
when the input prompt explicitly requests their reperformance, preserve the exact
source words and original language inside `<d>`. Write `[unclear]` for
unintelligible spans instead of guessing or paraphrasing. Standardize punctuation
to basic marks; remove repeated tildes, emoji, bullets, and decorative
punctuation.

> **When only timbre, rhythm, emotion, or delivery is referenced, do not carry
> the original dialogue from the reference audio into the target video.**

Assign `(Sx)` once according to the order of actual vocal events in the target
video. Reuse the corresponding ID at every actual vocal event. **Do not write
`(Sx)` in `retention_analysis`.**

## 6. `overall_soundscape` and `non_diegetic_music`

`overall_soundscape` summarizes ambience and physical sounds across the full
video. Dialogue, singing, and sound events synchronized to a particular shot
remain in `detailed_description`.

```text
overall_soundscape: Quiet indoor room tone and a low ventilation hum continue
throughout the video.
```

`non_diegetic_music` describes background music the characters cannot hear. State
instrumentation, tempo, and dynamic development.

```text
non_diegetic_music: A restrained solo-piano score at a slow tempo, with sustained
low cello underneath and no swell.
```

When reference audio is used, state its copy or reference relationship only in
the section matching the audible layer. Write complete dialogue and lyrics only
inside `<d>` in `detailed_description`; do not repeat them in these two sections.

## 7. Complete Example

```text

brick wall, an orange tufted sofa with patterned pillows, a neon sign, and a
wooden coffee table.

<Picture 4>, with thick white fur, pointed ears, a dark nose, and a curved tail.
<Subject 3> is the young blonde woman in <Video 1>, with long blonde hair and a
light-pink button-down shirt with rolled-up sleeves.
<Subject 4> is the young man in <Video 2>, with short wavy brown hair and a
dark-grey hoodie with drawstrings.
<Audio 1> is the voice-timbre reference for <Subject 3> (S1), containing a spoken
English vocal layer.

eating a cookie in <Subject 1>. <Subject 4> enters with <Subject 2>, which lunges
toward the cookie. The three-shot exchange uses <Audio 1> as the voice-timbre
reference for <Subject 3> and ends with a canned audience laugh.

exposed brick wall, orange tufted sofa, patterned pillows, neon sign, and wooden

<Subject 2> (appears in [Shot 1], [Shot 2]): fully_preserved - the Samoyed's
thick white fur, pointed ears, dark nose, and curved tail are retained.
<Subject 3> (appears in [Shot 1], [Shot 2], [Shot 3]): fully_preserved - the
blonde woman's identity, long hair, and light-pink shirt are retained.
<Subject 4> (appears in [Shot 1], [Shot 2]): fully_preserved - the young man's
short wavy brown hair and dark-grey hoodie are retained.

## Note the pattern this project extracted from the example

In two of the three shots above, the speaker's **mouth is closed in the clause

chunks.text:
# Reference — the official MiniMax H3 documentation, captured locally

Saved 2026-08-16 so the pipeline does not depend on network access or on pages
that may change. **These are the sources. `docs/H3_PROMPT_RULES.md` is what this
project actually does with them.**

| File | Source |
|---|---|
| `COMFYUI_MINIMAX_H3_TUTORIAL.md` | <https://docs.comfy.org/tutorials/video/minimax/minimax-h3> |
| **`MINIMAX_PROMPT_GUIDE_ref.md`** | MiniMax official **R2V** guide — **the one this project follows** |
| `MINIMAX_PROMPT_GUIDE_base.md` | MiniMax official base-mode guide (T2VA/I2VA/FL2VA/L2VA) |

MiniMax also publishes installable H3 skills, not captured here:
<https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/MiniMax-H3/tree/main/skills>

## The five things in here that changed this project

1. **`retention_analysis` with `<Audio N>: reference`** (ref guide §4.2) — fixed
   the doubled voice. Nothing had told H3 the master was a reference rather than
   a source to copy.
2. **Dialogue is `<d>[English] …</d>`** (base §4.4) — quotes mean on-screen text.
3. **`[Shot N]` marks a cut, not a beat** (base §4.2) — a continuous take is one
   `[Shot 1]` with no timestamp.
4. **The mouth closes in the clause right after `</d>`** — visible in two of the
   ref guide's three worked examples.
5. **`ref_image_size: max`** keeps a 2048px short edge for stronger identity
   fidelity (tutorial, R2V tips). This project has always run `match`, which
   downscales references at the moment identity is decided. **Untested here.**

## What the docs do NOT explain

Nothing in any of them addresses H3 filling unallotted time with invented speech.
That was found by measurement on this machine and is documented in
`docs/H3_PROMPT_RULES.md` §9: render only as long as the line needs, pad silence
at assembly.

# Reference-video motion transfer with character replacement — what this install can do (2026-09-25)

Written with `CHANGELOG/2026-09-25q_queued_analysis_honesty_and_motion_transfer_plan.md`.
Investigation of the request in `local_agent/chats/1f0e3e61bdb0487a.json` msg 0
(now under `chats/_deleted/`, evidence preserved): take a reference video, keep
its motion for its whole length, and put a different character, supplied as a
still, into it — "for MiniMax". The operator has said this kind of recasting of
*any* reference video is an ongoing need.

**Short answer.** Nothing in this tree does it today, and MiniMax H3 cannot do
it at all (its conditioning is stills, references and audio, not a motion
clip). Three ComfyUI approaches exist for this machine. One has every weight installed
right now (lowest quality; one node pack short of multi-window clips). The two better ones each need one weight file that
is not on disk, so they need the operator's download approval. What shipped in
this pass is the honest plumbing: the GVD router now knows the capability and
names exactly what is missing, a read-only planner tool reports the same per
approach with sizes, and the first stage every approach shares — turning the
reference clip into per-frame pose and depth maps — was run for real on a
benign clip through the owned ComfyUI backend (see §6). No generation path was
built; §7 says what a real `render_video_from_reference` still needs.

## 1. Why no existing path fits

| existing path | what it takes as motion input | why it cannot recast a reference video |
|---|---|---|
| `render_story_image` → Minimax FLF2V / `run_prompt_pack_production` | a first and a last **still** | motion is invented between two frames; a 70 s reference has thousands |
| MiniMax H3 `ref2va` / `fl2va` (Equal Shares) | reference **images** + audio + text | no video conditioning input exists on those nodes |
| `comfy_generate` (comfyui-mcp `generate_image`, action `video`) | whatever graph comfyui-mcp composes | it composes its own graph; no pose/reference-video control |
| `analyze_video` / `extract_video_actions` (+ 25c camera estimator) | — | analysis only: words and measured camera moves, not a conditioning signal |
| `repair_video` (ProPainter) | a clip + mask | inpainting/completion; weights are on disk (150 MB) but the GVD gate keeps it blocked without a VRAM profile |

### 6c. The inversion, root-caused (CHANGELOG 2026-09-25t)

Eight more owned-backend runs with the same seed, prompt, checkpoint and
IP-Adapter as 6b (plain SDXL, 4 independent frames, unless noted):

| control image | orientation |
|---|---|
| union `type=depth` on the pass-2 Depth-Anything-V2 maps | upright 4/4 |
| DWPose body + hands + face, xinsir-scaled sticks | inverted 4/4 |
| DWPose body + hands + face, default sticks (pass6 of 6b, re-read on all frames) | inverted 3/4 (frame 2 upright) |
| DWPose body + hands, no face, xinsir sticks | upright 4/4 |
| DWPose body + face, no hands, default sticks | upright 4/4 (frame 1 has a stray extra person) |
| DWPose body only, xinsir sticks / default sticks | upright 8/8 |
| **AnimateDiff `mm_sdxl_v10_beta`, 16 frames, body + hands, no face, xinsir sticks** | **upright 16/16, follows the reference motion** |

So the union-promax model, its loader, and ComfyUI's union code are fine
(core is unmodified upstream v0.36.0, no custom node patches the ControlNet
path, the file is byte-identical to xinsir's published
`diffusion_pytorch_model_promax.safetensors`, sha256 `9fae2e50…7cdc`). The
inversion appears only when the DWPose map carries face **and** hand
keypoints together, input the model was not trained on (xinsir's card:
body-only poses, thick sticks). Stick width makes no difference. **Any
template for this approach must set `DWPreprocessor detect_face: disable`**
(body-only is xinsir's documented preparation; hands may stay). Still
open for this approach: identity (the face IP-Adapter drifts on some
frames: a grey-haired woman instead of the reference in frame 1 of each
no-face pose run), SDXL softness, and clips longer than 16 frames need the
`ComfyUI-Advanced-ControlNet` pack (operator approval). Evidence:
`local_agent/runtime/motion_transfer_20260925/animatediff_v2v_manifest_pass8b…pass14*.json`,
`contact_25t_*.png`.

### 6e. Identity tuning without a download (CHANGELOG 2026-09-25v)

Cause of the drift: the character still was the full-body Kent master
(1672×941, lobby background). The PLUS FACE IP-Adapter's CLIP-ViT-H encoder
center-crops to a square and resizes to 224 px, leaving the face about
15 px across. Three 24-frame runs (same settings as §6d, one change each):

| change | identity (native-resolution head crops, frames 1/8/14/20/24) |
|---|---|
| baseline (§6d, full-body master) | drifts from frame ~13 into a long-haired, woman-like figure |
| **448×448 face crop** of the master (new file; original untouched) | **holds**: short dark hair, receding hairline, moustache, frames 1–20; frame 24 rounder/younger, moustache exaggerated; room picks up the crop's warm brown background |
| + IP-Adapter `attn_mask` over the man's region (left 400 of 768 px) | same man; the brown bleed stays on the left and the woman's side returns to the baseline palette |
| + weight 1.0 and `embeds_scaling K+V` | nearly indistinguishable from the row above; strength is not the limit |

Rule for a template: **pass a tight, square face crop, not the full
character sheet**, and mask the IP-Adapter to the character's region when
other people share the frame (a real template needs a per-frame mask, e.g.
from the DWPose person boxes; the static left-half mask only fits this
clip). Still open: softness, and the face drifting when the head turns
late in the clip (the only reference is face-on). The film's ensemble
master shows Kent face-on at ~60 px, so it adds no new angle. Next levers
need either a per-frame face-detail pass (a larger build, flicker risk) or
a download (FaceID, or Wan 2.2 Animate).

### 6f. Video face-detail pass (CHANGELOG 2026-09-26a)

Impact Pack, already installed: `UltralyticsDetectorProvider bbox/face_yolov8m.pt`
(the still renderer's detector) → `ImpactSimpleDetectorSEGS_for_AD` (one region

## 7. `render_video_from_reference` (built 2026-09-26, CHANGELOG 2026-09-26j)

Tools: `render_video_from_reference` (starts a background job, returns a
`job_id`) and `video_reference_job_status` (read-only). Code:
`local_agent/motion_transfer_render.py` (validation, target analysis, the
pinned graph, the job runner), `local_agent/motion_transfer_faces.py`
(InsightFace helper, ComfyUI venv, CPU, never downloads), tests
`local_agent/test_motion_transfer_render.py`.

- **What it runs:** the §6e–§6g recommended configuration. AnimateDiff-SDXL +
  union-promax openpose on DWPose body + hands (face keypoints off, xinsir
  sticks), ACN apply for multi-window clips, IP-Adapter PLUS FACE on an
  automatic square face crop of the still (masked to the target's region when
  others share the frame), and a video face-detail pass (denoise 0.5) through
  FaceID Plus V2 (PLUS FACE if the still has no detectable face or FaceID is
  absent). 768×448 landscape (measured) or 448×768 portrait (unmeasured),
  8 fps default.
- **Target person:** the helper samples 8 reference frames, picks `target`
  (`auto`/`largest`, `left`, `right`, `center`) and follows it by nearest
  face centre. The mask band is the part of the frame closer to the target
  than to its neighbours (median over samples, at least 25% wide). The detail
  pass takes the face at the target's left-to-right rank.
- **Discipline:** the same `router.gpu_busy` / Equal Shares owner / port 8188 /
  live image-owner refusals and `gpu_gate` approval as `render_story_image`,
  under the same launch lock. The job claims the shared image-render owner
  first, then does a thermal preflight, runs one private backend (900 s start
  limit), and always stops it and releases. Desktop only (phone calls are
  refused even if granted). Inputs under `outputs/equal_shares` are refused.
  Requires `likeness_attestation: true`.
- **Evidence:** `outputs/motion_transfer/<job_id>/` holds job.json,
  status.json, graph.json (with its sha256, plus the template sha256 pinned in
  the tests), manifest.json, runner.log, face crop, mask and track frames.
  The manifest holds every output with its sha256, ffprobe of both mp4s,
  planned vs source/pose/generated/detailed frame counts, peak GPU memory and
  temperature, and an ArcFace identity score with its caveat.
  `verified_outputs` is true only if every count equals the plan. Nothing is
  marked accepted.
- **Limits:** at most **64 frames per job** (8 s at 8 fps; `start_seconds` /
  `max_seconds` choose a section). The limit rises only after a measured

  can drift). Identity can soften in the last window. Output is 8 fps, with no
  audio.
- **Not done:** no GVD VRAM profile or promotion (the router still reports
  `motion_reference` blocked), no Wan approach, no interpolation or audio mux.
  A human frame-level check is still the acceptance step.

## 8. How to ask for it in chat

- "Plan a motion transfer from `<video>` with `<image>` as the character" →
  `plan_video_from_reference` reports feasibility. Nothing renders.
- "Render `<video>` with `<image>` as the character: `<describe character and
  scene>`" → `render_video_from_reference` (the model must pass
  `likeness_attestation: true`, confirming the character is fictional or
  consented and no real person's likeness goes into sexual content), then
  `video_reference_job_status` until `complete` with `verified_outputs: true`.

the snapshot is missing, stale (>90s), or not `status=="ok"`. Live CLI

## 3. Login item vs LaunchDaemon (who owns `utun5`?)

A GUI app login item and a system daemon can both try to own the same
WireGuard interface at boot. Disabling it as a "login item" in the UI
is **not** enough; disable the underlying launchd job.

Tonight: WireGuard.app login item **on**
(`gui/503/com.wireguard.macos.login-item-helper`). The Network
Extension owned `utun5` (`workstation_gateway`); handshake never

helper disabled; `workstation_gateway` Disconnected; no ifscoped
default on `utun5`; default via `en0`; `10.90.90.1/32` via `utun5`
only.

label: `com.local-agent.wireguard-wg0`.

Editing or relinting a LaunchDaemon/LaunchAgent plist **does not**
change what launchd is running. Only `bootout`+`bootstrap` of that
same job (or a real reboot) does.

`plutil -p` / a file diff is necessary and not sufficient.

plutil -p /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.local-agent.wireguard-wg0.plist
launchctl print system/com.local-agent.wireguard-wg0

Do not bounce the live tunnel "to pick up the plist" unless Rhine

launchd's default PATH is `/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`. `env bash`
