- Followed by natural, accurate description of the rest of the image (for an
  identity LoRA, typically including gender/descriptor right after the
  trigger).

Auto-generated captions are a reasonable starting point but need manual review
— they routinely omit the trigger word entirely or fixate on irrelevant
background details instead of the subject.

## Core training parameters (Kohya / sd-scripts, which your environment runs)

- **Learning rate:** `1e-4` (0.0001) is the standard, reliable starting point
  for SDXL LoRA training. This is the single most impactful setting to get
  approximately right before tuning anything else.
- **Network dimension (rank):** controls how much capacity the LoRA has to
  learn. `32` is a reasonable default for a small/medium dataset; `64` for a
  larger, more varied one. Higher rank = larger file, more capacity, more risk
  of overfitting on a small dataset.
- **Network alpha:** a scaling factor, effectively `alpha / dim`. Setting
  alpha equal to dim is a common, safe starting choice. An alpha lower than
  dim reduces the effective learning rate of the LoRA layers.
- **Steps/epochs:** highly dataset-dependent — there's no universal number.
  The practical approach is to save checkpoints periodically and evaluate
  against your held-out evaluation prompts rather than committing to a fixed
  step count up front.

## What "one bounded smoke run" (your TODO's next step) should look like

Given your project's existing safety posture (GPU-gated, thermal-guarded,
nothing runs without explicit approval), a reasonable first real run is:

1. Pick **one** objective — identity or style, not both.
2. 15-20 well-chosen, correctly captioned images with a unique trigger token
   present in every caption.
3. Conservative defaults: `1e-4` learning rate, `dim=32` / `alpha=32`.
4. A small, fixed set of evaluation prompts decided *before* training starts,
   so you're judging the result against a plan rather than post-hoc vibes.
5. One run, reviewed manually — no automated "looks good" acceptance criteria
   for a first LoRA. Your own eyes are the judge here.

## Sources

- [All-in-One Stable Diffusion Guide — LoRA Training](https://github.com/Haoming02/All-in-One-Stable-Diffusion-Guide/blob/main/LoRATraining.md)
- [LoRA Training Guide 2026 — ZSky](https://zsky.ai/blog/lora-training-guide)
- [Train an Image LoRA Locally (2026): Kohya, SDXL & FLUX](https://localaimaster.com/blog/image-lora-training-local-guide)
- [Kohya SS Wiki — LoRA training parameters](https://github.com/bmaltais/kohya_ss/wiki/LoRA-training-parameters)
- [Understanding LoRA Training, Part 1 — Medium](https://medium.com/@dreamsarereal/understanding-lora-training-part-1-learning-rate-schedulers-network-dimension-and-alpha-c88a8658beb7)
- [Stable Diffusion LoRA Training Settings for Kohya SS — Aituts](https://aituts.com/lora-training-settings/)

chunks.heading: # RealVisXL / SDXL LoRA training
chunks.text:
# RealVisXL / SDXL LoRA training

This runbook is for the local agent's RealVisXL image workflow. It is separate from the MiniMax H3 video LoRA process and must not modify it.

## Safety boundary

- The legacy `A:\Users\rhine\kohya_ss\.venv` is preserved; it is currently broken because its managed Python 3.11 runtime disappeared.
- Use only `A:\Users\rhine\kohya_ss\.venv-local-agent`, created by `work\setup_sdxl_lora_trainer.ps1`.
- Setup, verification, and dataset preflight never load the SDXL checkpoint or start a training job.
- A training run needs an explicit operator choice of dataset, objective, output name, and GPU permission.

## Decide the objective before collecting data

Train one objective per LoRA:

1. **Identity LoRA:** 20–30 varied, consented images of one adult subject. Use a unique trigger token. Do not mix artistic style teaching into this set.
2. **Style LoRA:** a consistent visual style with captions describing subject matter, composition, and lighting. Do not include private identities unless consented.

Keep source images and captions outside the project evidence tree. Store training outputs in a distinct local LoRA output directory after approval.

## Hardware-aware starting configuration

For RTX 5080 16 GB VRAM and an SDXL/RealVisXL checkpoint:

- resolution: 1024, with aspect-ratio buckets
- batch size: 1
- precision: bf16 when the isolated environment verifies it; otherwise fp16
- gradient checkpointing: enabled
- cache latents to disk: enabled
- first controlled run: UNet-only, rank 16, alpha 16
- UNet learning rate: `1e-4`; text encoder disabled for the initial run
- save every 250 steps; keep no more than three checkpoints

These are starting values, not a claim that a particular dataset will work. Evaluate before raising rank, steps, or adding text-encoder training.

## Setup and preflight

1. Run `work\setup_sdxl_lora_trainer.ps1 -Install`.
2. Run `work\setup_sdxl_lora_trainer.ps1 -Verify`.
3. Validate the selected dataset and generate its proposed training plan.
4. Produce baseline RealVisXL images using the final evaluation prompts.
5. Request a controlled training run. Do not automatically enqueue one.

## Acceptance check

Compare baseline and LoRA output with three fixed prompts: trigger-only, compositional variation, and an unrelated subject. Reject a run that merely memorizes training images, changes unrelated prompts, or has unstable faces, anatomy, lighting, or style.

# Source backup policy

`work/New-LocalAgentSourceBackup.ps1` creates a portable ZIP for cloud backup.
It includes source code and documentation, plus a `BACKUP_SCOPE.txt` manifest.

It deliberately excludes credentials, `.env`, paired identities, runtime state,
uploads, feedback/exemplar stores, virtual environments, models, media,
generated outputs, artifacts, logs, archival evidence, generated indexes, and
vendored third-party desktop/mobile binaries. The ZIP is therefore
safe for normal source-code backup but is **not** a complete project/evidence or
media backup.

Run it from the canonical repository root:

```powershell
.\work\New-LocalAgentSourceBackup.ps1
```

Verify the printed SHA-256 before uploading or restoring. Keep cloud backup
access private. A separate, explicit archival plan is required for raw media,
render evidence, and encrypted runtime artifacts.

chunks.heading: # Equal Shares — authoritative audio-first pipeline
chunks.text:
# Equal Shares — authoritative audio-first pipeline

Updated 2026-08-13 from the user's explicit workflow clarification. This file
supersedes the earlier Task-0/single-pass branch. There is no shortcut in which
the film is rendered at 0.9 MP before the soundtrack is complete.

## Outcome

Build and approve the complete MiniMax H3 soundtrack first. Only after every
story clip has accepted audio may high-resolution picture generation begin.

The two immutable gates are:

1. **Audio gate:** 124/124 clip soundtracks exist, have provenance back to a
   preserved MiniMax H3 audio-first raw, and pass the relevant speech, timing,
   voice, music, ambience, and sound-effect checks.
2. **Picture gate:** every clip has a visually accepted take generated against
   its approved soundtrack, or is explicitly marked `human_review_needed` after
   the 0.4 MP attempt fails.

Full-quality MiniMax H3 only. Never use Turbo.

## Phase 0 — establish canonical reference sounds

   voice, music, ambience, and sound-effect checks.
2. **Picture gate:** every clip has a visually accepted take generated against
   its approved soundtrack, or is explicitly marked `human_review_needed` after
   the 0.4 MP attempt fails.

Full-quality MiniMax H3 only. Never use Turbo.

## Phase 0 — establish canonical reference sounds

### Character voices

Each speaking character gets one canonical `h3_voice_ref.wav`. Use the first
appearance in story order whose **delivered** audio contains enough clean,
continuous speech to be a reliable reference. A first scripted line that is
silent, mixed with another voice, mostly noise, or unstable is not qualifying.

Selection rules:

- one contiguous passage from one preserved MiniMax H3 take;
- one stable speaker, no voice switching;
- at least 6 seconds of useful speech is required for an automatic canonical
  reference; a real-story passage of 2–6 seconds requires human voice review;
- speech density at least 60%, with no internal gap above 1 second;
- never concatenate separate takes;
- preserve and record the source MP4, extraction window, and character;
- once approved, never overwrite the reference—write a versioned sibling.

If no existing first-appearance candidate qualifies, render the character's
first qualifying actual story soundtrack at 0.2 MP with the original dialogue
and boundary images. That accepted story soundtrack becomes the voice source.
Never invent filler dialogue or create a reference-only VOX scene.

Ear review is an acceptance gate, not a Stage-1 generation stop. A pending
actual-story bootstrap may be labeled provisional and used only to keep voice
conditioning available while the remaining soundtrack candidates render. It
does not count as accepted and cannot open Stage 2. The resumable supervisor is
`work/continue_audio_generation_nonblocking.py`.

Narrator references are voice-identity conditioning, not soundtrack stems. A
take with the intended Narrator plus a quieter replay, echo, whisper, alternate
take, or doubled vocal layer fails even when the timbre is consistent. Use the
single-layer repair profile and preserve the original attempt. Static prompt
preflight is required before submission: every configured line appears exactly
once, every timing window fits, references and boundary frames exist, and
dialogue does not coexist with an absolute no-speech instruction.

`work/build_voice_reference_map.py` implements first-qualifying-appearance
selection and writes `story_voice_bootstrap_plan.json`. `work/render_audio_pass.py
--bootstrap-missing-voices` renders the planned story clips.

### Music, ambience, and recurring effects

Treat recurring sound as reference material just like a voice:

- The non-diegetic score is one continuous, approved master track laid across
  the edit. Do not ask H3 to invent a new song in every clip.
- For diegetic music, room tone, machine hum, phone tone, crowd bed, or another
  recurring sound, the first approved clean occurrence becomes the named sound
  reference for later clips in that continuity group.
- Store these under `outputs/equal_shares/audio/references/` with provenance in
  `outputs/equal_shares/audio_continuity_map.json`.
- MiniMax H3 ref2va allows at most three standalone audio references. Character
  voice references take priority during the audio harvest. If all reference
  slots are occupied, preserve continuity by carrying the approved bed in the
  soundtrack assembly rather than sacrificing a character voice.

## Phase 1 — generate the complete soundtrack at the lowest proven resolution

Render **all 124 clips**, including clips without dialogue, through
`MiniMaxH3ReferenceToVideo` at **0.2 MP**, 20 steps. The picture is disposable;
the sound is the deliverable.

Fixed settings:

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Checkpoint | `minimax_h3_ref2va_pruned_nvfp4.safetensors` |
| Node | `MiniMaxH3ReferenceToVideo` |
| Text encoder | `qwen3vl_32b_minimax_h3_nvfp4_awq.safetensors` |
| Video/audio VAEs | MiniMax H3 FP16 video / FP32 audio |
| Resolution | 16:9, 0.2 MP, multiple 32 |
| Sampling | 20 steps, `res_multistep` / `simple`, denoise 1.0 |
| Output | 24 fps, 8-bit video with native stereo H3 audio |

References for every audio-first job:

- `ref_image_0`: exact opening frame.
- `ref_image_1`: exact closing frame when `last_frame` exists. It must be wired,
  not merely described in prose.
- ordered character `h3_voice_ref.wav` files, based on first spoken appearance
  within the clip;
- a recurring sound reference when relevant and when a slot remains.

Prompt rules:

- Spoken words occur exactly once in the prompt, inside their timed beat.
- State which named speaker is on/off screen and who remains silent.
- Describe every necessary sound event and its window.
- Name the recurring music/ambience/effect reference and tell H3 to preserve its
  timbre, rhythm, level, and acoustic space without copying unrelated content.
- A single clip may be retried with tighter timing, clause-boundary splits,
  explicit silence locks, and then a new seed. Never solve dialogue with Turbo.

Every raw goes to `story/AUDIO_<clip>/` and every attempt is preserved. Accepted
full-clip audio is extracted to:

`outputs/equal_shares/audio/h3_dialogue/<clip>_<attempt>_full.wav`

Line-level inspection copies may sit beside it, but the full-clip WAV is the
authoritative soundtrack reference because it also contains timing, ambience,
music, and effects.

Do not use these older folders as native-H3 sources:

- `outputs/equal_shares/audio/dialogue/` — Kokoro and RVC material;
- `outputs/equal_shares/audio/_hybrid_parts/` — an older mixed assembly cache.

### Audio validation loop

After every audio-first generation:

1. Probe duration, sample rate, channels, clipping, silence, and missing audio.
2. Extract each scripted dialogue window with small timing padding.
3. Transcribe locally and compare normalized expected words, word recall, word
   order, insertions, omissions, and extra speech.
4. Flag likely gibberish, invented words, repeated lines, a second muttering
   voice, or speech outside assigned windows.
5. Compare the speaker and recurring-bed reference features when a reliable
   local comparison is available.
6. Listen to borderline/empty-recognizer results. A broken recognizer never
   converts an unknown result into a pass.

Automatic acceptance is intentionally strict. A dialogue line should normally
have at least 0.95 expected-word recall, high sequence agreement, no substantive
insertions, and correct timing. Store measurements, transcript, source raw,
prompt revision, seed, and verdict in `audio_pass_manifest.json`. Improve the
filter when a false pass or false reject is discovered; preserve the old result
as audit history.

Phase 1 is complete only when every clip is `accepted`, not merely rendered.

## Phase 2 — generate picture around the approved soundtrack

Phase 2 is blocked until the Phase-1 audio gate passes.

For each clip, use ref2va with:

- the exact opening image;
- the exact closing image when one exists;
- the accepted full-clip Phase-1 WAV as the principal audio reference;
- a prompt written for MiniMax that says the referenced audio is the exact
  soundtrack: preserve every word, speaker, pause, music cue, ambience, effect,
  and timing; generate the visual performance around it; do not paraphrase,
  replace, remix, repeat, or add speech.

Start at **0.9 MP**. If the visual gate rejects the take, create a new preserved
attempt at the next rung:

`0.9 → 0.8 → 0.7 → 0.6 → 0.5 → 0.4 MP`

Keep 20 steps on every rung. Resolution is the only automatic ladder variable;
prompt and seed may also change when the rejection explains what must be fixed.
Never go below 0.4 MP. If the 0.4 MP take still fails, stop automatic rendering
for that clip and set `status: human_review_needed`, including every attempt,
failure reason, prompt, seed, and resolution so the user can help diagnose it.

chunks.text:

Never go below 0.4 MP. If the 0.4 MP take still fails, stop automatic rendering
for that clip and set `status: human_review_needed`, including every attempt,
failure reason, prompt, seed, and resolution so the user can help diagnose it.

### Visual validation after every attempt

The filter must evaluate the full clip at native resolution against the prompt
and references, not merely a contact sheet. Check:

- missing, duplicated, merged, extra, or disappearing people;
- face/identity drift, facial collapse, and inconsistent hair or wardrobe;
- malformed hands, fingers, limbs, joints, gait, or object interactions;
- temporal morphing, severe flicker, unintended cuts, camera reversals, black
  frames, freezes, or unrelated scene changes;
- architecture, props, geography, screen direction, and start/end frame intent;
- visible gibberish text, logos, captions, or watermarks;
- action, blocking, and speaker behavior against the prompt.

Mechanical/video metrics may reject obvious failures. Agent vision must inspect
native-resolution frames and motion for semantic and anatomical faults. A
contact sheet may rank work but cannot accept a take. Upscaling cannot repair
identity or anatomy.

### Preserve the perfect soundtrack

H3 may reinterpret a reference even when prompted not to. Therefore the audio
from the high-resolution picture render is never the soundtrack authority.
Compare it for diagnostics, then mux the exact approved Phase-1 WAV onto the
selected video without rewriting it. This guarantees that accepted words,
voices, music, ambience, effects, and timing reach the film unchanged.

## Phase 3 — assembly and completion

- Assemble only visually accepted picture takes.
- Use only their corresponding accepted Phase-1 full-clip WAVs.
- Carry the continuous score as one track across cuts; do not restart it per
  generation.
- Preserve every raw, reference, manifest, validation report, assembly input,
  and versioned deliverable.
- The completion audit must include the audio gate, visual gate, provenance, and
  `human_review_needed` count. The film is not complete while that count is
  nonzero.

## Operational safeguards

- One ComfyUI backend and one GPU owner on port 8188 at a time.
- One clean backend per render job.
- Never download anything.
- Never use Turbo.
- Never delete or overwrite evidence.
- Never hand-edit a runner-owned manifest during a render.
- Mechanical validity is not audio or visual acceptance.

chunks.heading: # Voice cloning and approval gate
chunks.text:
# Voice cloning and approval gate

> **Legacy design; prohibited for the current workflow as of 2026-08-14.** The
> VOX/filler and external clone-API approach below is preserved only as design
> history. Do not run `work/voice_manager.py`. Current character references come
> only from first qualifying actual story soundtracks generated locally by
> non-Turbo MiniMax H3 at 0.2 MP and 20 steps. Use
> `work/render_audio_pass.py --bootstrap-missing-voices` and
> `outputs/equal_shares/story_voice_bootstrap_plan.json`.

`work/voice_manager.py` — plan, extract, gate, clone. `work/voice_review.ps1` — listen and approve.

Everything below the API section was executed against the real project. The MiniMax API
calls were **not** executed — no key in this environment — so treat those two functions as
reviewed-but-untested and check the response shapes on your first live call.

---

## The constraint that shapes the design

The MiniMax clone endpoint needs a reference sample of **10 seconds minimum**, 5 minutes
maximum, 20 MB maximum, in mp3/m4a/wav.

Measured against this script, by longest single take:

| | characters |
|---|---|
| One take already clears 10 s | **6** — Narrator, Kent, Doris, Avery, Terminal voice, Doris recording |
| No take clears 10 s | **12** |

Of those twelve, eight have less than 10 seconds of dialogue *in the entire film*. Male
Visitor Two has 2.0 s. Crew lead 2.0 s. Aid worker and Council member 3.0 s.

**A sample must come from a single take.** H3 re-derives a voice on every clip — that is
the drift you have been hearing. Concatenating two takes to reach 10 seconds would splice
two different-sounding performances together and teach the clone an average of both, which
is the opposite of what cloning is for.

So the twelve get a **VOX clip**: a throwaway 15-second render of that character speaking
filler, using their own approved anchor frame, existing only to harvest a voice. It is
never part of the edit.

## Render order

`plan` writes `outputs/equal_shares/runtime/render_priority.json` in two phases:

**Phase 1 — 12 voice sample clips**
`VOX_MALE_VISITOR_ONE  VOX_MALE_VISITOR_TWO  VOX_WEALTHY_COMMUTER  VOX_UNHOUSED_MAN
VOX_FAITH_WHITE  VOX_RYANN_SALLY  VOX_VOLUNTEER  VOX_HOUSING_REPRESENTATIVE
VOX_CONGREGATION_MEMBER  VOX_COUNCIL_MEMBER  VOX_CREW_LEAD  VOX_AID_WORKER`

**Phase 2 — 6 story clips whose audio doubles as a sample**
`00A  11B  13B  14D  22B  25A`

Eighteen renders and every character has a voice. Note phase 2 picks the *longest* take
per character, not the first — Kent's sample comes from `14D` (the driving shot, 15 s of
continuous speech), not from `02B` where he has 3.5 s.

**`render_queue_owner.json` is deliberately untouched.** That file is the GPU mutex —
the one lock preventing two backends. Queue ordering is a different concern and lives in
its own file. `render_until_complete.py` should read `render_priority.json` and take those
clips first; that wiring is the one integration step left to you.

`voice_sample_clips.json` holds the full spec for the twelve VOX clips — id, anchor,
duration, frame count already rounded to 5 mod 17, seed, dialogue and a complete prompt
following the house style. They are single-anchor by design; a closing frame would force
the take to arrive at a pose, which fights thirteen seconds of talking.

    }
  }
}
```

`strategy` is `single_clip` or `sample_clip_required`. `status` moves
`pending → approved`, or `pending → needs_reroll` and back. `fallback_voice` is the Kokoro
voice already assigned to that character, which stays available if cloning is abandoned.

The gate opens only when every character is `approved` with no `needs_reroll`. Rewriting
the file by hand works — set `approved: true` — but the CLI keeps `gate_open` and
`reviewed_at` consistent.

## Workflow

```powershell
$Py = "A:\Users\rhine\ComfyUI-Installs\Rockernow\ComfyUI\.venv\Scripts\python.exe"

# 1. plan: writes the VOX specs, the priority queue and the gate
& $Py work\voice_manager.py plan

# 2. render phase 1 and phase 2 (supervisor or by hand), then review them visually

# 3. extract reference samples from the rendered clips
.\work\voice_review.ps1 -Extract

# 4. LISTEN and decide - this is the human gate
.\work\voice_review.ps1 -Listen

# 5. anything unusable
.\work\voice_review.ps1 -Reroll "Kent" -Reason "too nasal, re-render 14D"

# 6. confirm before letting anything downstream run
& $Py work\voice_manager.py gate      # exit 0 open, 1 closed
```

`-Listen` plays each sample through `System.Media.SoundPlayer` and prompts
approve / re-roll / skip / quit per character. Extraction runs two-pass EBU R128
loudness normalisation, a 70 Hz high-pass and light denoise, then writes mono 44.1 kHz
PCM — H3's output level varies between clips and the clone endpoint is level-sensitive.

```

## Blocking downstream work

```python
from voice_manager import check_approval_gate

is_open, reasons = check_approval_gate()
if not is_open:
    raise SystemExit("voice gate closed:\n  " + "\n  ".join(reasons))
```

`check_approval_gate()` is read-only and never mutates state.

## MiniMax API integration

Three calls: upload the sample for a `file_id`, clone it into a `voice_id`, then
synthesise each line with that `voice_id`.

```python
file_id  = upload_reference("outputs/equal_shares/voices/narrator/reference_sample.wav")
voice_id = clone_voice("Narrator")          # POST /v1/voice_clone, records voice_id on the gate
synthesize_line("In a world of total equality...", voice_id,
                "outputs/equal_shares/voices/narrator/lines/00A_01.wav")
```

`clone_voice()` refuses to run on an unapproved character — the gate is enforced in code,
not just documented. The key comes from `MINIMAX_API_KEY` in the environment and is never
written to disk; `MINIMAX_GROUP_ID` is passed to upload if set.

`upload_reference()` validates the 10 s floor, the 5 minute ceiling and the 20 MB limit
before spending a call.

**Unverified:** the exact JSON envelope of the upload and clone responses, and whether
`t2a_v2` returns hex-encoded audio in `data.audio` for your account tier. Those are the
first things to check on a live call. Endpoints and the model name `speech-2.6-hd` come
from MiniMax's published docs.

## Replacing audio in the finished clips

Once voices are cloned and lines synthesised, `work/audio_decisions.py` already builds the
final timeline — mark clips `replace` and point its Kokoro source at the cloned line files
instead. The two modules are designed to meet there rather than duplicating the mixing
logic.

## What is left to wire

1. **`render_until_complete.py` should read `render_priority.json`** and take those clips
   before its normal sequence order. Nothing else consumes that file yet.
2. **The VOX clips need a render path.** They are not in `story_config.json` on purpose —
   adding them would put them in the edit and the completion audit. Either run them by hand
   through ComfyUI using the prompts in `voice_sample_clips.json`, or give the runner a
   `--spec` flag that accepts an alternate clip list writing to `story/VOX_*/`.
3. **Decide what happens to the Kokoro timeline** once voices are cloned. Both paths can
   coexist per clip through `audio_decisions.py`.

chunks.text:
# 10-node Worker Farm — architecture plan (2026-08-29)

## Purpose and boundary

This plan is now active only for the **local CPU-only Phase 1 bootstrap** in
`local_agent/worker_farm/`. It is not authorization to expose a queue, add a
remote worker, start a cluster, run a model, or process private historical
exports. The Ryzen/RTX 5080 workstation remains the only interactive control
plane. A future ten-node Intel cluster (60 CPU cores, 160 GB aggregate RAM,
1 GbE) is a private, asynchronous worker farm. It must never start ComfyUI,
edit workstation files, grant permissions, or make itself an authority over the
control plane.

The current Phase 1 implementation uses loopback-only Redis and a CPU-only
Celery worker with a single allow-listed, review-only sample distillation job.
It stores raw source/result artifacts with authenticated AES-256-GCM and has
no Chroma promotion, rendering, shell execution, model loading, or remote
listener. Its explicit readiness and activation sequence is documented in
`local_agent/worker_farm/README.md`.

Aggregate RAM is not unified memory. A multi-node model uses network transport
between partitions. At 1 GbE, do not make all ten nodes a sequential inference
pipeline. Batch work and use the smallest viable model partition; use remaining
nodes for independent horizontal workloads.

## Proposed minimum stack

| Concern | Planned component | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Durable ingress/backpressure | RabbitMQ | Publisher confirms, acknowledgements, bounded prefetch, priorities, dead letters. |
| General background work | Celery | Durable retries, fan-out/fan-in, schedules, explicit queue routing. |
| Batched model work | Ray Core / Ray Data | Long-lived model actors and independently parallel micro-batches. |
| Job authority | PostgreSQL | Idempotency keys, leases, state, reviews, provenance. |
| Raw artifacts | MinIO | Immutable source logs, PDFs, exports, outputs and encrypted archives. |
| Retrieval | ChromaDB gateway | One controlled writer, searchable encrypted-at-rest storage, source metadata. |

Messages must contain only a signed task envelope: task ID, artifact URI,
SHA-256, task type, expiration, idempotency key, and policy version. Raw logs,
documents, media, and exports stay in artifact storage.

## Phase A — capacity and trust gates

- Inventory all nodes and measure end-to-end 1-GbE throughput/latency.
- Reserve one CPU core per node for OS/network/monitoring; start with five
  CPU-heavy workers per six-core node.
- Establish private VLAN/LAN rules, TLS/authentication between services, and
  no public queue/model/database endpoints.
- Implement backup/restore and encrypted-artifact tests before production data.
- Benchmark a smaller single-node judge first. A distributed 70B judge is an
  experiment only after RAM, throughput, batch saturation, and recovery tests.

chunks.text:

- Establish private VLAN/LAN rules, TLS/authentication between services, and
  no public queue/model/database endpoints.
- Implement backup/restore and encrypted-artifact tests before production data.
- Benchmark a smaller single-node judge first. A distributed 70B judge is an
  experiment only after RAM, throughput, batch saturation, and recovery tests.

## Phase B — batch fabric

- RabbitMQ queues: judge, researcher fetch/extract/summarize/embed/ingest,
  Teacher, Student, synthetic evaluator, chat-export extraction/distillation,
  encryption, quarantine, and dead letter.
- Use publisher confirms and manual acknowledgement after durable output write.
- Set low prefetch for model workers; higher but bounded prefetch for lightweight
  fetching/parsing work. Set batch windows of 250 ms–2 s and benchmark batches
  of 4/8/16/32.
- Celery handles ordinary durable pipelines. Ray owns long-lived inference
  actors and micro-batch execution. Persist every output outside Ray memory.

## Phase C — four workflows

### 1. Judge evaluation

The workstation sanitizes a completed task log, uploads it to MinIO, and queues
a reference. The cluster batches jobs through a versioned evaluator rubric.
Structured output must cite exact artifact evidence for every criticism. Results
are advisory only; they cannot edit the workstation or change policy. Store raw
results as AES-256-GCM artifacts and promote only approved compact lessons.

### 2. Autonomous Researcher ingestion

Use an operator-maintained allowlist of URLs, PDFs and repositories. Preserve
the original source first, apply robots/rate-limit and private-address checks,
then extract, normalize, summarize, chunk, embed using `nomic-embed-text`,
deduplicate, and submit only through the Chroma gateway. Every chunk retains
URI/commit/page/hash/license/timestamp metadata. Treat source text as data, not
instructions; quarantine prompt injection and malformed material.

### 3. Teacher/Student synthetic data

Use separate Ray pools for Teacher, Student, evaluator and curator roles.
Queue scenario bundles of 8–64 independent examples, not sequential dialogues
across all nodes. Prefer smaller replicated models for throughput; reserve any
large distributed judge for high-value final scoring. Store schema-valid JSONL
with model versions, seed, task, rubric, output, score, and provenance. Human
review is required before training use.

chunks.text:

across all nodes. Prefer smaller replicated models for throughput; reserve any
large distributed judge for high-value final scoring. Store schema-valid JSONL
with model versions, seed, task, rubric, output, score, and provenance. Human
review is required before training use.

### 4. Historical memory distillation

Preserve incoming ChatGPT/Claude/other exports in encrypted raw storage. Never
embed full noisy transcripts. A deterministic parser and Extractor role create
only candidate preferences, hardware facts, verified project decisions, golden
code exemplars, and uncertain claims. Every candidate has source reference,
date, project scope, confidence and review status. Approved records go to
separate memory collections; uncertain records stay non-retrievable pending
review. Embeddings/search indexes remain technically searchable, so protect
Chroma with encrypted disks/backups, private networking and access control;
encrypt raw source text and sensitive fields rather than embedding ciphertext.

## Mandatory acceptance gates

- Workstation submission returns before any cluster result is available.
- Queue recovery never duplicates encrypted results, Chroma records, or JSONL.
- Worker crash, broker restart, database restart, Chroma failure and encryption
  failure all have tested recovery paths.
- No cluster worker can call workstation control endpoints.
- Every promoted RAG memory and training item has provenance and human approval.
- The 70B judge has measured throughput and a smaller fallback before use.

# Worker Farm — multiple idle LAN machines, before the 10-node cluster (2026-09-01)

## What this is, and what it is not

The operator has 4+ idle computers on the home LAN today (mixed Windows/
Linux/Mac) and a Pixel phone, and wants them contributing spare capacity now,
ahead of the dedicated 10-node/60-core/160-GB cluster hardware named in
`docs/WORKER_FARM_ARCHITECTURE_PLAN_2026-08-29.md` (that plan remains
"planning only" and unauthorized on its own). This document generalizes
`docs/WORKER_FARM_PHASE1_5_SECONDARY_NODE_PLAN_2026-08-29.md` — written for
exactly one additional laptop — to an arbitrary number of already-owned LAN
machines, and narrows the first milestone to **proving connectivity only**,
per the operator's own stated priority: get real machines securely joined and
completing real (if trivial) work before writing any new task logic.

It is **not** the RabbitMQ/Ray/PostgreSQL/MinIO ten-node stack or its four
production workflows (Judge, Researcher, Teacher/Student, historical-memory
distillation). Those stay exactly as scoped and gated in the architecture
plan. Nothing here authorizes starting that stack, downloading a model,
processing a real historical export, or granting a worker access to the
`distill` queue.

**The Pixel phone is explicitly out of scope for this document.** It has its
own, already-designed track: the inert, stdlib-only Termux edge-worker
contract (`local_agent/worker_farm/termux_powerinfer2_edge_worker.py`), which
deliberately never receives Redis/AES broker credentials or joins Celery —
see `docs/POWERINFER2_MOBILE_EDGE_PLAN_2026-08-29.md`. Mixing the phone into
this Celery/Redis track would cross a boundary that track was specifically
designed to keep closed. If the phone should contribute here too, that is a
separate, later decision — not a default of "it's idle hardware."

- The single-node Phase 1 broker + synthetic `--sample` job already completed

- `Add-Phase1SecondaryWorkerCredential.ps1` was already written generically

  change** to support more than one secondary node. It already refuses to
  grant the `distill` queue to any secondary credential.
- `local_agent/worker_farm/relay/tunnel_relay.py` already accepts up to 8
  concurrent connections through a semaphore — it needed **no code change**
  to relay more than one peer's traffic to Redis.
- `worker.py`'s pool selection (`solo` on Windows/Android, `prefork`
  elsewhere) already covers Windows, Linux, and macOS without change.
- The one real gap: `celery_app.py`'s `_is_authenticated_loopback_redis_url`
  accepted only `127.0.0.1`, which no other machine can ever reach. The
  Phase 1.5 plan doc flagged this exact gap and deliberately deferred fixing
  it until a secondary node was actually being implemented. **Fixed today** —
  see "Code changes made" below.
- No real task exists yet for a secondary node to run. `distill` is
  historical-export-only and forbidden to secondary credentials by the
  credential script itself; `preprocess`/`research` are named in the Phase
  1.5 doc but have no task functions written. A **new, minimal
  `connectivity_probe` task** (added today, see below) fills that gap for
  the "prove connectivity" milestone without inventing scope.

## Topology: hub-and-spoke instead of one point-to-point tunnel

The Phase 1.5 doc used a bare `/30` (workstation + one laptop only). With
4+ machines, the workstation becomes a small WireGuard hub with one peer
section per machine; each secondary machine's own WireGuard config lists
only the workstation as its one peer (a star, not a mesh — machines never
need to reach each other directly for this).

- Address plan: `10.90.90.0/28` (14 usable addresses — room for the current
  4+ machines plus headroom without renumbering). Workstation is
  `10.90.90.1` (unchanged from the Phase 1.5 doc — this is why
  `Add-Phase1SecondaryWorkerCredential.ps1`'s `-TunnelIp` default and the
  relay's `--bind-ip` did not need to change). Each secondary machine takes
  the next free address (`10.90.90.2`, `.3`, `.4`, `.5`, ...).
- Confirm `10.90.90.0/28` doesn't collide with the actual home LAN's router
  range before use — the same manual check the Phase 1.5 doc already named
  as something it cannot verify remotely.
- Each machine still generates its own WireGuard keypair locally; only
  public keys are exchanged once, over a channel the operator controls
  directly (never through this agent, never through the broker) — unchanged
  from the Phase 1.5 doc's rule.
- The workstation's WireGuard interface gains one `[Peer]` block per
  machine (each with that machine's public key and its `/32` allowed-IP);
  each secondary machine's config has exactly one `[Peer]` block, pointing
  back at the workstation's public key and `10.90.90.1`.
- Redis itself is still never reconfigured to bind to the tunnel interface.
  The existing `tunnel_relay.py`, run once on the workstation bound to
  `10.90.90.1`, still forwards every peer's traffic to the already-verified
  `127.0.0.1:6379` — this is exactly why its 8-connection semaphore already
  covers this case without modification.

least-privilege means not granting a queue before there's a reason to:

.\Add-Phase1SecondaryWorkerCredential.ps1 -Username media_server  -Queues probe
.\Add-Phase1SecondaryWorkerCredential.ps1 -Username old_laptop    -Queues probe
.\Add-Phase1SecondaryWorkerCredential.ps1 -Username linux_box     -Queues probe

(names are placeholders — use whatever identifies each machine to you). Each

transmitted by this agent; copy each one to its matching machine yourself.

same verification step the Phase 1.5 doc already specifies) before trusting
it for anything beyond the connectivity test below.

Note the script's own documented limitation: these ACL users live only in
the running Redis container's memory (no `aclfile` configured) and must be
re-applied if the container restarts — unchanged, not addressed here, to
avoid risking the verified Phase 1 foundation for a feature not yet live.

## Code changes made today

1. **`local_agent/worker_farm/celery_app.py`** — `_is_authenticated_loopback_redis_url`
   now also accepts `redis://<user>:<pass>@10.90.90.1:6379/{0,1}` (a single

   exact, narrowly-scoped change the Phase 1.5 doc pre-flagged as necessary
   once a secondary node was actually implemented. It does not open any
   network path by itself — Docker's `127.0.0.1:6379:6379` publish rule is
   unchanged, so nothing reaches Redis without the WireGuard tunnel and relay
   also being live, and nothing reads another user's keys without a
   correctly scoped ACL.
2. **`local_agent/worker_farm/tasks.py`** — added `connectivity_probe`, a
   Celery task that returns only `hostname`, `platform`, `worker_pid`, and
   `received_at`. It touches no file, no encryption, no job-registry state,
   and no historical-export data. Routed to its own `probe` queue in
   `celery_app.py`'s `task_routes` (never `distill`).
3. Tests: `test_farm_core.py` gained a test asserting the widened URL check
   still rejects an arbitrary private IP (`192.168.50.10`) and only accepts
   the one hub address, plus a subprocess registration test mirroring the
   existing `distill_export` one (worker.py's actual Celery load path must
   register the new task, not just the source file defining it), plus a
   direct call confirming the task body only ever returns the four harmless
   fields above. All pass; see `CHANGELOG/2026-09-01e_...md`.

chunks.text:
# Worker Farm Phase 1.5 — adding the secondary laptop node (2026-08-29)

## What this is, and what it is not

This is the runbook, scripts, and phased plan for the **single concrete next
step** named in `TODO.md` under "Phase 1 worker-farm bootstrap": *"Add the
secondary laptop only after it connects over a private encrypted overlay with
separate broker credentials."* It is scoped to exactly one additional trusted
node (the operator's laptop) joining the existing Celery/Redis foundation at
`local_agent/worker_farm/`.

It is **not** the ten-node Intel cluster. That larger vision, its RabbitMQ/Ray/
PostgreSQL/MinIO stack, and its four workflows (Judge, Researcher, Teacher/
Student, historical-memory distillation) stay exactly as scoped and gated in
`docs/WORKER_FARM_ARCHITECTURE_PLAN_2026-08-29.md` — "planning only... No
cluster service, model, download, network listener, or external account is
authorized by this roadmap alone." Nothing here authorizes starting that
cluster either. This document is the small, concrete bridge between "one
loopback-only worker on this machine" and that larger roadmap: it is Phase A's
first real node, sized to two machines instead of ten, so it can actually be
built and tested before the larger plan's capacity/trust gates are attempted.

It is also **not** the parked chat-offload idea in
`docs/design_notes/distributed_compute_assessment.md`. That note is about
moving the *interactive* reasoning LLM's Ollama server to a second box so the
RTX 5080 stays dedicated to ComfyUI — a different subsystem (`router.py`'s
GPU/CPU tiers), a different protocol (Ollama's HTTP API), and a different
trust model (a model-serving endpoint, not a task queue with private data
flowing through it). It remains paused on the question of whether the
candidate second box has a GPU, and nothing here un-pauses it. The two ideas
are related only in that both spend a second physical machine's spare
capacity — if the operator's laptop ever became both a Celery worker *and* a
remote Ollama host, `router.py`'s health-check/fallback design and this
plan's overlay would very likely reuse the same WireGuard tunnel, which is
the one implementation detail worth remembering if that note is ever
un-paused.

No script in this plan has been run. Nothing has been installed on a laptop.
No queue has been exposed beyond `127.0.0.1`. Writing this down is not
authorization to execute it — the live Phase 1 single-node sample (blocked on
Docker Desktop's engine, per `docs/CLAUDE_CODE_CONTINUATION_2026-08-29.md`)
should be accepted first, since this plan builds directly on that same broker
and its `.env`.

## Why a laptop node is safe to add and what changes

Today, Redis is authenticated (`--requirepass`) **and** unreachable from
anywhere but the workstation itself (`127.0.0.1:6379:6379` in
`compose.yaml`). Adding a second real machine means something other than
`localhost` must be able to reach port 6379. That is a genuine, deliberate
expansion of the trust boundary — exactly the one `worker_farm/README.md`
already names as requiring "a private encrypted overlay and separate broker
credentials" before it's allowed. Two independent layers do that work:

| Layer | Mechanism | Stops |
|---|---|---|
| Network | WireGuard point-to-point tunnel, workstation ⟷ laptop only | Anything else on the home LAN from reaching Redis at all, even if it later guesses a password |
| Application | A separate Redis ACL user for the laptop, scoped to its own queues/keys, distinct from the workstation's superuser password | The laptop (or anything using its credential) from reading `distill` jobs, historical-export artifacts, or other users' keys, even though it shares the same Redis instance |

Neither layer is optional. WireGuard without a scoped credential means a
compromised laptop gets the same access as the workstation. A scoped
credential without WireGuard means the password is the only thing standing
between the open LAN and a queue that will eventually carry private data.

## Phase 1.5-A — network: WireGuard tunnel

A point-to-point WireGuard tunnel, not a mesh VPN service (Tailscale/Nebula):
no third-party coordination account, no dependency on an external server
being reachable, keys never leave the two machines. This matches the existing
project bias against external accounts for core infrastructure (see `TODO.md`:
"No... external account is authorized by this roadmap alone").

- Address plan: a bare `/30`, only two usable hosts — `10.90.90.1`
  (workstation) and `10.90.90.2` (laptop). Chosen to be unlikely to collide
  with typical home-router LAN ranges (`192.168.x.x`, `10.0.x.x`); confirm it
  doesn't collide with the operator's actual LAN before use.
- Each machine generates its own keypair locally (`wg genkey | tee privatekey
  | wg pubkey > publickey`, or the WireGuard Windows client's built-in key
  generation). Private keys are never transmitted; only public keys are
  exchanged, once, over a channel the operator controls directly (not through
  this agent, not through the broker).
- The workstation's WireGuard peer listens on a UDP port (default 51820) on
  the LAN interface only — it does not need to be, and should not be, port
  forwarded on the home router. Both machines stay on the same LAN.
- Redis itself is **not** reconfigured to bind to the tunnel interface, and
  `compose.yaml`'s already-verified `127.0.0.1:6379:6379` publish rule is not
  touched. Whether Docker Desktop's WSL2-backed port publishing actually
  binds cleanly to an arbitrary secondary Windows adapter IP (the WireGuard
  interface) is untested here and not worth risking against a foundation that
  currently works. Instead:

### The relay, not a Docker networking change

`local_agent/worker_farm/relay/tunnel_relay.py` is a small stdlib-only TCP
byte relay (no third-party dependency, matching the project's existing
stdlib-only pattern in `termux_powerinfer2_edge_worker.py`). It binds
**only** to an explicit, non-loopback IP passed as a required argument — it
refuses `0.0.0.0` and refuses to guess — and forwards raw bytes to
`127.0.0.1:6379`. It adds no authentication of its own; it is plumbing, not a
security boundary. The two real security layers are WireGuard (below it) and
the Redis ACL credential (above it, inside the relayed connection). Run it on
the workstation, bound to `10.90.90.1`, only while a laptop worker session is
active — it is not part of `START_PHASE1_BROKER.ps1` and does not start
automatically.

## Phase 1.5-B — credentials: a scoped Redis ACL user

`redis:7-alpine` (already pinned in `compose.yaml`) supports full ACL
(`ACL SETUSER`, Redis 6+), not just the legacy single `--requirepass`. The
laptop gets its own username and password, generated the same way
`Initialize-Phase1Secrets.ps1` already generates the main Redis password
(`RandomNumberGenerator`, URL-safe base64, never printed) — never the
workstation's own broker password.

Draft ACL, applied through `redis-cli` inside the existing container (exact
command in the script below):

```
ACL SETUSER laptop_worker on >{generated-password} ~laptop_worker:* ~preprocess ~research ~_kombu.binding.preprocess ~_kombu.binding.research ~celery-task-meta-* ~unacked ~unacked_index resetchannels +@read +@write +@keyspace +@connection -@admin -@dangerous -@scripting -flushall -flushdb -config -shutdown -acl
```

This is a **draft, not a verified rule** — Celery/Kombu's exact Redis key and
command usage (delivery-tag bookkeeping, `unacked`/`unacked_index` for
`task_acks_late`, any event-pubsub channels if worker events are ever
enabled) needs confirming against a real Celery 5.6.3 client before this is
trusted, exactly the same way the task-registration fix in this session
needed a real Celery app object rather than reasoning from documentation
alone. Test it by pointing a throwaway worker at `laptop_worker`'s credential
and confirming both that its own queues work **and** that
`ACL DENY` correctly blocks a `GET` on a `distill`-queue or
`source_*`/`result_*` artifact-ledger key before this is used for anything
beyond the synthetic sample.

`local_agent/worker_farm/Add-Phase1SecondaryWorkerCredential.ps1` (below)
generates the password locally, applies the ACL rule above through the
running Redis container, and writes a laptop-side `.env.laptop_worker`
fragment containing only the `redis://laptop_worker:{password}@10.90.90.1:6379/0`
URL shape — it never prints the password to the console, matching
`Initialize-Phase1Secrets.ps1`'s existing convention, and it refuses to run
unless the main broker is already up (it needs a live Redis to apply the ACL
to).

## Phase 1.5-C — the laptop's own worker process

The laptop runs the exact same `local_agent/worker_farm/worker.py` already in
the repo — cross-platform pool selection (`solo` on Windows/Android, `prefork`
on Linux) is already implemented there and needs no laptop-specific fork. Two
new queues, `preprocess` and `research`, are added to `celery_app.py`'s
`task_routes` only once real task functions exist for them (none do yet —
per `worker_farm/README.md`'s policy table, the laptop is scoped to
"public/approved sources only," so its first real task is more likely a
Researcher-style fetch/extract job than anything touching private exports).
Writing those tasks is out of scope for this plan; it is the natural
follow-up once the tunnel and credential are live-verified.

The laptop's `.env` is **not** a copy of the workstation's. It contains:
- `FARM_BROKER_URL` / `FARM_RESULT_BACKEND` using the `laptop_worker`
  credential and the workstation's tunnel address (`10.90.90.1`), not
  `127.0.0.1` — `celery_app.py`'s existing
  `_is_authenticated_loopback_redis_url` check deliberately requires
  `127.0.0.1`, so it will (correctly) refuse this URL. That function needs a
  second, explicit allow-list entry for the tunnel address once this phase is
  actually implemented — not changed here, since loosening that check without
  the tunnel actually existing yet would just widen what the workstation's
  own worker/submitter accept. Flagging it now so it isn't missed later.
- `FARM_QUEUES=preprocess,research` (never `distill` — the laptop must not be
  able to claim historical-export jobs even if it could authenticate, and the
  ACL above already makes that a second, independent enforcement point).
- Its own `FARM_ENCRYPTION_KEY_B64`, if it ever produces artifacts that need
  encryption, is a separate concern from the broker credential and is not
  designed here — no task exists yet that would need it.

## What to run, once the operator decides to proceed

1. Confirm the existing single-node Phase 1 sample has been accepted (see
   `docs/CLAUDE_CODE_CONTINUATION_2026-08-29.md`'s numbered sequence). This
   plan assumes a working broker, not a blocked one.
2. Generate and exchange WireGuard keys on both machines; confirm
   `10.90.90.1` ⟷ `10.90.90.2` ping over the tunnel before touching Redis.
3. On the workstation: `local_agent\worker_farm\Add-Phase1SecondaryWorkerCredential.ps1`
   — applies the ACL, writes the laptop's env fragment to a file the operator
   copies across themselves (never transmitted by this agent).
4. On the workstation: run `tunnel_relay.py` bound to `10.90.90.1`, only for
   the duration of the test.
5. On the laptop: install the same `requirements.txt` into its own isolated
   `.venv`, place the generated `.env.laptop_worker` as its `.env`, and run
   `worker.py --queues preprocess,research`.
6. Verify with `ACL DENY` probes (step B above) before considering this done,
   and add the result to a same-session `CHANGELOG/` entry — this plan does
   not count as verification of itself, per this project's standing rule.

## Open questions this plan cannot resolve alone

- **Laptop OS is unknown here.** `worker.py`'s pool selection already handles
  Windows/Linux/Android; WireGuard has native clients for all three, so
  nothing above assumes one. Confirm before running step 3.
- **Whether Docker Desktop's WSL2 networking would have worked for a direct
  bind to the tunnel interface instead of the relay** is untested. The relay
  was chosen specifically to avoid depending on the answer, but if a future
  session confirms direct binding works, the relay becomes unnecessary
  overhead and can be dropped.
- **Whether `10.90.90.0/30` collides with anything already on the operator's
  network** needs a one-time manual check on the operator's side; it isn't
  something this agent can see.

These are recorded here rather than left as silent assumptions, in keeping
with `distributed_compute_assessment.md`'s own pattern of ending on its one
open question instead of guessing past it.

## 2026-08-30 — PowerInfer next-candidate research

The native RTX 5080 PowerInfer build and ReluLLaMA-7B bundle are mechanically
healthy, but the controlled quality comparison failed 9 of 10 basic
instruction/format cases. The bundle is diagnostic only: it is not registered,
not routed into the local agent, and its endpoint is stopped.

The next research target is the official PowerInfer Bamboo-DPO 7B sparse model,
which provides DPO alignment on the upstream dReLU architecture. This is a
candidate, not an approval: exact GGUF/predictor/activation lineage, revision,
hashes, mechanical serving, and the same bounded quality packet must pass
before promotion. Dense or Qwen checkpoints must not be relabeled as
PowerInfer models.

Running log. Append; don't rewrite history. The end goal is to fold these into a mostly
self-running automation program, so every entry should be specific enough to turn into a

## Generation — what works

**Locked settings, never varied, never a suspect.** 736×416 (0.3 MP), 16:9, multiple 32,
20 steps, `res_multistep` / `simple`, denoise 1.0, 24 fps, 8-bit, SageAttention, full
non-Turbo H3. Across 95 analysed takes, keepers and rejects had *identical* settings —
every difference that mattered was in the prompt.

**Frame count rule holds.** Round up to the next value congruent to 5 modulo 17. Every
correct render obeys it: 8 s → 192, 10 s → 243, 12 s → 294, 15 s → 362.

**One clean backend per clip.** The supervisor starts ComfyUI, renders one clip, stops it,
clears GPU, repeats. Roughly 8 minutes per clip. 124 clips rendered this way without a
VRAM failure.

**A single anchor is viable.** `1.mp4` was kept from a render with no last frame wired.
Dual anchors give control of the endpoint; they are not required for a usable take.

## Generation — what does not work

**Undirected time.** Any second not described in the shot list gets invented. `10B` had
nothing scripted after 3 s and filled the room with 8–10 people. `11C` had nothing after
the opening beat and cut to a new angle, putting "MiniMAX H3 BRNTWOOD" on the counter.
Rule: **every second of a clip must be accounted for in a timed beat.**

**Two people in the same screen position across two anchors.** In `boundary_03_v2 →
boundary_04_v2` the standing man is centre in frame 1 and the Narrator is centre-right in
frame 2, so the model grows one into the other. Rule: **when a new person appears mid-clip,
name their entry edge, state they are nearer to camera, and explicitly forbid anyone
already in frame from transforming.**

**Small faces.** At 736×416 a face in a medium shot is 20–30 px. Identity cannot survive
there. Six clips were rejected purely for face distortion. This is a resolution problem,
not a prompt problem — no wording fixes it. Reference frames are already 1672×941, so
raising megapixels needs no new assets.

**Dark scenes.** The daylight driving clip `14D` is among the cleanest in the film; the dim
interiors in scenes 13, 16 and 17 are the worst. Small face plus compressed tonal range
compounds. Rule: **light interiors generously even when the mood is sombre.**

**Counting without a number.** "They repeatedly offer the chair" produced either one limp
gesture or a blur. "Exactly three offer-and-refusal exchanges, no more and no fewer"
produced three. Rule: **every countable action states its integer.**

## Prompts — what works

**Quotation marks mean speech, and only speech.** A quoted string with no named speaker
gets assigned to the nearest person in the beat. This is the single highest-value rule
found. The one keeper on the `03 → 04` shot differed from the reject before it by putting
`Narrator speaking` in front of the quote.

**Narration is never quoted.** Write it plain: `Narration over, off screen: …`. It only
exists to time the picture — H3 audio is discarded, so the model never needs to perform it.

**Per-beat mouth locks.** "Mouth closed" belongs inside the beat that gives someone
business, not only in a rule at the bottom. The model decides what a face does at the same
moment it decides what the body does.

**Positive cardinality.** "Exactly three people are in this shot… no one enters" works.
The negative-prompt token `duplicate person` did not prevent two Kents in `13A`.

**Naming a discriminator between similar characters.** The two visitors wear near-identical
suits; the standing one has a white pocket square. Stating that stops role swaps.

## Prompts — what does not work

**Repetition.** Saying a thing twice is not emphasis; the model has to reconcile two copies
and guess which governs. 73 of 78 clips with dialogue were sending each spoken line to the
model **twice** — once in the prompt body, once in the AUDIO LOCK the runner appends.

**Contradiction after an edit.** Adding a line of dialogue leaves stale absolutes behind:
"nobody speaks to anybody" three sentences below a character who now speaks. Two hand-edits
both had this.

**Copying prompt text out of the CSV.** CSV wraps fields in quotes and doubles internal
quotes. **0 of 7 quote-wrapped prompts were ever kept.** Copy from `prompts/<clip>.txt`.

**Describing something not in the shot.** Several opening prompts lit "the Narrator" in
shots he isn't in. Anything you tell the model to light, it may draw.

## Review — what works

**ComfyUI's PNG metadata is a complete record.** Every generation writes a PNG with the
full API graph embedded: prompt text, both anchor filenames, seed, steps, resolution,
duration, every model path. The whole session is reconstructable after the fact.
`work/analyze_takes.py` and `work/scan_manual_runs.py` read it.

**Pairing a take to its keeper needs two signals.** Timestamp alone produced a false match
— a Clipchamp export landing near a render read as its keeper. Require timestamp proximity
**and** duration equal to frames ÷ 24.

**Wiring faults are detectable.** 14 takes loaded a second anchor image never connected to
the model; anyone appearing only in that frame was invented. Two more used the same image
as both first and last frame. Now flagged automatically.

## Review — what does not work

**Contact sheets for faces.** At reduced scale a face is unreadable. A machine pass over
sheets caught every large-area fault — invented crowds, duplicate bodies, camera jumps,
burned-in text — and missed **every** face-level fault. Rule: **"no fault visible at
reduced scale" means not reviewed, not passed.** Faces need native-resolution crops.

**Instability scores as verdicts.** `16A` scored highest of anything unreviewed and was a
clean pass — the spike was a character standing up. Useful for ranking what to look at
first; never a reason to reject.

**Trusting the progress counter.** "N/124 valid clips" counts renders, not approvals.
124/124 was reached on 2026-08-12; human acceptance stands at 43 with 22 rejects found in a
sample of 30.

## Audio

**Kokoro is the working path and is already built.** `EQUAL_SHARES_DIALOGUE_TIMELINE.wav`,
1266.000 s, 48 kHz stereo, 113 segments, one fixed voice per character. A fixed voice
cannot drift, which was the whole problem. 157 voice files on disk.

**H3 voices drift per clip.** Same mechanism as faces — the model re-derives a voice from
the prompt every time. Not fixable by retrying.

**A clone reference must come from one take.** Concatenating two takes to reach a length
minimum splices two different-sounding performances and teaches the clone an average.

**Ten reference samples exist**, 12–15 s each, extracted and normalised: Narrator, Kent,
Doris, Doris recording, Avery, Terminal voice, Faith White, Ryann Sally, Volunteer,
Housing representative.

**RVC is not the same tool as a zero-shot cloner, and the sample sizing differs.**
XTTS/F5/Chatterbox clone zero-shot from 6–15 s — the reference samples suit them. RVC
*trains* a model and wants minutes, so it should be trained on all of a character's speech
pulled from the 124 rendered clips instead: Kent ~201 s, Narrator ~169 s, Ryann ~95 s,
Avery ~74 s, Doris ~42 s, Faith White ~28 s, Volunteer ~22 s, Housing rep ~17 s. The
remaining eight have 2–6.5 s in the whole film and stay on Kokoro.

**Gibberish speech does not block voice work.** RVC learns timbre, not words, so invented
syllables train a voice model as well as real dialogue. Of 138 validation transcripts, 132
contain recognised speech, median 19 words. Only `04C`, `06A`, `14B`, `14E`, `16E` and
`17C` are silent. What does poison training is a second voice inside the assigned window,
invented music under the speech, or a window that is actually room tone — filter for those,
not for intelligibility.

**RVC preserves duration**, which is why it was chosen over a TTS cloner. Kokoro already
holds the correct words and timing across 1266.000 s; conversion changes timbre only, so
the timeline never has to be rebuilt. Any converted file whose duration differs from its
input is a failure, not a variation.

**RVC does not require `rmvpe.pt`.** `harvest` and `pm` pitch extraction are algorithmic
and need no download. `rmvpe` is a quality upgrade for later.

### Harvest vs rmvpe

The brief says to use `harvest` to avoid downloading `rmvpe.pt`. **harvest is not
implemented in this Applio version.** The `extract.py` `compute_f0()` only has branches
for `crepe`, `crepe-tiny`, `rmvpe`, and `fcpe`. When `f0_method="harvest"` is passed,
`f0` is never assigned and every extraction throws `"cannot access local variable 'f0'
where it is not associated with a value"`, producing an empty filelist and a training
run with zero valid samples.

Since `rmvpe.pt` is already on disk, the bandwidth concern does not apply. **Use
`rmvpe` for all future RVC training and inference in this installation.**

### assets/config.json was missing

Applio's `extract_model()` reads `assets/config.json` for the `model_author` field. The
file was absent, so the per-epoch checkpoint saving failed silently after every epoch
("An error occurred extracting the model"). Training itself succeeded and wrote
`G_<iter>.pth` / `D_<iter>.pth`. Fix: copy `assets/config_template.json` to
`assets/config.json`. Done on 2026-08-12.

## Toward the automation program

Notes for the eventual self-running build, not tasks.

**What is already chained:** the render loop and final assembly. Everything else is a
standalone command. See `README.md` for the map.

**What the automation will need that does not exist yet:**

1. A single orchestrator that owns phase order — priority queue → render → review gate →
   audio → assemble → audit — rather than the current set of independent scripts.
2. Priority queue consumption in the supervisor.
3. A real review gate. Human acceptance is the only step that cannot be automated, so the
   program must be designed to *stop cleanly* and resume, the way the voice gate does.
4. Pre-flight validation as a hard gate: prompt integrity, anchor wiring, aspect ratio,
   frame count. Every one of these has already cost a batch of renders.
5. Post-render fault detection: unwired anchors, identical anchors, quote-wrapped prompts,
   instability spikes. All exist as separate tools; they should run automatically after
   each clip.

**Local LLM assistant — noted, not built.** The intent is a local model that reads the
logs, manifests, audit files and review notes and produces the kind of summary an agent
gives now, so state can be understood without reading everything by hand. Requirements
when the time comes: read-only over `outputs/equal_shares/`, summarise render progress,
acceptance counts, open faults and what changed since last asked. Ollama is already
installed and was used for Open Interpreter with `qwen2.5-coder:14b` pinned to CPU
(`num_gpu=0`) so it does not compete with H3 for VRAM — that pattern is the right one to
reuse.

## Resolution — the sweet spot, found 2026-08-12

**0.9 MP is the setting.** Tested on `00J` (aerial descent to Kent, single anchor, 12 s,
294 frames — the hardest case in the film for camera control):

| megapixels | dims | latent vs 0.3 | 60 px face lands at | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.3 | 736×416 | 1.00× | 27 px | faces warped, camera perfect |
| 0.4 | 864×480 | 1.35× | 31 px | faces warped, camera perfect |
| **0.9** | **1248×704** | **2.87×** | **45 px** | **faces fixed, camera held** |
| 1.0 | 1312×736 | 3.15× | 47 px | faces fixed, **camera broke** |

**There are two opposing failure modes and 0.9 MP sits between them.**

Too low and faces deform — not enough pixels to hold identity. Too high and the model loses
its grip on the anchor: at 1 MP `00J` descended past Kent, travelled through the ground, and
rendered a *second* cityscape with Kent repeating the same move. That is not a glitch, it is
the model losing the anchor, re-reading the prompt, and starting the described shot over.

**The mechanism is conditioning dilution.** One anchor frame has to constrain the whole
latent volume. At 3.15× the volume, with the same 20 steps and the same single anchor over
294 frames, the anchor no longer dominates. Camera-movement shots break first because they
are already being told to travel.

**The window is narrow — roughly 10% of latent volume between working and broken.** Do not
assume 1.0 MP is "basically the same as 0.9". It is not.

**What this predicts.** The clips most at risk when raising resolution are **single anchor +
camera movement**: `00J`, `00K`, `00L`, `00M`, `00N`, `13C`, `14D`, `21C`, `30C`. Dual-anchor
clips should tolerate the bump better because both ends are pinned. Static single-anchor
shots should also be fine.

**Mitigations if a clip still wanders at 0.9 MP**, in order of leverage:

1. **Add a closing frame.** Biggest lever and usually free — the frame often already exists
   as the next clip's opener. `00J` should end on `frames/scene_000/boundary_05.png`, which
   is exactly what `00K` opens on.
2. **Raise steps with resolution.** 20 steps resolving 2.87× more latent is not equivalent
   to 20 steps at 0.3 MP. Try 30–36.
3. **Shorten the shot.** Fewer frames is less room to drift.

**Cost.** 2.87× the latent means substantially longer renders than the ~8 min/clip baseline,
and more VRAM. Measure before committing to a full re-render pass.

## Speaker attribution — convention adopted 2026-08-12

Every prompt now carries a **SPEAKERS IN THIS SHOT** block before the dialogue, and every
dialogue line is tagged with the speaker's screen status. The purpose is that there is never
any ambiguity about who is talking or whether their mouth should move.

```
SPEAKERS IN THIS SHOT
Narrator — OFF-SCREEN voice only. He is never visible in this shot, and no one on screen
is him. Nobody in frame mouths his words.
Male Visitor One — ON-SCREEN. Visible in this shot; their mouth moves only to their own
assigned line and is closed at all other times.
Everyone else in frame is silent for the whole shot.

DIALOGUE
[1s-9s] Narrator, OFF-SCREEN: "..."
[3s-5s] Male Visitor Two, ON-SCREEN: "..."
```

Five statuses: `ON-SCREEN`, `OFF-SCREEN`, `ON-SCREEN THEN OFF` (`00C`, camera passes him),
`OFF-SCREEN THEN ON` (`00I`, `00K`, he walks in), `DEVICE VOICE` (`Terminal voice`,
`Doris recording` — comes from a machine, no human mouths it).

**Screen status could not be inferred from the config and is asserted, not derived.** Two
heuristics were tried and both failed: matching "off screen" phrases in the prompt gave
false positives from the shot-list preamble, and reading the `Character continuity:` block
put Kent off-screen for 36 lines because that block only names characters needing identity
preservation, not everyone present. The map now lives in
`work/apply_speaker_attribution.py`: the Narrator is mapped per clip from each clip's own
action text, `Terminal voice` and `Doris recording` are device voices, and **everything else
defaults to ON-SCREEN**. Correct that file if any character is wrong.

**The two prompt variants diverge here and it matters.** The config holds the runner variant,
where the dialogue block names the speaker and window but omits the quoted words, because
`minimax_story_runner.py` appends an AUDIO LOCK carrying them. The `prompts/*.txt` files are
the manual-paste variant and carry the quoted line in full, because nothing appends a lock on
that path. Regenerating the .txt files straight from the config silently strips the dialogue
— it happened once. Always rebuild them through the manual-variant path.

### The first generation that spoke correctly

words, correct timing, no gibberish. First time in this project.

Graph: `minimax_h3_ref2va_pruned_nvfp4.safetensors` on `MiniMaxH3ReferenceToVideo`, **0.2 MP**,
16:9, multiple 32, 20 steps, `res_multistep`/`simple`, denoise 1.0, 24 fps, 8-bit,
`ref_image_size: match`.

**The reference sockets are a dynamic list**: `ref_images.ref_image_0`,
`ref_audios.ref_audio_0`, `ref_audio_1`, … A second character in a scene gets
`ref_audio_1`. That was the open question and it is answered.

The audio reference came from `VHS_LoadVideoPath` **output 2** (the audio output) on
`video/1.mp4`, with `select_every_nth: 3` decimating the frames. A `LoadAudio` on a trimmed
WAV does the same job with less risk of the picture leaking in.

### The prompt is the bigger half of that result

Four differences from the 124 story prompts, all now applied by
`work/build_audio_pass_prompts.py`:

1. **A REFERENCE JOBS block at the top** giving every reference an explicit job —
   `ref_audio_0` is voice only, `ref_image_0` is the opening composition.
2. **`SHOT LIST and DIALOGUE TIMING` is one section**, not two.
3. **The words sit inside the beat that contains them**, with speaker and screen status in
   the same sentence: `Narrator says off screen "…"` / `Narrator continues "…"`.
4. **The dialogue appears exactly once.** No DIALOGUE block, no AUDIO LOCK.

The story prompts said `Narration phrase 1 of the assigned line plays over` in the beat and
kept the words elsewhere. That indirection is the most likely cause of the timing failure —
the model had to work out which words belonged to which second.

### Lipsync — the tool on disk is the wrong shape

Only Sonic is installed: `models/sonic/UNet.pth`, `models/sonicLipsyncFor_comfyui/sonic/*`,
`workflows/DBZ-Voice-Sonic-Lipsync.json`. That workflow is
`LoadImage → SONICTLoader → SONIC_PreData → SONICSampler` on an `ImageOnlyCheckpointLoader`
— **it animates one still portrait from audio.** It cannot re-lipsync an existing
15-second two-hander while preserving the original motion.

Video-to-video options: Wav2Lip ~500 MB (soft at 1248×704, its mouth crop is 96×96),
LatentSync ~5 GB (out of budget on a hotspot). Both blocked on bandwidth.

**Do not lock mouths closed for a lipsync pass.** Lipsync models mask and regenerate the
lower face, so a still mouth buys nothing, and a rigid face under a moving mouth reads as
pasted-on. More importantly, dialogue in the prompt drives the turn, the gesture and the
reaction — strip the lines and H3 stops performing the scene.

lower face, so a still mouth buys nothing, and a rigid face under a moving mouth reads as
pasted-on. More importantly, dialogue in the prompt drives the turn, the gesture and the
reaction — strip the lines and H3 stops performing the scene.

## 2026-08-13 (later) — the voice references were wrong, and how it was caught

**The user listened to `voices/kent/h3_voice_ref.wav` and heard a few seconds of
speech in a mostly-empty 15 seconds.** Two automated checks had passed it. Both
were measuring the wrong thing.

**Fault 1 — the scripted window is not the delivered window.** v1 cut straight
from `dialogue_timing`. That is when a line is *supposed* to be spoken. H3 comes
in early by about a second and often does not fill the window at all.

**Fault 2 — level cannot tell speech from noise.** Kent's reference came from
`14D`, the **driving clip**. Mean −19.8 dB and 100% "voiced" under an ffmpeg
`silencedetect=noise=-35dB` gate, because road and engine noise never drops
below the gate. It was 14.6 s of car interior containing ~2 s of dialogue.

Its envelope gives it away: floor −25.4 dB, peak −10.4 dB, **no silence
anywhere**. Real speech has gaps. Continuous loud content with a 15 dB range is
noise, not a performance.

### `work/speech_density.py` — score speech, not level

Speech puts most of its energy in roughly 300–3400 Hz; engine rumble sits below
300 Hz. Per-frame band ratio separates them cleanly.

**Calibrated against ground truth, not tuned by eye:**

| set | file | want |
|---|---|---|
| positive | Kokoro TTS lines (pure clean speech) | > 0.85 |
| positive | `1.mp4`, `MiniMax_H3_00002_.mp4` | > 0.40 |
| negative | Kent's `14D` window (car interior) | < 0.30 |

Final: `BAND_RATIO_MIN=0.25`, `REL_FLOOR_DB=35`, `BRIDGE_GAP=0.5`. Scores 0.82–0.87
on Kokoro, 0.56–0.76 on real takes, **0.20 on the driving clip**.

**An early band gate of 0.45 scored a pure Kokoro speech file at 35%**, because a
deep male voice puts a lot of energy in its fundamental below 300 Hz. Always
calibrate against a positive *and* a negative. One file will mislead you.

The syllable-modulation gate (3–9 Hz envelope energy) is implemented but disabled
— at any threshold high enough to matter it also rejected genuine speech. Band
ratio alone suffices here.

### The selection rule that replaced it

**Cheap filter first, from the script:** sole speaker in the clip, and scripted
lines covering ≥55% of its duration. Free, and it eliminates almost everything
unsuitable. **Then confirm from the audio:** one contiguous speaking passage,
internal gaps ≤1.0 s, ≥60% actual speech.

**One contiguous passage from one take. Never stitched.** Splicing two passages
teaches an average of two deliveries — the drift the reference exists to prevent.

## 2026-08-15 — the prompt format was wrong all along

Full spec now in `docs/H3_PROMPT_RULES.md`. This entry records how it was found.

### The project had never used H3's native prompt format

Reading the official guides — the ComfyUI H3 tutorial plus MiniMax's own
`VIDEO_PROMPT_WRITING_GUIDE_ref_en.md` — showed the R2V format is six named
sections: `subject_definitions`, `summary`, `retention_analysis`,
`detailed_description`, `overall_soundscape`, `non_diegetic_music`. The project
had none of them.

chunks.heading: ## 2026-08-15 — the prompt format was wrong all along
chunks.text:
.

### The project had never used H3's native prompt format

Reading the official guides — the ComfyUI H3 tutorial plus MiniMax's own
`VIDEO_PROMPT_WRITING_GUIDE_ref_en.md` — showed the R2V format is six named
sections: `subject_definitions`, `summary`, `retention_analysis`,
`detailed_description`, `overall_soundscape`, `non_diegetic_music`. The project
had none of them.

### `retention_analysis` was the doubled-voice bug

Every reference needs a line declaring its relationship to the output. For audio
the markers are `fully_copy`, `partially_copy`, `reference`, `weak_reference`.

Nothing in any prompt had ever told H3 that the voice master was a **reference**
rather than a source to **copy**. A partial copy of the master laid under freshly
generated speech is exactly the quieter-second-vocal symptom that had blocked the
project for days, and that no amount of prose forbidding echo or chorus removed.

Adding one line fixed it on the first attempt:

```
<Audio 1>: reference - S1 follows <Audio 1>'s voice timbre, pitch, accent, and
delivery without copying the original signal; none of its words, breaths, or
room tone appear in the target video.
```

**Lesson: a missing required section is invisible. Absent structure produced a
default behaviour, and the default was wrong.**

### Two gibberish faults, both positional, both found by listening

**Fault 1 — a split line.** A hand-written `00B` prompt split the Narrator's
sentence across two beats at `…so they are no longer without,` /
`but in the process…`. The render put about a second of gibberish at exactly that
seam. Two quoted fragments read as two utterances and H3 fills the gap between
them. **One scripted line, one `<d>` block, always.**

**Fault 2 — delivery prose after the tag.** The user's own diagnosis, and
correct: text referring to a character speaking, placed after `</d>`, reads as
speech still in progress. `00B` carried `The Narrator's delivery cools.`
immediately after the tag and the model kept talking past the scripted words,
producing a tail of gibberish.

The guide's examples confirm it — two of its three dialogue examples close the
speaker's mouth in the clause right after `</d>`:

> `…<d>[English] Hey! Watch your dog!</d> She closes her lips and guards the cookie…`

So: **delivery before the tag, mouth closes after it.**

### Other format corrections

- **Dialogue is `<d>[English] …</d>`.** Double quotes are for on-screen lettering
  only. This inverts the project's old rule, which existed because the previous
  format had no `<d>` tag.
- **`[Shot N]` marks a cut, not a beat.** A continuous take is one `[Shot 1]`
  with no timestamp; timing inside it is prose. The `[0-1 s]` bracket notation
  was never the model's grammar.
- **Speaker IDs `(S1)`, `(S2)`**, by order of first vocal event.
- **Identity-only images get no `<Picture N>` entry** — cite them inside the
  `<Subject N>` definition. Standalone picture entries are frame anchors only.
- **`ref_image_size: max`** keeps a 2048px short edge for stronger identity
  fidelity; the project has always run `match`, which downscales references at
  the moment identity is decided. Untested here — worth one clip.
- The docs name the R2V checkpoint `ref2va_pruned_int8_convrot`; this project
  runs the more aggressively quantised `nvfp4`. Untested, and a multi-GB
  download, so blocked on bandwidth.

### Two converter bugs worth not repeating

`work/build_native_r2v_prompts.py` regenerates all 124.

1. Header detection required full capitalisation, so `SHOT LIST and DIALOGUE
   TIMING` — lowercase "and" — was missed and the first run wrote **124 prompts
   with no dialogue at all**. A structural check caught it; reading one file
   would not have.
2. The mouth-close clause was appended to every line, telling a character with
   two lines to fall silent before the second. Now only a speaker's final line
   closes the shot.

Verified on every run: 78 dialogue clips, one `<d>` per scripted line, zero
splits, exact word fidelity against `dialogue_timing`, a mouth-close after every
`</d>`, no delivery prose after any `</d>`, and correct pronoun/verb agreement.
