chunks.text:
# Resource and safety hardening — 2026-08-25

## What changed

- `ollama_client.py` now accepts and transmits an explicit `keep_alive` value.
  Interactive agent turns retain the selected model for five minutes; planner
  and queued Ollama vision calls request zero retention.
- `media_queue.py` records `interactive` or `batch` priority, drains direct
  operator work first while preserving FIFO within each tier, and can return a
  pre-empted processing job to pending with its audit history intact.
- `media_tools.py` and `media_watcher.py` re-check for a render between video
  frames/action batches. A render pre-empts media work cooperatively; it never
  kills the render or marks a partial analysis as done.
- `tools.py` adds `propose_file_diff`, a protected-file-aware unified-diff
  preview. `agent.py` directs the model to preview a file edit before applying
  one.

## Why

Background model retention could delay VRAM recovery; old bulk media work could
delay a live attachment; and a render arriving mid-video analysis used to leave
the watcher with no safe recovery path. Direct file edits also needed an
operator-visible review step.

## Evidence and verification

- `test_native_tool_calling.py` verifies native schema registration, protected
  diff refusal, non-destructive diff output, and explicit keep-alive payloads.
- `test_media_gpu_queue.py` verifies priority order, duplicate promotion, and
  invalid-priority refusal.
- `test_media_preemption.py` verifies a pre-empted video action job returns to
  pending with a preserved audit record.
- Full local-agent test suite, agentic harness baseline, and 124/124 H3 prompt
  validation are run after this entry is written.

## Still unverified

- The exact 14B Ollama Flash Attention/q8 KV-cache comparison remains blocked
  because that exact primary model is not currently installed. No substitute
  model, live model load, render, or configuration switch was used here.
- A real CPU Whisper transcription remains a separately requested live model
  check; regression tests verify the available runtime gate and routing without
  loading Whisper during every test run.

# 2026-08-25 — Sideband Tier B Android build status

## What was attempted

The opt-in forked-Sideband Android debug build was resumed in its isolated WSL
toolchain. This work is limited to the companion-phone package; it did not
start ComfyUI, a render, a desktop model, or the Equal Shares pipeline.

## Progress

- The original host-Python recipe lacked the pip helper expected by the pinned
  python-for-android version. The staged build-only recipe was repaired with
  the upstream-compatible `pip`/`fix_pip_shebangs` helpers.
- NumPy then progressed through the dependency collection and into its Android
  recipe, proving the first repair was effective.

## Current blocker

The pinned python-for-android NumPy recipe selects the modern Meson build path.
Its isolated build environment still cannot import `mesonpy`, even after the
host environment has the package. No APK was produced.

This is a packaging compatibility issue, not a runtime or transport failure.
Do not claim Tier B is installable until a signed/debug APK exists and is
installed on a device. Tier A remains the working, paired LXMF path.

## Attempts recorded

- Confirmed `sideband/audioproc.py` imports NumPy, so NumPy cannot be removed
  from the package requirements.
- Added a staged NumPy-recipe overlay that exposes the host recipe's
  site-packages path in both host and compile environments.
- The overlay was loaded by the build, but the isolated PEP 517 environment
  still failed to import `mesonpy`. Repeating that same build will not provide
  new evidence.

## Next safe action

Make a versioned local NumPy recipe compatible with the pinned
python-for-android/Android-NDK combination, or move the build to a Sideband
source/toolchain revision whose NumPy recipe is known to work. Preserve the
current cache and do not reset the desktop agent or media pipeline.

chunks.text:
# 2026-08-26 — exact Qwen2.5-VL lifecycle benchmark, run 1

## Scope

One controlled, unattended lifecycle run using only the approved local pair:

- `Qwen2.5-VL-7B-NSFW-Caption-V4.Q4_K_M.local.gguf`
- `Qwen2.5-VL-7B-NSFW-Caption-V4.mmproj-Q8_0.local.gguf`

The input was a synthetic geometric still created only for this measurement.
No user upload, project media, render, download, or ComfyUI job was used.

## Measured evidence

Metadata-only report:
`artifacts/benchmarks/qwen25_vl_lifecycle_2026-08-26.json`.

| Metric | Result |
|---|---:|
| GPU before | 0 MB |
| Cold lazy load | 52.844 s |
| GPU after load | 10,530 MB |
| First factual analysis | 30.281 s; non-empty |
| GPU after first analysis | 10,624 MB |
| Second factual analysis | 0.375 s; non-empty |
| GPU after second analysis | 10,628 MB |
| Release to idle | 22.187 s |
| GPU after release | 0 MB |

The report identifies runtime `llama.cpp` and exact model
`qwen25-vl-nsfw-caption:v4-q4_k_m`; it stores result hashes and sizes, not
caption text, image content, local file paths, or user information.

## Lifecycle reliability repair

The benchmark exposed a Windows ownership-probe flaw: `os.kill(pid, 0)` can
return access-denied for a live process, which the old helper treated as gone.
`capabilities._runtime_pid_alive()` now uses `tasklist` on Windows and treats a
failed probe as still live. Cleanup therefore fails safe and preserves its
ownership record rather than falsely claiming VRAM was released.

The first run's VLM cleanup needed a one-time elevated termination of the exact
owned `llama-server` process after the old probe misreported it. The repaired
probe is covered by `local_agent/test_qwen25_release.py` (2/2). Final telemetry
after cleanup: 0% GPU, 0 MB VRAM, 31 C.

## Remaining evidence

## Follow-up runs and negative controls

Two more identical synthetic-image runs completed after the first run. All
three used the same exact model/runtime, returned the same two output hashes,
peaked at 10,626–10,628 MB, and released to 0 MB.

| Run | Process-start/load s | First analysis s | Second analysis s | Release s |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 52.844 | 30.281 | 0.375 | 22.187 |
| 2 | 38.015 | 2.640 | 0.407 | 2.015 |
| 3 | 5.563 | 1.141 | 0.406 | 2.047 |

The later launch times are materially faster because Windows retained filesystem
and/or driver caches after run 1. Therefore the three values are **not** a
reproducible cold-load metric and must not be averaged or published as one.
They do establish stable exact-model output, VRAM peak, warm-process latency,
and release behavior.

Two negative controls were added and passed without loading any model:

- an ordinary text chat cannot call the exact VLM runtime;
- active render ownership blocks VLM work before a VRAM/runtime check.

Evidence: native tool suite 22/22; exact-Qwen watcher suite 5/5;
`test_qwen25_release.py` 2/2; H3 validator 124/124. No chat model or ComfyUI
render was started for these controls.

chunks.text:
# 2026-08-27 — Architectural safety locks

## Completed high-priority fixes

### Verified GPU eviction before CPU routing

`local_agent/router.py` now unloads every resident local Ollama GPU model and
polls `/api/ps` for up to 15 seconds before allowing a CPU handoff. A stale,
unreadable, or timed-out inventory is an explicit safe refusal rather than a
possible VRAM collision with ComfyUI. Status polling never triggers eviction.

### Lease-before-send phone scheduling

`local_agent/phone_scheduler.py` now writes a durable dispatch lease before it
queues any LXMF message. A second bridge loop observes that lease and cannot
send the same counter. If a process dies while a send result is unknown, the
job becomes `uncertain`; it is not silently retried and duplicated over mesh.

### Bounded feedback encryption queue

`local_agent/feedback_manager.py` now bounds its idle-only AES-GCM work queue
to 256 records. On overflow, the oldest record is displaced and a metadata-only
fingerprint is quarantined. Records that cannot be encrypted after three tries
are likewise quarantined without persisting a plaintext payload.

## Verification

- `python local_agent/test_phone_scheduler.py` — 12 passed.
- `python local_agent/test_feedback.py` — 7 passed.

`local_agent/artifacts.py` now keeps oversized tool results in a local,
fingerprinted JSON artifact and returns a compact pointer for the live model
context. `agent.py` applies that boundary to every tool result at 2,400
characters. The GUI/audit event keeps its operator-facing output behavior,
while the next model hop avoids reprocessing a giant raw response.

- `python local_agent/test_artifacts.py` — 3 passed.

  end-to-end multi-hop artifact-pointer check.

and scoped-project prefix renderers. `agent.system_prompt()` now assembles them
in one stable order before dynamic turn evidence, helping compatible local
Ollama/llama.cpp runners reuse their prefix/KV cache across turns.

# 2026-08-27 — Opt-in read-only loop-engineering controller

## What changed

- Added `local_agent/loop_controller.py`, a stdlib-only durable controller for
  explicit verification goals.
- Its fixed check registry contains only local non-rendering test and validation
  commands. Its only optional tool handoff is the existing non-writing diff
  preview after a failure and explicit request; it never starts a model,
  downloads, accesses the network, edits a project file, or controls ComfyUI.
- Added durable, redacted state under `local_agent/runtime/loop_engineering/`:
  goal records, one-result-per-run audit logs, triage records, review queue,
  configuration, and a compact status file.
- Added explicit default-off `loop_enabled` state. One `run-once` call executes
  exactly one pending fixed check; success advances to the next check only on a
  future invocation, while failure stops at `needs_operator` and opens a
  review record.
- Added a read-only status summary to the existing localhost app. It has no
  endpoint that can enable or run a loop.
- Added controller documentation and `test_loop_controller.py` coverage.
- Added a 20-scenario golden safety/maintenance contract and an evidence-only
  metrics report. They make no model calls and report unknown metrics as
  unmeasured instead of estimating them from nothing.
- Added a Phase-2 review-only repair-proposal handoff: only after a failed,
  operator-reviewed fixed check and an explicit request, it can call the
  existing non-writing unified-diff tool. It stores only a redacted audit item
  and diff hash; it cannot apply a file edit or approve its own proposal.
- Added `loop_verifiers.py`, a separate deterministic evidence registry for
  SHA-256 checks, JSON required-key checks, and captured-result predicates. It
  has no command runner, network access, model call, or authority to mark a
  goal complete.

## Why

This implements the safe first phase of the Loop Engineering design: durable
state, bounded discovery, constrained action, deterministic verification, and
an operator gate. It does not grant the agent recursive or self-modifying
authority.

- `python local_agent/test_loop_evaluation.py`

# 2026-08-27 — Loop Engineering design and persistent goal

## Request

The operator asked the local-agent project to remember Addy Osmani's June 7,
2026 “Loop Engineering” article and determine how its approach applies here.

## Recorded

The operator's interest is stored as durable local-agent memory id 40. The
preference is for measured, safety-gated loops with persistent state,
discovery/triage, separate implementation and verification, explicit
evaluations, and operator review. It explicitly excludes loops that bypass
render, download, permission, or evidence safeguards.

## Design added

`local_agent/UPGRADE/22_loop_engineering.md` maps the article's automation,
state, skill, connector, and independent-verifier ideas onto existing local
agent components. It defines a phased build beginning with read-only discovery
and testable state, then approved repair proposals, deterministic verification,
and finally worktree-isolated parallel work.

## Not enabled

No automation, render, download, model load, model training, unattended edit,
or remote permission was enabled by this design record. Implementation remains
operator-approved and must begin with the Phase 0 baseline/evaluation work.

chunks.heading: # 2026-08-27 — optional-dependency guards; scheduler live test pending
chunks.text:
# 2026-08-27 — optional-dependency guards; scheduler live test pending

## What changed

### Job 2 — optional package import guards (complete)

Four files modified, one new test file created.

#### `local_agent/exemplar_embeddings.py`

The two chromadb imports (`import chromadb` and `from chromadb.config import
Settings`) were bare top-level statements. Any missing or broken chromadb
installation raised `ImportError` at import time, preventing `agent.py` and
`server.py` from loading at all.

**Change:** wrapped in try/except ImportError. On failure: `_CHROMADB_AVAILABLE
= False`, `_CHROMADB_REASON` carries the package name and install command.

Five public functions guarded:

| function | behaviour when chromadb absent |
|---|---|
| `retrieve()` | raises `RuntimeError(_CHROMADB_REASON)` — not silently empty |
| `semantic_duplicate()` | returns `{"available": False, "reason": ..., "install": ...}` |
| `embed_record()` | returns `{"status": "unavailable", "reason": ..., "install": ...}` |
| `sync_approved()` | returns `{"embedded": 0, "unavailable": True, "reason": ...}` |
| `start_worker()` | returns immediately; no background thread starts |
| `_client()` | raises `RuntimeError(_CHROMADB_REASON)` (private guard for any missed path) |

`retrieve()` raises rather than returning `[]` because the existing caller in
`agent.py` already has `except Exception` around it and emits a named note.
Returning `[]` would be silent; raising is not.

#### `local_agent/feedback_manager.py`

`from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM` was a bare
top-level import. Missing cryptography prevented `server.py` from loading.

**Change:** wrapped in try/except ImportError. On failure: `_CRYPTOGRAPHY_AVAILABLE
= False`, `_CRYPTOGRAPHY_REASON` carries the package name and install command.

Four public functions guarded:

| function | behaviour when cryptography absent |
|---|---|
| `decrypt_envelope()` | returns `{"available": False, "reason": ..., "install": ...}` |
| `flush_pending()` | `_encrypt()` raises `RuntimeError`; flush re-raises it; no unencrypted file is written |
| `start_idle_worker()` | returns immediately; no background thread starts |
| `status()` | returns `{"available": False, "last_error": _CRYPTOGRAPHY_REASON, ...}` |

`enqueue()` is unchanged: it puts a record on `_PENDING`. If `flush_pending`
cannot encrypt, it leaves the record in the queue and re-raises — the record
stays in RAM and is never silently dropped or written in plaintext.

# 2026-08-27 — tool description collision fix

## What changed

**`local_agent/tools.py`** — two tool description strings modified.

### The observed problem

A 26-message phone conversation (`chats/87017e91b2ab4fac.json`, model
`huihui_ai/qwen3-abliterated:14b`) showed the model systematically choosing
`start_current_chat_render` over `schedule_phone_messages` when the user asked
to "send me a message every 10 seconds for 20 minutes, counting from 0".

The model responded with text descriptions of `start_current_chat_render
--duration 1200 --interval 10 --start 0` starting at message 5 and never
deviated. The user echoed the model's own output back three times. When the user
said "yes" at message 24, the model actually called `start_current_chat_render`
and received an H3 prompt-set error.

The model never called `schedule_phone_messages` once. The wiring is confirmed
working by `test_phone_scheduler` (10/10 green) and by `phone_schedule_audit.jsonl`
which shows earlier sessions successfully queuing messages to LXMF.

chunks.heading: ### The observed problem
chunks.text:
ree times. When the user
said "yes" at message 24, the model actually called `start_current_chat_render`
and received an H3 prompt-set error.

The model never called `schedule_phone_messages` once. The wiring is confirmed
working by `test_phone_scheduler` (10/10 green) and by `phone_schedule_audit.jsonl`
which shows earlier sessions successfully queuing messages to LXMF.

### Root cause

The `schedule_phone_messages` description ended with a single low-signal hint:
`Use for "message me every N seconds/minutes".` That hint appeared at the end
after the JSON schema and interval constraints, where it competed with the
H3-render context that saturated the system prompt from CLAUDE.md.
`start_current_chat_render` contained no explicit exclusion for messaging tasks,
so the model picked the more structurally prominent render tool and reinterpreted
`interval 10`, `duration 1200`, and `start 0` as render parameters.

### Change — `schedule_phone_messages`

Old (end of string):
```
interval 10-3600s, count 1-120, within 24h. Use for "message me every N seconds/minutes".
```

New (full replacement):
```
PERIODIC TEXT MESSAGES TO THIS PHONE — call this tool whenever the caller asks
to "send me a message every N seconds/minutes", "message me every", "text me
every", "keep messaging me", or "count up to me". This is NOT video rendering;
it sends repeating text messages back to the caller's phone only — the recipient
is always the caller and cannot be changed. {...schema...} interval 10-3600s,
count 1-120, within 24h.
```

All triggering phrases from the failure conversation are now named explicitly at
the front of the description. The anti-collision note `NOT video rendering`
appears in the body.

### Change — `start_current_chat_render`

Old (beginning):
```
Prepare and start the current chat's latest complete H3 prompt set...
```

New (beginning):
```
GPU VIDEO RENDERING ONLY — use this tool ONLY when the operator explicitly says
'render it' or 'start render' for H3 video generation. Never use this tool to
send periodic text messages or any other messaging task. Prepare and start...
```

The explicit exclusion eliminates the residual ambiguity that let the model
reinterpret a scheduling request as a render command.

## Verified after

Read-back of lines 1270 and 1280 confirmed the strings are in place. No
functional code was changed; the tool implementations are unchanged. Schema
count unchanged at 48.

## Still unverified

Whether the description change alone is sufficient to overcome `huihui_ai/
qwen3-abliterated:14b`'s tendency to latch onto the render tool when the system
prompt is heavy with CLAUDE.md render rules. This requires a live test: start a
fresh phone conversation with no prior render context, ask "send me a message
every 15 seconds five times counting from 0", and confirm the model calls
`schedule_phone_messages` without narrating.

chunks.heading: # 2026-08-27 — scheduled phone messages: the orphaned half connected
chunks.text:
# 2026-08-27 — scheduled phone messages: the orphaned half connected

## The reported failure

From the phone: *"start sending a message every 30 seconds for the next 20 or 30
minutes starting with 0 and counting up."* The agent replied as though it had
started. **Nothing was ever sent**, and its reply also mentioned permissions,
which had nothing to do with the request.

## Root cause — two missing connections, not one

`local_agent/phone_scheduler.py` already existed (created 2026-08-27 17:14) and
is complete and correct: durable JSON state, bounded intervals and counts,
per-identity isolation, an audit trail, and a `dispatch_due(send)` entry point.

It was **orphaned at both ends**:

1. **No tool registered it.** `tools.py` contained no scheduler entry — the only
   match for "schedul" was `scheduler="karras"`, a ComfyUI sampler argument. The
   model therefore had no way to create a schedule.
2. **Nothing called `dispatch_due`.** `lxmf_agent.py` never imported the module.
   Even a schedule created by hand would have sat in the file forever.

So the model had no capability, and did what a model does with no capability and
a confident-sounding request: it narrated success. It then reached for a gated
execution tool as a substitute, which is exactly where the unrelated permission
language came from. **The permission system behaved correctly** — it refused
something that should be refused. The bug was the absent feature behind it.

## What changed

### `tools.py` — three phone-only tools

| tool | |
|---|---|
| `schedule_phone_messages` | `{"message":"count {n}","interval_seconds":30,"count":40}`, optional `start` |
| `list_phone_schedules` | this phone's jobs and their status |
| `cancel_phone_schedule` | `{"job_id":"phone_schedule_..."}` |

**Source-bound by construction.** The recipient is always the calling identity,
injected by the trusted dispatch seam in `call()` — the same mechanism already
used for `__remote_render_identity`. There is **no recipient parameter in the
schema**, so the model cannot name, choose or forge a target. A desktop call has
no identity to inject and is refused with a clear message.

This is a new capability, not a relaxed permission. No existing gate was widened.

### `lxmf_agent.py` — the delivery half

- `_scheduled_send()` resolves the pairing and replies through the existing
  `_reply()` path with `kind="scheduled"`. If the pairing is no longer active it
  raises `ScheduleBlocked`, so revoking a phone stops its schedules rather than
  retrying forever.
- `drain_scheduled()` wraps `dispatch_due` and swallows its own errors — a
  scheduler fault must never kill the bridge loop.
- The existing 1-second `run()` loop now drains on every tick.

chunks.text:

- `drain_scheduled()` wraps `dispatch_due` and swallows its own errors — a

- The existing 1-second `run()` loop now drains on every tick.

## Verified

`local_agent/test_phone_scheduler.py`, **10 tests, all passing**:

- all three tools registered **with schemas**
- the schema exposes **no** `identity` / `recipient` / `to` / `target` / `address`
- a desktop call is refused
- a model-supplied `__remote_schedule_identity` is **stripped** and refused —
  the forgery path is closed
- a phone call binds to its caller
- **counts up correctly**: `count 0` at t, nothing at t+1s, then `count 1/2/3` at
  30-second intervals, and **no fifth message** after the count completes
- unpairing mid-run marks the job `blocked`, not retried
- a transient send failure does **not** increment `queued_count` — a failed queue
  is never recorded as a sent message
- the run loop really calls `drain_scheduled()`, and `_scheduled_send` reaches
  `_reply` with the right bytes, text and `scheduled` kind

Unaffected: 48 tools, 48 schemas, none missing; `project_state` still dispatches;
`validate_h3_prompt.py` still **124/124**.

## Still unverified

- **No message has been sent to the real phone yet.** Every test above uses an
  injected send callback. The first live run is the real test.
- Wording only: whether the model reliably chooses `schedule_phone_messages` for
  a plain request like "message me every 30 seconds" is unmeasured.
- The bridge must stay running for a schedule to continue; there is no catch-up
  for messages whose due time passed while it was stopped. `dispatch_due` sends
  one message per due job per tick, so a long outage does not produce a burst —
  but it does mean missed intervals are skipped, not replayed.

## Note for the operator

Limits are deliberate: interval **10–3600 s**, count **1–120**, total span within
**24 hours**. "Every 30 seconds for 30 minutes" is 60 messages — within range.

A queued LXMF message is **queued, not delivered**. The workstation cannot
promise radio delivery, and the tool's own response says so rather than claiming
success — which is the failure mode this entry exists to fix.

# 2026-08-28 — Correct false GPU-busy state from Codex desktop

## Fault

The router treated the Codex/ChatGPT desktop executable's small WDDM display
context as a foreign GPU compute process. With no ComfyUI listener, no render
owner, no resident Ollama model, 81 MB VRAM used, and 0% utilization, that still
forced the agent to CPU-only routing.

## Fix

- Classified `ChatGPT.exe` / Codex desktop alongside browser/Electron display
  contexts, which are already non-blocking telemetry on Windows WDDM.
- Preserved all real blockers: live queue ownership, port 8188, unknown GPU
  telemetry, high unowned VRAM, Python/ComfyUI compute processes, and all
  gateway permission controls.

## Verification

- Added regression coverage for the exact Codex UI process path and for a real
  foreign Python compute process.
- No model was loaded, evicted, or rendered while diagnosing or fixing this.

## Activation

The desktop launcher's revision is now `2026-08-28-gpu-idle-r63`, so it replaces
an earlier local-agent server and imports this router revision. This restart
only targets the loopback local-agent listener; it does not touch ComfyUI.

chunks.text:
# 2026-08-28 — LXMF bridge scheduler startup repair

## Fixed

`LXMFBridge.run()` called `self.drain_scheduled()`, although the scheduler
delivery adapter belongs to its transport-agnostic `BridgeCore` instance. The
bridge therefore opened the RNode and then crashed on its first timer tick with
`AttributeError: 'LXMFBridge' object has no attribute 'drain_scheduled'`.

The loop now calls `self.core.drain_scheduled()`. No scheduler policy, pairing
rule, permission boundary, or delivery semantics changed.

## Verification

- `python -m unittest test_phone_scheduler -v` from `local_agent/`: **12/12**
  passed, including source binding, durable pre-send leases, cancellation,
  no duplicate concurrent dispatch, and the bridge wiring assertion.
- A controlled four-second live bridge run opened `COM11`, configured the
  `Equal Shares RNode LoRa` transport at **914.875 MHz / 500 kHz / SF12 / CR5**,
  remained alive through the scheduler tick, and exited normally on its timer.
- The configured Wi-Fi AutoInterface still reports multicast echo failures.
  That does not prevent the independently configured USB LoRa transport and is
  not treated as successful Wi-Fi delivery.

## Still pending

The real paired-phone acceptance remains: receive five timed messages, cancel
one active schedule, and verify safe recovery across a bridge restart. LXMF
queueing alone is not claimed as phone delivery.

chunks.heading: # 2026-08-28 — Phone counter default and scheduler-test isolation
chunks.text:
# 2026-08-28 — Phone counter default and scheduler-test isolation

## Fixed

- `schedule_phone_messages` now treats an omitted `message` template as
  `"{n}"`. A natural phone request such as “send five messages, counting from
  0” can therefore schedule `0`, `1`, `2`, `3`, `4` even if the model omits a
  redundant presentation field. An explicitly supplied blank message remains
  invalid. The phone-only, source-bound recipient rule is unchanged.
- Its native function schema now makes `message` optional and documents the
  counter-only default.
- `phone_scheduler.py` resolves state and audit paths at call time rather than
  capturing the live runtime paths as Python default parameters. Scheduler
  tests now use their temporary queue as intended; they cannot create future
  fake jobs in the live phone queue.
- Successful queue audit records now preserve the counter that was actually
  queued. Previously `queued_count` was incremented before the record was
  written, making the evidence label one ahead of the message. Existing audit
  evidence remains unchanged; the bridge was restarted for the corrected logic.

## Evidence

- A real phone message reached the bridge over the paired LoRa route and the
  CPU agent selected `schedule_phone_messages`. The refusal was specifically
  `message must contain 1 to 500 characters`, caused by the omitted template;
  it was not a radio, pairing, or permission failure.
- `python -m unittest test_phone_scheduler -v`: **14/14 passed**, including
  the counter-only default, source binding, pre-send lease, cancellation, and
  bridge wiring tests, plus exact queued-counter audit evidence.
- The bridge was restarted after the patch so the live phone path uses the
  updated tool implementation.

## Live acceptance evidence

The paired phone identity `62ce…cdde` completed two five-message, 15-second
counter schedules over the RNode transport. For the final controlled run,
`phone_schedule_12c978519bce4130` reached `complete` with five queue attempts;
the operator confirmed receipt on the phone. This verifies the phone → bridge
→ CPU agent → scheduler → LoRa reply path. It does not yet replace the separate
cancel-midway and restart-during-active-schedule checks.

## Preservation

Existing runtime schedule/audit records were preserved. No evidence was
deleted or rewritten.

chunks.heading: # 2026-08-29 - GPU busy false positive: idle Steam client
chunks.text:
# 2026-08-29 - GPU busy false positive: idle Steam client

## Problem

On Windows WDDM, `nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps` reported the idle Steam
launcher (`steam.exe`) alongside ordinary desktop GPU contexts. The local-agent
router classified every non-browser process as a foreign compute owner, so this
small display allocation forced chats onto the CPU even when ComfyUI was closed,
port 8188 was not listening, no render owner was live, and GPU utilization was
zero.

## Change

- Added the Steam launcher executable to the router's explicit low-VRAM desktop
  display-context allowlist.
- Preserved every real GPU reservation boundary: live render queue ownership,
  ComfyUI on port 8188, unknown process owners, active game executables, and
  material foreign VRAM use above the 2500 MB threshold.
- Added a router regression case for an idle `steam.exe` context at 121 MB.

## Verification

`python -m unittest local_agent.test_router_switching -v` passes after this
change. The test suite does not load a model, start ComfyUI, or start a render.

checkpoints.

# 2026-08-29 — Pixel mobile sparse-runtime evaluation boundary

## What changed

- Added `docs/POWERINFER2_MOBILE_EDGE_PLAN_2026-08-29.md`, a staged Pixel 10
  Pro plan that distinguishes the PowerInfer-2 paper from the currently
  documented upstream Android SmallThinker runtime.
- Added an inert, stdlib-only
  `local_agent/worker_farm/termux_powerinfer2_edge_worker.py` gateway contract
  and offline tests. It limits phone jobs to small `edge_text_inference`
  requests, requires an HTTPS private-overlay gateway, launches a configured
  local binary with a shell-free argument list, and performs at most one job in
  its required initial `--once` mode.
- Updated the TODO, worker-farm README, and Claude/current-handoff notes with
  the same security and verification boundaries.

## Security and architecture decisions

- Pixel 10 Pro is Tensor G5/TPU hardware, not a Qualcomm/Hexagon device. No
  NNAPI/Tensor runtime path is claimed because the inspected upstream Android
  guide documents no such backend.
- Android NDK compilation belongs on an x86_64 Linux/WSL build host; the
  documented NDK host tools are not Termux arm64 executables.
- The phone cannot connect directly to the loopback Redis/Celery broker and
  must never receive the workstation broker password or AES key. A future
  private-overlay, per-device authenticated gateway is required before any
  phone worker is enabled.

## Deliberate non-changes

- Did not download, convert, compile, install, root, launch, or route a mobile
  model/runtime.
- Did not start a queue, service, render, ComfyUI, desktop PowerInfer process,
  or GPU workload.

## Evidence

- Upstream SmallThinker documentation inspected on 2026-08-29 describes an
  Android NDK arm64 build, sparse Q4_0 models, `libaio`/`liburing`, and notes a
  possible Termux root requirement for its memory-efficient path. It does not
  document NNAPI/QNN/Hexagon options.
- Google Pixel 10 Pro official specifications list Tensor G5 and 16 GB RAM.
- Offline test evidence is recorded alongside the contract after the command
  below succeeds; no mobile live claim is made:

  `python -m unittest local_agent.worker_farm.test_termux_powerinfer2_edge_worker -v`

## Why (blocked here)

All subsequent stages (`dump`, `train`, `convert`, `quantize`, `validate`, `bench`,
and the server launch) require compiled binaries from `setup`.

  execute            : True (intake run)

```

## prosparse-7b retirement rationale

`SparseLLM/prosparse-llama-2-7b` was the original `hf_id`. The downloaded
`config.json` shows `hidden_act: "fatrelu"` with `hidden_act_param: 0.01` and
`model_type: "sparsellama"` / `architectures: ["SparseLlamaForCausalLM"]`.

FATReLU(x) = max(x, threshold) is **not plain ReLU**. PowerInfer's CUDA solver
builds GPU index tensors from activation sparsity — it pre-computes which
neurons fire and routes computation accordingly. That analysis assumes exactly
relu(x) = max(x, 0): a neuron is either zero or positive with no floor.
FATReLU keeps neurons at ≥ 0.01 even when they would otherwise be zero, so
the sparsity pattern is materially different; the solver's offload decisions
would be made against an incorrect sparsity map. The risk is not a hard crash
— it is subtly wrong outputs that look plausible and are difficult to detect.

The gate (`pipeline_lib.relu_gate`) was correct to reject this. It is left
unchanged.

`PowerInfer/ReluLLaMA-7B` is the model the PowerInfer team actually built the
pipeline and paper results around: LLaMA-2-7B retrained to use plain ReLU in
place of SiLU, so every neuron is truly zero or positive with no floor.
Its config.json is expected to show `hidden_act: "relu"` and `model_type:
"llama"`, which the gate will accept without modification.

## relu-gate failure on prosparse-7b (context for the retirement decision)

After intake completed (all 16 files, exit 0), `relu-gate` was run immediately:

```json
{
  "ok": false,
  "hidden_act": "fatrelu",
  "model_type": "sparsellama",
  "architectures": ["SparseLlamaForCausalLM"],
  "reason": "FATReLU is not supported by PowerInfer",
  "shape_mismatches": ["model_type='sparsellama'"]
}
```

`SparseLLM/prosparse-llama-2-7b` (the `hf_id` in `models.json`) ships with
`hidden_act: "fatrelu"` and a custom `SparseLlamaForCausalLM` architecture.
The gate in `pipeline_lib.relu_gate()` has `fatrelu = act.startswith("fatrelu");
ok = act == expected_act.lower() and not fatrelu` — FATReLU is explicitly
excluded regardless of the threshold value (here `hidden_act_param: 0.01`).
`models.json` records `expected_hidden_act: "relu"` and `expected_model_type:
"llama"` for this target; neither matches.

The downloaded model IS the correct HuggingFace checkpoint (6 shards,
~26.9 GB total, matching ProSparse-LLaMA-2-7B); the gate is catching a real
property of the model, not a download error. FATReLU(x) = max(x, 0.01) is
not the same activation function as ReLU, and whether PowerInfer's CUDA
solver handles it correctly is an open question that the gate is designed to
force explicit human sign-off on.

**This gate should not be crossed without operator instruction.** See the
main report below for what the operator needs to decide.

- No render or ComfyUI process touched; GPU remains idle.

chunks.heading: # 2026-08-29 — Scheduled Sideband delivery fallback and final-outcome audit
chunks.text:
# 2026-08-29 — Scheduled Sideband delivery fallback and final-outcome audit

## Finding

A live six-message, 30-second phone schedule was created for the paired phone
identity and the scheduler submitted counters `0` through `5` to the LXMF
router. The phone received none. `queued to LXMF` was router submission, not
delivery evidence.

The bridge hard-coded every outbound message to LXMF `DIRECT`. That works for
the immediate answer while a phone link is open, but a later scheduled message
can have no active direct link even though the paired session has an established
ratchet.

## Fixed

- The bridge now follows Sideband's delivery selection: retain `DIRECT` while
  a delivery link exists; otherwise use compact opportunistic delivery when a
  ratchet exists for the paired destination.
- Every outbound message now records its eventual LXMF `delivered` or `failed`
  callback in `runtime/lxmf/outbound_delivery_audit.jsonl`, including method,
  state, request ID and message hash. Router submission remains explicitly
  distinct from receipt.
- Added mocked coverage for both link-present and ratchet-only routing cases.

## Verification boundary

The corrected bridge must be restarted before a live re-test. A phone receipt
is still required to claim live delivery; this change does not turn queued
records into proof of receipt.

# 2026-08-29 — Source backup snapshot policy

## What changed

- Added `work/New-LocalAgentSourceBackup.ps1`, a repeatable ZIP builder for
  source code and documentation. It safely skips unreadable filesystem entries
  instead of failing or attempting to alter them, and records the skipped count
  in its archive manifest. The first local dry run identified bundled Sideband,
  ADB, and generated-index binaries as out of scope; the builder now excludes
  those third-party/generated trees and nested ZIPs as intended.
- Added `docs/SOURCE_BACKUP_POLICY.md` and a tracked backup-hygiene section in
  `TODO.md`.

## Safety boundary

The backup excludes `.env`, paired identities, runtime stores/uploads,
virtual environments, model weights, media, generated outputs, logs, artifacts,
and archive evidence. It writes a scope manifest and SHA-256 so a cloud copy can
be checked. This protects source continuity without moving private runtime data
or pretending the ZIP is a complete evidence/media archive.

## Deliberate non-changes

- No source file, model, render, queue, ComfyUI process, or local-agent service
  was altered or started.
- No raw media/evidence/runtime archive was copied by this backup workflow.

chunks.heading: # 2026-08-29 — Worker-farm Docker credential-helper path repair
chunks.text:
# 2026-08-29 — Worker-farm Docker credential-helper path repair

## What changed

`local_agent/worker_farm/START_PHASE1_BROKER.ps1` now prepends Docker Desktop's
installed `resources\\bin` directory to **its own process** `PATH` when the
`docker-credential-desktop.exe` helper exists but is absent from `PATH`.

## Why

After Docker Desktop's runtime-socket recovery, the guarded loopback Redis
launcher reached the engine but Compose could not pull `redis:7-alpine` because
it could not locate `docker-credential-desktop`. The helper was installed at
the standard Docker Desktop location; only the launcher environment lacked its
directory.

## Safety / verification

- No credentials, Docker configuration, or system-wide environment variable was
  changed.
- The path change exists only for the launcher process.
- The failed pre-repair launcher stopped before creating the Redis container.
- The next step is to rerun the guarded broker launcher, verify its loopback
  binding, then start the CPU-only worker and benign sample separately.

Redis container's environment, in addition to using it in the Redis command.

## Why

The container correctly required the configured password and accepted loopback
connections, but the Compose health check used `$REDIS_PASSWORD` within the
container where that variable had not been supplied. It therefore stayed
`health: starting` despite a healthy server.

## Safety / verification

- The port remains `127.0.0.1:6379` only.
- The password is not printed, committed, or exported beyond the Redis
  container and the existing local `.env`.
- Recreating the Redis service applies only the checked-in health-check fix;

chunks.heading: # 2026-08-29 — worker_farm: distill_export was never registered on the real worker process
chunks.text:
# 2026-08-29 — worker_farm: distill_export was never registered on the real worker process

## Context

Found while re-reading `local_agent/worker_farm/*.py` to match existing patterns
before adding a new smoke-test task the same way. Before copying the pattern,
checked whether the existing one actually works end to end, rather than
assuming it does.

## Root cause

`worker.py` launches the real worker as:

```
celery -A local_agent.worker_farm.celery_app:app worker --queues ... --pool ...
```

That `-A` target only ever imports `celery_app.py`. `celery_app.py` builds the
`Celery(...)` app with no `include=` and no `autodiscover_tasks()`. `tasks.py`
(which defines `distill_export` behind `@app.task(...)`) is imported by
`submit_distillation.py` and by the test suite, but **never by the worker
process itself** — and `submit_distillation.py` dispatches by name via
`app.send_task("local_agent.worker_farm.tasks.distill_export", ...)`, not
`.delay()`, so the submitter succeeds and returns a task ID regardless of
whether the worker actually knows that task. `local_agent/worker_farm/__init__.py`
is a docstring only, so package import doesn't pull `tasks.py` in either.

Net effect: `RUN_PHASE1_SAMPLE.ps1` would appear to queue successfully, and the
worker would silently discard every job with Celery's standard "Received
unregistered task" behavior. Nothing in the existing 12-test suite caught this
— all of it tests task-body logic directly (`tasks._run_distill(...)`) or
patches `submit_distillation.app`, never the worker's actual app-loading path.

chunks.heading: ## Root cause
chunks.text:
`RUN_PHASE1_SAMPLE.ps1` would appear to queue successfully, and the
worker would silently discard every job with Celery's standard "Received
unregistered task" behavior. Nothing in the existing 12-test suite caught this
— all of it tests task-body logic directly (`tasks._run_distill(...)`) or
patches `submit_distillation.app`, never the worker's actual app-loading path.

## Verification

No live Redis was available in this sandbox, and none was needed — task
registration is decided entirely by Python import wiring, before any broker
connection is opened. Copied `celery_app.py`, `tasks.py`, `worker.py`,
`farm_core.py`, `job_registry.py`, `status.py`, `doctor.py`, `submit_distillation.py`,
and `test_farm_core.py` into an isolated sandbox tree, installed `celery==5.6.3`
and `cryptography` fresh, and used Celery's own `celery.app.utils.find_app`
(the exact function the `-A` flag resolves through) plus
`app.loader.import_default_modules()` (the exact call `celery worker` makes
during startup, before consuming) to reproduce the real load path without a
broker:

**Before fix** — `Celery(broker=..., backend=...)`, no `include=`:
```
registered tasks: ['celery.accumulate', 'celery.backend_cleanup', 'celery.chain',
'celery.chord', 'celery.chord_unlock', 'celery.chunks', 'celery.group', 'celery.map',
'celery.starmap']
distill_export registered: False
```

**After fix** — `include=["local_agent.worker_farm.tasks"]` added:
```
registered tasks: [..., 'local_agent.worker_farm.tasks.distill_export']
distill_export registered: True
```

Confirmed the `include=` list itself is not read eagerly at app-construction
time (so `celery_app.py`'s docstring promise — "importing this module never
starts a broker or worker" — still holds): right after `find_app()`,
`distill_export` is absent; it only appears after `import_default_modules()`
runs, matching real worker startup order.

## Changes

### `local_agent/worker_farm/celery_app.py`

Added `include=["local_agent.worker_farm.tasks"]` to the `Celery(...)`
constructor in `create_app()`. This is Celery's standard mechanism for a
worker to lazily pull in a sibling task module by dotted path instead of a
top-level `import` — which was not an option here anyway, since `tasks.py`
already does `from .celery_app import app` and a direct top-level import in
the other direction would be circular.

### `local_agent/worker_farm/test_farm_core.py`

Added `test_worker_app_registers_the_distill_task`, imports `os`, `subprocess`,
`sys`. It shells out to a fresh interpreter (mirroring what `worker.py` itself
does) that resolves the app exactly as `-A local_agent.worker_farm.celery_app:app`
would, runs `import_default_modules()`, and asserts `distill_export` is
registered. A subprocess is required, not optional: this test module already
imports `local_agent.worker_farm.tasks` at file scope for the existing tests,
which caches it in `sys.modules` with `app=None` (no `FARM_BROKER_URL` set at
that point). An in-process retry against a freshly-constructed app would hit
that stale cache and silently no-op instead of re-registering — which would
have made the regression test pass regardless of whether the real bug was
fixed. Caught this by running the first version of the test against the
already-fixed code and watching it fail for the wrong reason.

Negative-control run (reverted `include=` in the sandbox copy only, real
project file untouched): the new test fails with `'REGISTERED' != 'MISSING'`.
Restored the fix: passes. Full suite: 13/13 (12 pre-existing + 1 new).

## What is unverified

This was proven against an isolated sandbox copy running `celery==5.6.3`
installed fresh, not against the project's actual `local_agent/worker_farm/.venv`
on the Windows machine, which may pin a different Celery version — `include=`
is core, stable Celery behavior across the 4.x–5.x line, so this is low risk,
but the closing step is still to run
`.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m unittest local_agent.worker_farm.test_farm_core -v`
from that real environment and confirm 13/13 there. No broker was started; this
is import-wiring verification only, not a live end-to-end submit → worker →
result run. That live run still needs Docker Desktop's engine confirmed
running and should happen from the normal Windows desktop account per the
existing Phase 1 foundation note.

# 2026-08-29 — Worker Farm Phase 1.5: secondary-node runbook, scripts, plan

## What changed

Added `docs/WORKER_FARM_PHASE1_5_SECONDARY_NODE_PLAN_2026-08-29.md`, the
runbook/scripts/phased plan for `TODO.md`'s next concrete worker-farm step —
"Add the secondary laptop only after it connects over a private encrypted
overlay with separate broker credentials" — scoped to exactly one additional
trusted node, not the ten-node cluster already planned in
`docs/WORKER_FARM_ARCHITECTURE_PLAN_2026-08-29.md`.

Added two scripts the plan describes:

- `local_agent/worker_farm/relay/tunnel_relay.py` — stdlib-only asyncio TCP
  relay. Binds only to an explicit, non-loopback IP (refuses `0.0.0.0` and
  any loopback address); forwards raw bytes to the existing loopback Redis.
  Adds no authentication of its own by design — WireGuard and the Redis ACL
  credential are the two real security layers, this is plumbing between them.
- `local_agent/worker_farm/Add-Phase1SecondaryWorkerCredential.ps1` —
  generates a fresh random password the same way `Initialize-Phase1Secrets.ps1`
  does, applies a scoped Redis ACL user (`ACL SETUSER`) restricted to the
  laptop's own queue/key patterns, and writes a `.env.<user>.generated`
  fragment locally. Never prints the password. Refuses to grant the `distill`
  queue to a secondary node.

Widened `local_agent/worker_farm/.gitignore` from the literal `.env` to also
match `.env.*`, since the new script writes `.env.laptop_worker.generated`
and the existing pattern would not have caught it.

Cross-referenced the plan from `TODO.md`, `local_agent/UPGRADE/00_INDEX.md`'s
design-notes list, and both current handoff docs.

Blocked on the operator's own hands for Phase 1's final live check (Docker
Desktop's engine, from the normal desktop account), which this session cannot
do. `TODO.md`'s explicit next worker-farm step doesn't depend on that check
being finished to be *designed*, so this is the useful parallel work: have
the next phase's runbook and scripts ready rather than idle until Phase 1
clears.

# 2026-08-29 — Cross-checked the concurrent PowerInfer pipeline against the coordination prompt

## Context

Earlier this session, replied to Grok's PowerInfer control-plane plan with two
specific asks: (1) record hashes/versions/benchmarks as evidence, not just log
them; (2) make `--vram-budget` a required argument with no silent default, and
print a GPU-gateway/idle-status reminder before launching. Grok's
`tools/powerinfer/` landed while this session was doing the worker_farm work
(see `CHANGELOG/2026-08-29_powerinfer_native_pipeline.md`). Checked it against
those two asks rather than assuming they were honored, and independently
re-ran the claimed test evidence rather than trusting the changelog's "8/8" by
itself.

## What was verified as correct

- Native Windows build (VS 2022 x64, `-DLLAMA_CUBLAS=ON`,
  `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120`), not WSL2 — matches the reply prompt.
- `record_acceptance_gate.py` writes `acceptance_gate.json` with cold/warm
  20-turn latency, tokens/sec, host RAM, VRAM, and SHA-256 of the GGUF,
  predictor tree, and `activation/` files — matches the "record evidence, not
  just log it" ask.
- `check_gpu_preflight.py` is called from `Assert-Execute` before any GPU
  stage and refuses with the blocking owner list if ComfyUI/another render
  process holds the GPU — this is actually stronger than what was asked for
  (an automated refusal instead of just a printed reminder).
- Independently reran `python -m unittest test_powerinfer_pipeline -v` from
  an isolated copy (`pipeline_lib.py`, `models.json`, and the test file only,
  no GPU/network needed) in this session's sandbox: **8/8 passed**, matching
  the claimed evidence.

## What was not honored, and the fix

`run_pipeline.ps1` declared `[double]$VramBudget = 12` — a real default, not
`Mandatory`, and not what was asked. A silent 12 GiB would have reached
`main.exe`/`server.exe`/`record_acceptance_gate.py` on any `validate`/`bench`
run where the operator forgot to pass `-VramBudget` explicitly.

Fixed directly rather than only flagging it, since it's small and matches the
original request precisely:

- Changed the parameter to `[Nullable[double]]$VramBudget = $null`.
- `Invoke-ValidateAndBench` — the only function that actually forwards
  `$VramBudget` to a GPU binary — now throws before doing anything if it's
  still `$null`, with a message naming the GPU gateway/idle check explicitly.
  `-Stage show` and every non-GPU stage remain usable with zero required
  flags beyond `-ModelId`, since the plan-preview mode was never the problem.
- `Show-Plan`'s output now prints `(not set -- required before validate/
  bench)` instead of a numeric default, so a dry-run preview doesn't imply a
  budget is already chosen.

chunks.heading: # 2026-08-29 — Wired run_pipeline.ps1 to actually call vault.init_vault()
chunks.text:
# 2026-08-29 — Wired run_pipeline.ps1 to actually call vault.init_vault()

## What changed

`tools/powerinfer/run_pipeline.ps1` computed `$VaultRoot` from
`vault.default_vault_path()` and then joined bundle paths with raw
`Join-Path`/`New-Item` calls throughout every `Invoke-*` function. It never
called `vault.init_vault()`, `assert_outside_repo()`, or `preflight()` at
all — `TODO.md`'s own note already said as much ("not yet wired to fail
closed if this vault is uninitialized"), but the actual consequence is
broader than that phrasing suggests: on any machine without a `D:` drive
(confirmed true of the sandbox this session runs in, and possibly true of
others), `default_vault_path()`'s fallback is `REPO_ROOT/artifacts/
powerinfer_vault` — **inside the git tree** — and nothing stopped the
pipeline from writing GGUFs, activation tensors, and predictor mmaps there
with no `.gitignore` protecting them from `git add`.

Added `Invoke-VaultInit`, called once right after `-Stage show` returns (so
the zero-side-effect preview path is untouched), which shells out to
`vault.init_vault(Path($VaultRoot))` and throws with a clear message if it
refuses — which it will, on the in-repo fallback, unless `-Vault` or
`$env:POWERINFER_VAULT` is set explicitly.

## Why

Found while reviewing `run_pipeline.ps1` end to end to understand exactly
what `TODO.md`'s vault caveat meant, rather than taking the one-line note at
face value. This project's own standing rule elsewhere (`SOURCE_BACKUP_POLICY.md`,
the backup builder's exclusion list) treats "large binaries or secrets landing
in the git tree" as a real, specifically-guarded-against failure mode; this
was a live path to exactly that on any machine without the preferred drive.

## Verification

- Reran `python -m unittest test_powerinfer_pipeline -v` after the edit
  (unaffected — the test file doesn't exercise `run_pipeline.ps1`): 18/18.
- Directly exercised the exact command `Invoke-VaultInit` runs, in isolation,
  against an isolated copy of `vault.py`/`pipeline_lib.py`:
  - `init_vault(Path('<repo>/artifacts/powerinfer_vault'))` (the in-repo
    fallback) raised `VaultError` with the expected message.
  - `init_vault(Path('/tmp/.../outside_vault'))` (an explicit outside path)
    succeeded, created `production/quarantine/scratch/private/keys`,
    `.gitignore`, and `vault.json` as expected.
- The PowerShell wrapper itself (`Invoke-VaultInit`'s `& $Py -c "..."` call,
  its `$LASTEXITCODE` check, and the call site right after `-Stage show`)
  was not run — no `pwsh` in this sandbox, same limitation as the earlier
  `-VramBudget` fix. Read through twice for the backtick escaping in the
  throw message (`` `n `` for newline, `` `$env:POWERINFER_VAULT `` to print
  the variable name rather than expand it).

## Deliberately not done

Did not route the per-stage directory creation (`Invoke-Intake`,
`Invoke-Calib`, `Invoke-Convert`, etc.) through `vault.create_bundle()` /
`vault.bundle_paths()` — that would replace several already-working,
individually Force-gated overwrite checks scattered through the script with
a single shared one, which is a larger and riskier rewrite of a file another
session is actively iterating on. The narrower fix (call `init_vault` once,
up front) closes the actual safety gap — in-repo writes with no
`.gitignore` — without touching the rest of the stage logic. Flagging the
bundle-creation consolidation as a reasonable follow-up, not doing it now.

## What is unverified

Whether `run_pipeline.ps1` actually refuses cleanly end-to-end on a real
Windows machine with no `D:` drive, and proceeds cleanly on one that has it
or an explicit `-Vault`. Needs a `pwsh` run to confirm; the Python-level
behavior it depends on is proven above.

# 2026-08-29 — PowerInfer native toolchain gate

## What changed

- Cloned the upstream PowerInfer source into `external/PowerInfer` and prepared

  installed explicitly because modern pip rejects the upstream bare `./...`
  requirement lines.
- Verified the environment imports the PowerInfer Python packages and CUDA
  12.8 PyTorch reports CUDA available. This was an availability probe only;
  it did not load a model or execute inference.
- Hardened `tools/powerinfer/run_pipeline.ps1`: it now requires a Visual Studio
  2022 (17.x) C++ instance and its matching `Visual Studio 17 2022` generator.
  It preflights that requirement before cloning or installing Python packages,
  and will not auto-select Visual Studio 2026 merely because that is newest.

  rather than the retired ProSparse example, and to state the VS 2022 host

  the CUDA-supported VS 2022 generator rather than silently selecting VS 2026.
- Passed CMake the verified CUDA runtime-library path explicitly; this avoids a
  CMake Windows host-architecture discovery edge case that otherwise misses
  `lib\\x64\\cudart.lib` even though CUDA itself is installed.
- Made the native toolchain probe find `nvcc.exe` from the standard installed
  CUDA roots when its `bin` folder is not already on the invoking shell's PATH.

  rather than treating a file-system object as a command-discovery object.
- Scoped new native output to `external/PowerInfer/build-vs2022`; the runner
  preserves the failed VS 2026 CMake cache rather than deleting or reusing it.
- Updated the matching control-plane and runner documentation to use that
  compiler-scoped binary location.

  asset, model download, PowerInfer server, render, or GPU inference was
  started.

chunks.heading: # 2026-08-29 — PowerInfer as a normal local-agent chat-picker backend
chunks.text:
# 2026-08-29 — PowerInfer as a normal local-agent chat-picker backend

## What changed

- Design: `docs/POWERINFER_CHAT_PICKER_DESIGN_2026-08-29.md`. The router is
  still an Ollama CPU/GPU handoff, not a multi-engine registry. PowerInfer
  joins the picker the same way `gpt-oss-20b-heretic` does: always visible,
  GPU-only, never an automatic default, never a silent Huihui/CPU substitute.
- `local_agent/router.py`
  - `chat_models()` always appends `POWERINFER_MODEL_ALIAS` (default
    `powerinfer-local`) with `backend: "powerinfer"`.
  - `available` is true only when both the OpenAI proxy (`127.0.0.1:8091`)
    and `server.exe` (`POWERINFER_BACKEND_URL`, default `http://127.0.0.1:8080`)
    accept a 0.4s loopback TCP probe. A down backend cannot hang a status poll.
  - `decide(model="powerinfer-local")` returns `host=POWERINFER_PROXY_HOST`
    and `backend="powerinfer"`, or `model is None` with an explicit reason
    (proxy down, server down, ComfyUI/foreign GPU owner). It does not start
    `server.exe` or the proxy.
  - `gpu_busy()` treats a configured PowerInfer `server.exe` as this agent's
    GPU occupant: ordinary Ollama auto-chat yields to CPU; a PowerInfer pin
    is allowed to talk to the already-running proxy. Queue owner and port
    8188 still win.
- `local_agent/powerinfer_client.py` — OpenAI `/v1/chat/completions` client
  for that host. Flattens tool-role history to text. Does not send native
  tool schemas. The proxy contract is unchanged.
- `local_agent/ollama_client.py` — `chat` / `chat_stream` dispatch to that
  client when `host == POWERINFER_PROXY_HOST`, so planner and other callers
  do not post `/api/chat` at the proxy.
- `local_agent/agent.py` — a PowerInfer pin does not request an Ollama GPU
  load, does not run the extra planner hop, and does not send native tools.

## Why

The OpenAI proxy was built and tested but was not in the GUI picker, so the
operator still had to call it by hand. The existing picker already had a
pattern for an opt-in GPU choice that may be unusable (Heretic). PowerInfer
is that shape plus a different HTTP contract. Auto-starting `server.exe`
from the router was rejected: the proxy is specified not to spawn that
process, the production pipeline owns lifecycle, and another session is
using those files live.

# 2026-08-30 — Bamboo-DPO isolated mechanical gate authorized

The operator approved the next isolated candidate gate after the byte-verified
Q4 runtime intake. The allowed operation is one bounded native `main.exe`
raw-completion smoke run against the exact locked Bamboo-DPO Q4 PowerInfer
GGUF and its 32 adjacent activation files.

This authorization does not permit a server, registry entry, proxy, router or
picker change, a render, ComfyUI, training, conversion, or a substitute model.
The runner records the exact model SHA-256, output logs, GPU before/after state,
and exit status under the candidate's `validation/` directory.

The first preflight invocation exposed a runner-only stale-exit-code defect in
the GPU status check and exited before model launch. The check was corrected to
validate the actual status line rather than an inherited native-command code;
the candidate, GPU, and runtime receipt were untouched.

The second preflight invocation also exited before model load: Windows split a
space-containing prompt while forwarding it through `Start-Process`. The runner
now invokes `main.exe` with PowerShell's native argument array, so the bounded
raw-completion prompt is forwarded as one argument. This is a runner repair,
not a model or candidate change.

The first actual bounded run exited cleanly and produced text, but its native
log showed that the solver called the unrelated system Python and therefore
failed to generate the sparse GPU split. That is a mechanical **failure**, not
a pass. The gate now requires confirmed sparse load, CUDA use, a successful
split, and non-zero FFN GPU offload. It scopes the matching PowerInfer venv on
`PATH` and `PYTHONPATH` only for the child process; no persistent environment,
model artifact, or route is changed.

chunks.text:
# 2026-08-30 — Bamboo-DPO mechanical PowerInfer gate passed

The byte-verified candidate at
`A:\PowerInferModels\bamboo-dpo-7b\20260830-q4-runtime-intake` passed one
isolated native PowerInfer mechanical smoke run. The source tree was not
changed. No server, registry, proxy, router, picker, ComfyUI process, render,
training, or conversion was started.

## Frozen candidate facts now confirmed locally

- Exact model SHA-256:
  `9661890635b4f986ebe523eba10404cbb5481be57266cb6d5a894fb63cac527c`
- `BambooMLP.forward()` applies `relu(gate_proj(x)) * relu(up_proj(x))` before
  `down_proj`, so the locked revision is dReLU, not merely an unclassified
  `bamboo` model.
- 32 matching `activation_*.pt` files were present and the local source lock
  remained valid.

## Result

The deterministic raw-completion smoke used a 512-token context, 12 GiB VRAM
budget and 16 generated tokens. Native logs prove PowerInfer sparse loading,
CUDA acceleration, and **3,024 MiB** FFN offload. Load time was 4,186.65 ms;
prompt evaluation was 241.73 tokens/s and generation was 65.86 tokens/s for
this tiny smoke. GPU temperature moved 29 C → 32 C and returned to 30 C with
102 MiB resident after exit.

Evidence is stored next to the candidate:
`validation/bamboo_dpo_mechanical_gate_20260830_232453.json` and its paired
stdout/stderr logs.

The first executable attempt exposed that native PowerInfer invokes literal
`python -m powerinfer` to calculate its split. The system Python did not have
the module, produced zero FFN offload, and is recorded as a mechanical failure.
The gate now scopes the matching repository venv for the child process and
requires successful split plus nonzero FFN offload before reporting a pass.

## Still blocked

This is not an instruction-following or quality result. The frozen tokenizer
has no chat template, so a prompt contract must be established before the fixed
ten-case quality test. The candidate remains `candidate` only and must not be
registered or exposed in the local-agent picker without a separate approval
after that quality gate.

## Why

Two GPU-only pins (Heretic and PowerInfer) were the same ordering bug: an
earlier `Decision(tier="cpu")` short-circuited a later pin check that is
supposed to win with `tier="gpu", model=None`. That is a pattern. Walking
every return once is cheaper than finding the next instance during a feature
add.

## The evidence — every `decide()` return, in execution order

Setup that is **not** a return, but runs **before** the pin checks:

| Step | What it does | Before/after pin checks | Same-bug candidate? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gpu_busy()` | fills `busy`, `why`, `detail` | before | no — no `Decision` |
| CPU `/api/tags` | `cpu_have` | before | no |
| `skip_gpu_inventory` | if busy **and** Huihui 8B is on CPU, set `gpu_have = []` and skip GPU `/api/tags` | before | no — not a return. Heretic/PowerInfer busy paths do not use `gpu_have`. Idle Heretic still inventories GPU because `busy` is false. |

Pin checks (these **are** the checks that must win):

| Return | Condition | Decision | Before/after itself |
|---|---|---|---|
| PowerInfer, foreign GPU owner | `is_powerinfer_model` and busy and not PowerInfer-owned | `tier="gpu"`, host=proxy, `model=None`, "will not fall back to Ollama or CPU" | **is** the pin check |
| PowerInfer, `prefer=="cpu"` | pin + CPU preference | `tier="gpu"`, `model=None`, will not fall back to CPU | pin check |
| PowerInfer, proxy/backend down | pin + not ready | `tier="gpu"`, `model=None`, explicit down reason | pin check |
| PowerInfer, ready | pin + GPU free or PowerInfer already owns it | `tier="gpu"`, model=alias, backend=powerinfer | pin check |
| Heretic busy | `is_gpu_only_opt_in_model` and busy | `tier="gpu"`, `model=None`, "will not fall back to CPU" | pin check |
| Heretic `prefer=="cpu"` | pin + CPU preference | `tier="gpu"`, `model=None` | pin check |
| Heretic, GPU Ollama down | pin + `not up(GPU_HOST)` | `tier="gpu"`, `model=None` | pin check |
| Heretic not installed | pin + missing tag | `tier="gpu"`, `model=None` | pin check |
| Heretic success | pin + GPU free + installed | `tier="gpu"`, model=selected | pin check |

Returns **after** the pin checks (GPU-only / PowerInfer pins never reach these
when `is_*` matches):

| Return | Condition | Decision | Covered? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unverified eviction | `busy and ensure_gpu_evicted` and `/api/ps` not verified | `tier="cpu"`, `model=None`, "eviction could not be verified" | `test_unverified_gpu_eviction_refuses_cpu_handoff` (primary pin). ## What changed

chunks.heading: # 2026-08-30 — JSONL append in learning.py / phone_scheduler.py is not a gap
chunks.text:
# 2026-08-30 — JSONL append in learning.py / phone_scheduler.py is not a gap

Closes the loose end from
`CHANGELOG/2026-08-30_architecture_refactor_reverify.md`: two of the 14
audited writers still use `open(..., "a")` for JSONL. Production code was
not changed.

## What those files actually re-read

**`learning.py`**

- `record()` appends one JSON object + newline to `runtime/learning/failure_ledger.jsonl`.
- It then updates `runtime/learning/self_review.json` with
  `atomic_write_text`.
- `_load()` / `prompt_block()` read **only** `self_review.json`
  (`json.loads(REVIEW.read_text(...))`, empty dict on any exception).
- Nothing in `learning.py` parses the JSONL ledger. A truncated last ledger
  line is unused forensic residue; the counts that affect prompts live in
  the atomically replaced JSON file.

**`phone_scheduler.py`**

- Durable job state is `runtime/lxmf/phone_schedules.json` via `_load` /
  `_save` → `atomic_write_text`.
- `_load` already treats `JSONDecodeError` as empty `{jobs: {}}`, so a
  corrupted **state** file fails closed rather than poisoning dispatch.
- `_audit()` appends to `phone_schedule_audit.jsonl`. `dispatch_due`,
  `list_for_identity`, `create`, and `cancel` never read that file.
- The only JSONL parse in-tree is a test helper:
  `json.loads(AUDIT.read_text().splitlines()[-1])` in
  `test_audit_records_the_counter_that_was_queued`. That is not a runtime
  reader.

A crash mid-`write()` of a JSONL line can leave a truncated **last** line.
That cannot destroy earlier lines, and it cannot break the next operational
read, because those reads do not parse the JSONL files.

Atomic tmp-replace of the whole log would be the wrong tool: it rewrites
history on every event. Skipping a truncated last line would only matter if
something replayed the ledger; nothing does.

```
python local_agent/test_phone_scheduler.py -v
Ran 14 tests in 0.804s
OK
```

`learning.py` has no dedicated test file. `test_prompt_prefix.py` only
mentions learning in passing and was not needed for this read-path check.

## Verdict

Not a gap. No writer or reader change.

  harmless hidden-state means with a 4-bit CUDA copy.

  activation/sparsity drift.

chunks.text:
# 2026-08-30 — TurboSparse projected abliteration: independent re-execution completed

## Session context

An independent diagnostic and abliteration pass was run against the same task
specification used to produce `turbosparse-mistral-abliterated-projected-20260830b`.
All streaming-loader infrastructure (`abliterate_loader.py`,
`abliterate_turbosparse_v2.py`, `diagnose_turbosparse_loader.py`) was found
already in place from the prior session. No code was changed; the session
confirmed diagnostics, re-ran smoke, and ran the full abliteration to a
separately named output directory.

Operator-accepted canonical checkpoint remains:
`A:\Users\rhine\Documents\Codex\PowerInferStaging\turbosparse-mistral-abliterated-projected-20260830b`
(see `2026-08-30_turbosparse_abliteration_docs_accepted.md`).

---

## Diagnostics

**Environment** (Python: `A:\Users\rhine\.unsloth\studio\unsloth_studio\Scripts\python.exe`):

| Package | Version |
|---|---|
| torch | 2.10.0+cu130 |
| transformers | 5.5.0 |
| bitsandbytes | 0.50.2 |
| accelerate | 1.14.0 |
| safetensors | — |
| GPU | RTX 5080 (sm_120) |
| VRAM free (pre-run) | 15,872 MB |
| Host RAM free | ~15 GiB |

**Shard inventory** (`turbosparse-mistral-instruct-source-20260830`):

| Shard | Tensors | Size |
|---|---|---|
| model-00001-of-00004.safetensors | 108 | 4,760.7 MB |
| model-00002-of-00004.safetensors | 117 | 4,664.2 MB |
| model-00003-of-00004.safetensors | 110 | 4,686.7 MB |
| model-00004-of-00004.safetensors | 20  | 1,119.5 MB |

All 4 shards readable via `safe_open`. Tokenizer and config load successfully
in isolation (`model_type=bamboo`, `hidden_act=relu`, 32 layers, `hidden_size=4096`).

**Transformers 5.5.0 lazy-load verified** (alternative path, not used for abliteration):
`device_map='auto'` + `max_memory={0: '14GiB'}` loaded the full model in 96.7 s
with VRAM = 5,209 MB and a finite forward-pass hidden norm of 136.4542.

**Root cause confirmed**: matches prior CHANGELOG (`2026-08-30_turbosparse_projected_abliteration_loader_fix.md`).
Transformers 4.41.x `load_file` full-shard mapping causes pagefile thrashing at
shard 2/4 boundary (~15 GiB RAM, ~9.4 GiB combined shard 1+2 working set plus CUDA pins).
Streaming loader avoids this by reading one tensor at a time via `safe_open`.

**bitsandbytes cpp-extension warning**: non-blocking. `bnb 0.50.2` warns about
`torch >= 2.11.0` requirement for cpp extensions but core CUDA NF4 kernels work.
4096×14336 tensor quantizes in ~1.1 s.

---

chunks.text:
# 2026-08-30 — TurboSparse 4-bit shard-load stall: root cause and streaming fix

## Root cause

The stall at Transformers' `Loading checkpoint shards` **2/4** was **not** a Bamboo
import failure, a FlashAttention scanner hang, a bitsandbytes/sm_120 deadlock, or
a Windows inability to open shard 2.

Evidence on this host (RTX 5080 / sm_120, 32 GiB RAM, ~15 GiB free, GPU idle):

| Hypothesis | Result |
|---|---|
| 1. Custom Bamboo remote-code incompatibility | **Rejected.** `BambooConfig` / 1-layer and 32-layer construct succeed with `trust_remote_code` and the existing `check_imports` bypass. |
| 2. Transformers/bitsandbytes version mismatch as a hard API break | **Not the hang.** `transformers==4.41.2` + `bitsandbytes==0.50.2` NF4-quantizes a 4096×4096 matrix in 0.3 s and 4096×14336 in 1.2 s. |
| 3. CPU RAM / pagefile pressure | **Primary.** ~15 GiB free physical RAM. Each shard is 4.55–4.65 GiB. |
| 4. Incorrect device-map behavior | **Trigger, not a mis-map.** `device_map={"": "cuda:0"}` is the intended 4-bit measurement placement. Combined with (5) it keeps a whole shard in the working set while CUDA pins copies. |
| 5. Safetensors shard loading | **The mechanism.** Transformers 4.41.2 calls `safetensors.torch.load_file` (full 4.5 GiB mmap) then `param.to(float16)` + `Params4bit(...).to(cuda)` for every tensor **before** tqdm advances. `safe_open` + `get_tensor` on shard 2 is milliseconds; `load_file` returns immediately because it is mmap, then touching/quantizing the whole mapping pages ~4.5 GiB and looks frozen at 2/4. |
| 6. Flash-attention/import scanning | **Already mitigated** in the original script; eager attention is used. |
| 7. Other | Contributing: `create_quantized_param` copies `old_value.__dict__` into `Params4bit` (4.41 vs bnb 0.50). Accelerate 1.14 is installed but the stall is Transformers' own shard loop, not `dispatch_model`. |

A later `from_pretrained` of the **full** 15 GiB CPU copy would hit the same host-RAM ceiling. The v2 editor therefore streams safetensors on CPU and never instantiates the 15 GiB `nn.Module` for writing.

chunks.heading: # 2026-08-30 — ReluLLaMA quality review: failure diagnosis
chunks.text:
# 2026-08-30 — ReluLLaMA quality review: failure diagnosis

**Status: UNVERIFIED diagnosis — awaiting operator-approved re-run to confirm.**

Continuation of `2026-08-30d_quality_review_responses_recorded.md`.
Root-cause analysis of the 7/10 empty and 3/10 prompt-echo responses
recorded in `quality_review_packet.json`.

---

## Evidence base

Files read (no server.exe started, no inference run, no GGUF touched):

- `validation/quality_capture_server_20260830b.log` — server-side timing for the 10 `/completion` requests
- `validation/quality_review_packet.json` — the 10 prompt/response pairs
- `validation/quality_capture_meta_20260830.json` — capture session metadata
- `validation/acceptance_gate_20260830_175953.json` — acceptance gate benchmark turns
- `validation/main_smoke_bench_20260830_175953.log` — acceptance gate `main.exe` invocation
- `A:\PowerInferModels\relu-llama-7b\relu-llama-7b-source-20260829\source\hf\README.md` — model card
- `A:\PowerInferModels\relu-llama-7b\relu-llama-7b-source-20260829\source\hf\config.json` — model config
- `A:\PowerInferModels\relu-llama-7b\relu-llama-7b-source-20260829\source\hf\tokenizer_config.json` — tokenizer config
- `manifest.json` — staging pipeline classification

---

## Findings

### Finding 1 — ReluLLaMA-7B is a base model with no instruction fine-tuning

**Evidence:**

- `manifest.json` line: `"class": "base"` — the staging pipeline itself classifies this as a base model.
- `config.json`: `"_name_or_path": "meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf"` — this is the BASE Llama-2 model (not `Llama-2-7b-chat-hf`).
- `README.md` training data (lines 25–26): Wikipedia, Pile, StackOverflow — raw text, no instruction pairs.
- `README.md` training objective (line 29): "conventional language modeling objective and the knowledge distillation objective" — pure LM loss + KL from the base teacher. No RLHF, no SFT on instruction data, no DPO.
- `tokenizer_config.json`: No `chat_template` key. `"add_eos_token": false`. Standard Llama tokenizer with no chat format registered.

**Conclusion:** This model was fine-tuned exclusively for ReLU activation sparsity. It has no instruction-following capability and knows nothing about `[INST]` / `[/INST]` wrappers. Applying an instruction template to it is a category error.

---

chunks.heading: ### Finding 1 — ReluLLaMA-7B is a base model with no instruction fine-tuning
chunks.text:
izer_config.json`: No `chat_template` key. `"add_eos_token": false`. Standard Llama tokenizer with no chat format registered.

**Conclusion:** This model was fine-tuned exclusively for ReLU activation sparsity. It has no instruction-following capability and knows nothing about `[INST]` / `[/INST]` wrappers. Applying an instruction template to it is a category error.

---

### Finding 2 — The quality capture used a malformed instruction template, and the acceptance gate does NOT use instruction format

The existing CHANGELOG entry (`2026-08-30d`) states:

> "llama-2 `[INST]` wrap **as the gate uses**"

**This is incorrect on both counts.**

**The acceptance gate does not use `[INST]` wrapping.**

Evidence from `main_smoke_bench_20260830_175953.log` line 2:

```
Once upon a time, the phrase "the third age" referred to three generations: one generation
```

The acceptance gate invokes `main.exe` with a raw text continuation prompt — no template wrapper of any kind. From that same log (line 529):

```
generate: n_ctx = 2048, n_batch = 512, n_predict = 16, n_keep = 0
```

The benchmark sent plain prose continuations and measured throughput only. It never tested instruction-following behavior.

**The quality capture DID use an `[INST]`-style wrapper, but it was malformed.**

The echoed responses in `quality_review_packet.json` show the exact prompt strings the model received back:

- `constraint_following` (case 0, 128 tokens generated):
  `</s\n<s>[Inst] Give exactly three short steps for organizing a folder. Do not use bullets or headings. [Inst]</s</s...`

- `format_repair` (case 6, 128 tokens generated):
  `</s\n<s>[Inst] Repair this JSON and return valid JSON {name: local-agent, active true} [Inst]</s</s...`

- `bounded_plan` (case 7, 34 tokens generated):
  `</s\n<s>[Inst] Give a two step plan to compare two local text models. mention one measurement and one human review step.[/Inst]</s`

**Two defects in the template string:**

1. **Case error:** `[Inst]` (mixed case) instead of `[INST]` (all caps). Cases 0 and 6 show this clearly. The correct Llama-2 chat format uses ALL CAPS throughout.

2. **Missing slash in closing tag:** In cases 0 and 6, the closing tag is `[Inst]` — identical to the opening tag — instead of `[/INST]`. Case 7 has `[/Inst]` (slash present but wrong case). None of the three match the canonical `[/INST]`.

Even if both defects were corrected, the model would not respond usefully — it has no instruction fine-tuning (Finding 1). But the malformed tags are a secondary failure that also explains why the 3 non-empty cases produced prompt-echo instead of silent EOS.

---

chunks.heading: ### Finding 2 — The quality capture used a malformed instruction template, and the acceptance gate does NOT use instruction format
chunks.text:
NST]`. Case 7 has `[/Inst]` (slash present but wrong case). None of the three match the canonical `[/INST]`.

Even if both defects were corrected, the model would not respond usefully — it has no instruction fine-tuning (Finding 1). But the malformed tags are a secondary failure that also explains why the 3 non-empty cases produced prompt-echo instead of silent EOS.

---

### Finding 3 — The 7 empty responses are immediate EOS from the base model

From `quality_capture_server_20260830b.log`, tasks 1–5 and 8–9 (the 7 empty responses):

```
print_timings: eval time = ~13–17 ms / 2 runs
```

Two eval runs = the model generated exactly one token and that token was EOS (token id=2, `</s>`). The server strips EOS from returned content, leaving `""`. A base model that encounters a context pattern absent from its training distribution has high confidence in immediately ending generation. The malformed `[INST]` prefix is not in Wikipedia/Pile/StackOverflow, so the model routes to EOS.

This is not a malfunction of the model; it is correct base-model behavior on an out-of-distribution input.

---

### Finding 4 — The 3 non-empty responses are prompt echo + EOS repetition, caused by missing stop sequences

From `quality_capture_server_20260830b.log`:

- Task 0 (`constraint_following`): `eval time = 1796.78 ms / 128 runs` — exhausted `n_predict=128` budget
- Task 6 (`format_repair`): `eval time = 1658.74 ms / 128 runs` — exhausted `n_predict=128` budget
- Task 7 (`bounded_plan`): `eval time = 478.57 ms / 34 runs` — stopped at 34 tokens

For tasks 0 and 6 the model echoed the prompt text and then produced the string `</s>` repeatedly until the token budget expired. The `</s>` text here is the model generating individual characters (`<`, `/`, `s`, `>`) that spell out the EOS string — NOT the EOS token (id=2). The llama.cpp server halts on the actual EOS token, but these are text-level tokens that happen to spell it out.

**The direct cause of the 128-token runaway is that no `stop` parameter was passed in the `/completion` request.** Had `"stop": ["</s>"]` been present, the server would have halted on the first occurrence of the EOS string in the text output.

Task 7 stopped at 34 tokens because the model happened to generate the actual EOS token (id=2) after producing the partial echo, not because of any stop sequence.

---
